docs.title: Redis Mastery Path
docs.text:
Mastery Path BOOTCAMP VINOD BHANUJA

Redis looks like the simplest database there is: SET, GET, done. That simplicity is real, and it's also why so many Redis problems surprise people. A counter that loses 89% of its increments, a session that never expires because of one plain SET, a cache that keeps serving a stale price for five minutes no matter how you invalidate it, a lock that two clients both hold, a queue that silently drops jobs when a worker dies, a write the server acknowledged and then lost in a failover: none of those are Redis bugs. They're the consequences of how Redis actually works, and they can all be reproduced in a few lines.

This course teaches Redis by reproducing them. Every lesson runs against a real server and measures what happens: how long one slow command blocks everyone else, what each data structure costs in memory, how often a cache stampede hits the database, which writes survive which crashes. It assumes you can program (examples are mostly Python, with some Node.js) and have used a database before. It doesn't assume any Redis experience.

Level 1 covers the foundations: a throwaway lab and what one command thread means, redis-cli and the RESP protocol, strings and expiry, safe keyspace iteration, hashes, lists, sets and sorted sets, and the client libraries (including a retry default that applied one INCR twice), ending with a tested URL shortener. Level 2 goes deeper: memory encodings and why one extra member made a key 12× larger, bitmaps, HyperLogLog and Bloom filters, geospatial indexes, streams and consumer groups, Pub/Sub, transactions with WATCH, and Lua and Functions, ending with a leaderboard and activity feed. Level 3 is application patterns: cache-aside and its stale-write race, eviction policies, stampedes, rate limiting, distributed locks and fencing tokens, sessions and client-side caching, reliable job queues, JSON documents, and the query engine with vector search, ending with a caching and rate-limiting layer for a real API. Level 4 is production: RDB and AOF, replication, Sentinel, Cluster and resharding, ACLs and TLS, monitoring, Redis vs Valkey and upgrades, ending with a secured cluster proven by an automated failover test.

Every lesson has a How It Actually Works section: why SCAN can return a key twice but never miss one, why a hash with 513 fields costs five times as much as one with 512, why XREAD $ drops messages, why kill -9 doesn't lose everysec writes but a power cut can, why a lock lease can't protect you from a paused process, and how a replica decides whether it needs a full resync.

Versions and what was actually run

Everything in this course was run on Redis 8.10.2 (Homebrew, macOS on Apple Silicon) with its bundled JSON, search and probabilistic modules, using redis-py 8.1.0 on Python 3.14 and node-redis 6.3.0 on Node.js 26. Level 4 · 09 also uses Valkey 9.1.2. Every output shown is the output it produced, including the failures. Some of those failures were findings: a BITCOUNT that returned wrong totals above 2^21 on this build, a race in a project's caching layer that only a concurrency test caught, and TLS certificates that one client accepted and another rejected. Timings come from a laptop and show proportions, not benchmarks.

Several commands used here are very recent (SET … IFEQ and DELEX from 8.4, idempotent XADD from 8.6, XNACK from 8.8, atomic slot migration from 8.4). Each lesson says when a feature arrived, so you can check it against your own servers. Things that couldn't be run are stated where they come up, never shown with invented output: OS-crash and power-loss durability, Linux-only copy-on-write instrumentation, Redlock across independent primaries, managed cloud services, and Valkey's own modules.

docs.text:
Level Focus Modules What you can do after 1 · Redis Foundations The server, redis-cli/RESP, strings, keys, hashes, lists, sets, sorted sets, clients 10 Write correct application code against Redis 2 · Data Structures in Depth Encodings, bitmaps, sketches, geo, streams, Pub/Sub, transactions, Lua 10 Pick the right structure and make multi-step operations atomic 3 · Caching & Application Patterns Caching, eviction, stampedes, rate limits, locks, sessions, queues, JSON, search 10 Build the patterns Redis is hired for without their classic bugs 4 · Operations & Production Persistence, replication, Sentinel, Cluster, security, monitoring, upgrades 10 Run Redis in production and prove what survives a failure

Each level has 9 teaching modules plus a hands-on project (module 10), for 40 lessons total.

docs.title: How to use this site
docs.text:
• Run your own server. Level 1 · 01 sets up a lab you can wipe and restart in seconds. Later lessons start several servers on other ports. Use a laptop or a disposable VM, never a shared or production Redis.
  • Reproduce the outputs. Your IDs, timings and sizes will differ; the behaviour should not. When something differs in kind, find out why. Version differences are a likely cause, and each lesson names the version.
  • Break things on purpose. Kill a primary, run twenty clients against one key, fill memory to the limit. Most of what matters about Redis only shows up under concurrency and failure.
  • Do the projects. Each one combines its level into something you could adapt for real work, and each was tested end to end, including the bugs its tests caught.

docs.title: Level 1 · Redis Foundations
docs.text:
Level 1 takes you from "Redis is a cache" to writing correct application code against it. That's more than learning GET and SET. You need to know why one KEYS * made an unrelated PING wait 149 ms, why a plain SET quietly removed a session's expiry, why read-then-write counters lost 89% of their increments, and why a client library's helpful automatic retry applied one INCR twice.

Every lesson is built from commands run against a real server, Redis 8.10.2, and every output shown is what that server (or the client library) actually returned, errors included.

Prerequisites: basic programming in Python or JavaScript, and comfort at a terminal. No Redis experience is needed. If you know a relational database, you'll see where Redis's model differs.

docs.title: Modules
docs.text:
1. What Redis Is: One Thread, Memory & a Local Lab — install Redis, start a throwaway server, measure memory per key, and watch one slow command block every client.
  2. redis-cli & the RESP Protocol — speak RESP2 and RESP3 by hand, raw vs formatted output, --pipe loading 100,000 keys in 79 ms, MONITOR and --bigkeys.
  3. Strings, Counters & Expiry — SET's options including 8.4's IFEQ, atomic counters vs lost updates, float pitfalls, TTLs and the overwrite trap.
  4. The Keyspace: Naming, SCAN & Safe Deletes — key naming, cursor iteration and its guarantees, UNLINK vs DEL on a 2-million-field hash, pattern deletes that don't block.
  5. Hashes & Per-Field Expiry — objects as hashes, HEXPIRE/HSETEX/HGETDEL, and why a small hash beat both JSON and separate keys on memory.
  6. Lists: Queues, Stacks & Blocking Pops — capped lists, which list commands are really O(N), BLPOP workers and LMOVE for safer handoff.
  7. Sets: Membership, Set Algebra & Random Picks — dedupe with SADD, intersections and SINTERCARD, random draws, and the cost of algebra on million-member sets.
  8. Sorted Sets: Rankings, Ranges & Time Windows — leaderboards, ZADD flags, score and lex ranges, delayed jobs, sliding windows and O(log N) measured.
  9. Clients: redis-py & node-redis — shared clients and pools, RESP3 defaults, pipelines vs transactions, and timeouts with retries that can double-apply writes.
  10. Project — URL Shortener with Click Analytics — a tested shortener using every type in this level, including the overwrite bug its tests caught.

docs.title: After Level 1
docs.text: You can store and change data correctly with Redis's five core types. Level 2 goes underneath and beyond them: how each type is encoded in memory and how to shrink it, bitmaps and HyperLogLog for counting at scale, geospatial indexes, streams with consumer groups, Pub/Sub, and the two ways to make several commands atomic, MULTI/WATCH and server-side Lua functions.

docs.title: 01 · What Redis Is: One Thread, Memory & a Local Lab
docs.text:
Redis is usually introduced as "a cache" or "a key-value store". Both undersell it and both mislead. Redis is a data structure server: a process that keeps strings, hashes, lists, sets, sorted sets, streams and a few more exotic types in RAM, and lets many clients run small, atomic operations on them over a network socket. A cache is one thing you can build with that. So are leaderboards, rate limiters, job queues, session stores, presence indicators, distributed locks and event logs.

Two facts shape everything else in this course:

  1. The data lives in memory. Reads and writes don't touch a disk on the request path. That's why Redis is fast, and it's also why the dataset must fit in RAM and why durability is something you configure rather than something you get.
  2. Commands execute one at a time, on one thread. Each command runs to completion before the next one starts. That's why INCR never loses an update. It's also why one slow command makes every client wait.

This lesson sets up a lab, then measures both facts on a real server.

docs.title: Installing Redis
docs.text:
Everything in this course was run on Redis 8.10.2, installed with Homebrew on macOS (Apple Silicon):

brew install redis
redis-server --version

Redis server v=8.10.2 sha=00000000:1 malloc=libc bits=64 build=764b3e45065a66fb

The formula installs six programs:

redis-benchmark  redis-check-aof  redis-check-rdb  redis-cli  redis-sentinel  redis-server

On Linux, the Redis project publishes its own APT/RPM repositories and an official redis container image; your distribution's package may be several major versions behind, so check redis-server --version before assuming a feature exists. (Those install paths weren't used for this course. Commands are the same once the server is running.)

Valkey

If your platform ships Valkey instead of Redis, most of Levels 1–3 still applies. Valkey is a fork of Redis 7.2 and speaks the same protocol and core commands. The two projects have diverged since then. Level 4 · 09 compares them directly on the same machine.

docs.title: A throwaway lab
docs.text:
You want a server that you can wipe and restart freely, separate from any Redis that something else on the machine depends on. Command-line flags override config file settings, so you don't need a config file to start one:

mkdir -p ~/redis-lab && cd ~/redis-lab
redis-server --port 6400 --dir ~/redis-lab --save '' --enable-debug-command local
  • --port 6400 keeps it off the default port 6379.
  • --dir is where any snapshot or append-only file would be written.
  • --save '' turns off automatic snapshots, so nothing lands on disk unless you ask.
  • --enable-debug-command local allows DEBUG from localhost. It's off by default since Redis 7, and we use it here to generate test data. Never enable it on a shared server.

The server logs to the terminal:

97838:C 13 Oct 2026 06:54:46.616 * oO0OoO0OoO0Oo Redis is starting oO0OoO0OoO0Oo
97838:C 13 Oct 2026 06:54:46.616 * Redis version=8.10.2, bits=64, commit=00000000, modified=1, pid=97838, just started
97838:C 13 Oct 2026 06:54:46.616 * Configuration loaded
97838:M 13 Oct 2026 06:54:46.616 * monotonic clock: ARM CNTVCT @ 24 ticks/us
97838:M 13 Oct 2026 06:54:46.616 * Running mode=standalone, port=6400.
97838:M 13 Oct 2026 06:54:46.616 # WARNING: The TCP backlog setting of 511 cannot be enforced because kern.ipc.somaxconn is set to the lower value of 128.
97838:M 13 Oct 2026 06:54:46.617 * Server initialized
97838:M 13 Oct 2026 06:54:46.617 * Ready to accept connections tcp
97838:M 13 Oct 2026 06:54:46.617 # WARNING: Redis does not require authentication. Redis will accept connections from any local client.

Each line starts with the PID and a role letter: C is a child or startup phase, M is the main process. The two warnings are worth reading rather than ignoring. The backlog warning means the OS caps how many not-yet-accepted connections can queue up, which matters on busy Linux servers (raise net.core.somaxconn). The authentication warning says plainly that anyone who can reach this port can run any command. Level 4 · 07 deals with that.

In a second terminal:

redis-cli -p 6400 ping

PONG

The lab convention for the rest of the course: a lab server on the default port 6379, started the same way with its own --dir. Lessons that need several servers (replication, Sentinel, Cluster) start them on other ports and say so. Shut a lab server down with redis-cli -p <port> shutdown nosave. The nosave means "don't write a snapshot on the way out".

docs.title: Loading the bundled modules
docs.text:
Redis 8 ships JSON, the query engine (search and vector indexes), probabilistic types (Bloom, Cuckoo, Count-Min, Top-K, t-digest) and time series as modules that are part of the Redis Open Source distribution. Homebrew's /opt/homebrew/etc/redis.conf loads them with loadmodule lines, but a server started only with flags, like the one above, doesn't:

redis-cli -p 6400 MODULE LIST

1) 1) "name"
   2) "vectorset"
   3) "ver"
   4) (integer) 1
   ...

Only the built-in vectorset type is there. For the lessons that use JSON, search or Bloom filters (Level 2 · 03, Level 3 · 08–10), start the lab from a small config file instead:

# ~/redis-lab/redis.conf
port 6379
dir /Users/you/redis-lab
save ""
appendonly no
loadmodule /opt/homebrew/opt/redis/lib/redis/modules/redisbloom.so
loadmodule /opt/homebrew/opt/redis/lib/redis/modules/redisearch.so
loadmodule /opt/homebrew/opt/redis/lib/redis/modules/rejson.so
loadmodule /opt/homebrew/opt/redis/lib/redis/modules/redistimeseries.so

redis-server ~/redis-lab/redis.conf

On Linux the module paths depend on how Redis was packaged. Look for the loadmodule lines in the redis.conf your package installed.

docs.title: Fact 1: the data lives in memory
docs.text:
Ask the empty server how much memory it's using:

redis-cli -p 6400 INFO memory | grep -E '^used_memory(_human|_rss_human)?:'

used_memory:930608
used_memory_human:908.80K
used_memory_rss_human:4.72M

used_memory is what Redis's allocator has handed out. used_memory_rss is what the operating system says the process occupies, including allocator overhead and fragmentation. Now generate a million keys, each a 64-byte string. DEBUG POPULATE exists for exactly this kind of test:

redis-cli -p 6400 DEBUG POPULATE 1000000 user 64
redis-cli -p 6400 DBSIZE
redis-cli -p 6400 INFO memory | grep -E '^used_memory_human|^used_memory_rss_human'

OK
1000000
used_memory_human:121.20M
used_memory_rss_human:126.12M

About 120 MB for 64 MB of values. That's roughly 120 bytes per key for keys like user:42 holding 64 bytes. The difference is overhead: the hash table entry, the key object, the value object and the allocator's size classes. Ask about one key:

redis-cli -p 6400 GET user:42
redis-cli -p 6400 MEMORY USAGE user:42

value:42
106

DEBUG POPULATE pads the value to 64 bytes, which is why value:42 has trailing spaces. MEMORY USAGE estimates 106 bytes for this key, its value and its share of the table. When you size a Redis server, count the overhead per key and not just the payload. With many small keys, the overhead can be bigger than the data. Level 2 · 01 shows how to shrink it.

Memory is volatile, so what happens to those million keys if the process stops? It depends entirely on configuration. Write a snapshot by hand, kill the server without saving, and start it again:

redis-cli -p 6400 SAVE
ls -la dump.rdb
redis-cli -p 6400 SHUTDOWN NOSAVE
redis-server --port 6400 --dir ~/redis-lab --save ''

OK
-rw-r--r--@ 1 bhanuja  wheel  36777608 Oct 13 06:55 dump.rdb

97881:M 13 Oct 2026 06:55:06.833 * Loading RDB produced by version 8.10.2
97881:M 13 Oct 2026 06:55:07.524 * Done loading RDB, keys loaded: 1000000, keys expired: 0.
97881:M 13 Oct 2026 06:55:07.524 * DB loaded from disk: 0.692 seconds

The 121 MB in memory became a 37 MB file. RDB is a compact serialization and compresses repetitive strings. On startup Redis found dump.rdb in its dir and loaded it before accepting connections. Without that SAVE, the restart would have come up empty, because this lab disabled automatic snapshots.

A server started with no configuration at all is not in that state:

redis-server --port 6401 &
redis-cli -p 6401 CONFIG GET save
redis-cli -p 6401 CONFIG GET appendonly

save
3600 1 300 100 60 10000
appendonly
no

The built-in default snapshots after 3600 s if at least 1 key changed, after 300 s if 100 changed, and after 60 s if 10,000 changed. So by default you can lose up to an hour of writes in a crash, and the append-only file that narrows that window is off. Whether that's acceptable depends on what you store. Level 4 · 01–02 cover persistence properly.

docs.title: Fact 2: one command at a time
docs.text:
Look at the threads of the running server:

ps -M -p $(pgrep -f 'redis-server.*6400')

USER      PID   TT   %CPU STAT PRI     STIME     UTIME COMMAND
bhanuja 97838   ??    0.2 S    31T   0:00.01   0:00.01 redis-server *:6400
        97838         0.0 S    31T   0:00.00   0:00.00
        97838         0.0 S    31T   0:00.00   0:00.00
        97838         0.0 S    31T   0:00.00   0:00.00

There are four threads. The main thread runs the event loop and executes every command. The other three are background ("bio") threads that close files, fsync the append-only file and free large values lazily, so that none of those slow system calls stall the main thread. None of them runs client commands.

The consequence is easy to measure. This script pings the server every millisecond from one connection while another connection runs KEYS *, a command that walks the entire keyspace:

import threading, time, redis

r = redis.Redis(port=6400)

def slow():
    t = time.perf_counter()
    n = len(r.keys('*'))
    print(f"KEYS * returned {n} keys in {time.perf_counter()-t:.3f}s")

worst = 0.0
def pinger(stop):
    global worst
    c = redis.Redis(port=6400); c.ping()
    while not stop.is_set():
        t = time.perf_counter(); c.ping()
        worst = max(worst, time.perf_counter() - t)
        time.sleep(0.001)

stop = threading.Event()
th = threading.Thread(target=pinger, args=(stop,)); th.start()
time.sleep(0.3); print(f"worst PING before: {worst*1000:.2f} ms"); worst = 0.0
slow()
time.sleep(0.2); stop.set(); th.join()
print(f"worst PING while KEYS ran: {worst*1000:.1f} ms")

worst PING before: 0.34 ms
KEYS * returned 1000000 keys in 0.192s
worst PING while KEYS ran: 149.1 ms

A PING normally takes a third of a millisecond. While KEYS * ran, one PING waited 149 ms. Nothing was wrong with that client; it was just queued behind someone else's command. On a laptop with a million keys that's a hiccup. With 50 million keys in production, it's an outage. That's why Level 1 · 04 replaces KEYS with SCAN, and why "what's the time complexity of this command?" is a question you'll keep asking all course.

The same property is a gift. Because nothing else runs while INCR counter executes, the read-add-write inside it can't interleave with another client's. You get atomicity for every single command without writing a lock.

docs.title: When Redis is the wrong tool
docs.text:
• The data doesn't fit in RAM, or RAM costs too much at your size. Redis is priced per gigabyte of memory.
  • You need ad-hoc queries. There's no general query language over values. You design keys and data structures around the questions you'll ask. The query engine (Level 3 · 09) adds secondary indexes, but you still declare them up front.
  • Losing the last second of writes is unacceptable and you can't prove your persistence and replication setup meets that. A relational database with synchronous commit is the safer default for records of truth.
  • Large values. A single 50 MB string has to be serialized on the one thread that serves everyone.

Most production systems use Redis alongside a primary database: the database holds the truth, and Redis holds fast, derived or short-lived state.

docs.title: How It Actually Works
docs.text:
When redis-server starts, it parses flags and the config file, creates a listening socket and enters an event loop (Redis's small ae library). On macOS the loop waits on kqueue (the multiplexing_api:kqueue line in INFO server); on Linux it uses epoll. Each iteration asks the kernel which sockets are readable, reads whatever bytes have arrived into each client's query buffer, parses complete commands out of it, and runs them one after another. Replies go into per-client output buffers and are written back when the sockets become writable. Timers also run in that loop. The serverCron function, at hz times per second (10 by default), expires keys, checks whether a snapshot is due and updates statistics.

Because one thread owns all the data, the data structures need no locks. A command reads and modifies the in-memory structures directly and finishes before the loop moves on. This is the source of both the atomicity and the head-of-line blocking you measured. Redis can be configured with io-threads (it was 1 on the lab server) to move reading and writing of sockets onto helper threads. That helps when a large server spends most of its time in network I/O. Command execution itself stays on the main thread.

The keyspace is a hash table from key to value object. Each key is a compact string type (SDS, "simple dynamic string") that stores its length up front, so strings are binary-safe and STRLEN is O(1). Each value carries a type tag and an encoding: the same logical type may be stored in different ways depending on its size. Level 2 · 01 explores this. The per-key overhead you measured is the table entry plus those headers, rounded up to the allocator's size classes.

SAVE serialized the whole dataset into the RDB format on the main thread, blocking clients while it wrote. On startup Redis reads the file back before opening for business, which is why loading a million keys took 0.69 s with the server unavailable. That gap is one reason restarting a large Redis isn't free.

docs.title: Common mistakes
docs.text:
• Treating Redis as durable by default. The default snapshot schedule can lose an hour of writes, and many managed or containerized setups disable persistence entirely. Know your configuration.
  • Running O(N) commands on big keyspaces. KEYS *, FLUSHALL (synchronous), SMEMBERS on a huge set, or HGETALL on a huge hash all block every other client for the whole time they run.
  • Sizing by payload. A million 64-byte values took 121 MB, not 64 MB. Measure used_memory with a realistic sample before you buy RAM.
  • Exposing the port. With no password, anyone who reaches the port can read, delete or reconfigure everything. Protected mode only stops connections from outside localhost when no password and no explicit bind address are set.
  • Testing against the shared server. Use a lab you can wipe. Several lessons in this course deliberately break things.

docs.title: Exercise
docs.text:
1. Start a lab on port 6400 with --save '' and --enable-debug-command local. Populate 200,000 keys with DEBUG POPULATE 200000 k 16, then with 200,000 keys of 1,000 bytes (flush in between with FLUSHALL). Record used_memory each time and work out the overhead per key in both cases. Which case has the larger overhead as a percentage?
  2. Run the KEYS * blocking script with 100k, 1M and 3M keys. Does the worst PING latency grow roughly linearly with the key count?
  3. Run INFO server and find multiplexing_api, process_id and config_file. Why is config_file empty for your flag-started lab?
  4. Without SAVE, shut the --save '' server down with plain SHUTDOWN (no NOSAVE) and restart it. Were the keys kept? Then repeat with a server started with --save '60 1' and compare the shutdown lines in the two logs. What does SHUTDOWN decide based on the save setting?

docs.title: 02 · redis-cli & the RESP Protocol
docs.text:
Every Redis client, whether it's redis-cli, redis-py, node-redis or Jedis, does the same job. It turns a command like SET city Porto into bytes, sends them over TCP and parses the reply. The format of those bytes is RESP, the Redis Serialization Protocol. It's simple enough to speak by hand, and it pays to have done that once: it shows you why pipelining is so fast, what (nil) really is, and why a client library can return a float from one server and a str from another.

All examples use the lab server on port 6379.

docs.title: Speaking RESP by hand
docs.text:
A request is an array of bulk strings. *1 means "an array of one element", and $4 means "a string of 4 bytes follows". Every line ends with . Here is a small Python script that opens a raw socket and sends RESP:

import socket, time

s = socket.create_connection(("127.0.0.1", 6379))
def send(raw):
    s.sendall(raw)
    time.sleep(0.05)
    print(repr(s.recv(65536)))

send(b"*1
$4
PING
")
send(b"*3
$3
SET
$4
city
$5
Porto
")
send(b"*2
$3
GET
$4
city
")
send(b"*2
$3
GET
$7
missing
")
send(b"*2
$4
INCR
$4
hits
")
send(b"*2
$4
INCR
$4
city
")

b'+PONG
'
b'+OK
'
b'$5
Porto
'
b'$-1
'
b':1
'
b'-ERR value is not an integer or out of range
'

The first byte of every reply tells the client what type follows:

Prefix RESP2 type Example above + simple string (status) +PONG, +OK - error -ERR value is not an integer… : integer :1 from INCR $ bulk string (length-prefixed, binary-safe) $5 Porto $-1 null bulk string GET missing * array replies to LRANGE, HGETALL…

Two details matter in practice. Bulk strings carry a length, so a value can contain , NUL bytes or a JPEG, and nothing has to be escaped. And an error is a normal reply, not a dropped connection: the client stays connected and the next command works.

Because the format is just bytes on a stream, you can send several commands in one write and read all the replies afterwards:

send(b"*4
$5
RPUSH
$1
q
$1
a
$1
b
"
     b"*4
$6
LRANGE
$1
q
$1
0
$2
-1
")

b':2
*2
$1
a
$1
b
'

Both replies arrived in one read, in order. That is pipelining, and it's the single biggest performance lever on the client side (measured below).

Redis also accepts inline commands, which are plain space-separated text, mainly so you can poke a server with telnet or nc:

send(b"EXISTS city hits nope
")

b':2
'

Clients never use inline commands: they can't carry binary data or spaces inside arguments.

docs.title: RESP3: richer types after HELLO 3
docs.text:
RESP2 has no maps, no floats and no sets. HGETALL returns a flat array [field, value, field, value] and ZSCORE returns a number as a string. RESP3 (Redis 6+) adds real types, and a connection opts in with HELLO 3:

send(b"*2
$5
HELLO
$1
3
")

b'%7
$6
server
$5
redis
$7
version
$6
8.10.2
$5
proto
:3

  $2
id
:16
$4
mode
$10
standalone
$4
role
$6
master
 ...'

(Wrapped for width.) %7 is a map with seven entries. Compare the same commands on a RESP2 connection and a RESP3 connection:

RESP2  ZSCORE z m      ->  b'$3
1.5
'          bulk string "1.5"
RESP3  ZSCORE z m      ->  b',1.5
'               double
RESP3  HGETALL h       ->  b'%1
$1
f
$1
v
'   map
RESP3  SMEMBERS s      ->  b'~1
$1
x
'       set
RESP3  GET missing     ->  b'_
'                   null

RESP3 also adds booleans (#t), big numbers ((), verbatim strings (=) and push messages (>). Push messages are out-of-band data that the server sends without being asked. They're how Pub/Sub messages and client-side-cache invalidations can share a connection with normal commands (Level 3 · 06).

This difference reaches your application code. A client that negotiates RESP3 can hand you a native float for a score and a dict for a hash, while a RESP2 client may give you bytes that you have to convert. Level 1 · 09 shows what redis-py 8 does about that.

docs.title: redis-cli in interactive mode
docs.text:
Run redis-cli with no command to get a prompt. It formats each reply type so you can tell them apart:

127.0.0.1:6379> SET city Porto
OK
127.0.0.1:6379> GET city
"Porto"
127.0.0.1:6379> GET missing
(nil)
127.0.0.1:6379> INCR hits
(integer) 2
127.0.0.1:6379> INCR city
(error) ERR value is not an integer or out of range
127.0.0.1:6379> RPUSH q a b
(integer) 4
127.0.0.1:6379> LRANGE q 0 -1
1) "a"
2) "b"
3) "a"
4) "b"
127.0.0.1:6379> ZSCORE z m
"1.5"

"Porto" with quotes is a bulk string, OK without quotes is a status reply, and (nil) is the null bulk string. (RPUSH returned 4 because the raw-socket demo had already pushed a and b; lists keep duplicates.) Switch the same session to RESP3 and the formatting follows the new types:

127.0.0.1:6379> HELLO 3
1# "server" => "redis"
2# "version" => "8.10.2"
3# "proto" => (integer) 3
...
127.0.0.1:6379> HGETALL h
1# "f" => "v"
127.0.0.1:6379> ZSCORE z m
(double) 1.5

You can also start in RESP3 with redis-cli -3. Other things worth knowing at the prompt:

  • HELP SET prints the syntax, and the prompt shows grey hints as you type. In Redis 8.10 the SET hint already includes newer options like IFEQ.
  • SELECT 2 switches to logical database 2, and the prompt becomes 127.0.0.1:6379[2]>.
  • After MULTI, the prompt shows (TX) until EXEC or DISCARD.
  • Command names are case-insensitive. Key names are not.

docs.title: redis-cli in scripts
docs.text:
Give redis-cli a command as arguments and it runs it and exits. When stdout is not a terminal it switches to raw output, with no quotes, no 1) numbering and no (nil):

redis-cli RPUSH q a b c
redis-cli LRANGE q 0 -1
redis-cli --no-raw LRANGE q 0 -1
echo "[$(redis-cli GET nothere)]"

3
a
b
c
1) "a"
2) "b"
3) "c"
[]

In raw mode a missing key and an empty string both print as an empty line, so a shell script can't tell them apart. If the difference matters, check EXISTS first or use --no-raw. For machine-readable output there's --json:

redis-cli HSET user:1 name Ana city Porto
redis-cli --json HGETALL user:1

{"name":"Ana","city":"Porto"}

Reading a value from stdin with -x makes the last argument come from stdin, byte for byte:

printf 'line one\nline two\n' > note.txt
redis-cli -x SET note < note.txt
redis-cli --no-raw GET note

OK
"line one\nline two\n"

Databases. A server has 16 numbered databases by default. -n picks one:

redis-cli -n 2 SET only-in-db2 yes
redis-cli GET only-in-db2
redis-cli -n 2 GET only-in-db2
redis-cli INFO keyspace

OK

yes
# Keyspace
db0:keys=3,expires=0,avg_ttl=0,subexpiry=0
db2:keys=1,expires=0,avg_ttl=0,subexpiry=0

Numbered databases are namespaces, not isolation. They share one memory limit, one thread and one set of users, and Redis Cluster supports only database 0. Prefer key prefixes (app1:…) or separate servers.

Repeating a command uses -r (count) and -i (interval in seconds):

redis-cli -r 3 -i 0.5 INCR tick

1
2
3

docs.title: Round trips are the cost: three ways to load 100,000 keys
docs.text:
Here is a file of 100,000 SET product:N value commands, loaded three ways:

python3 -c "
for i in range(100000): print(f'SET product:{i} {i*3}')" > cmds.txt

One redis-cli process per command (only 2,000 of them, because the full set would take minutes):

time (head -2000 cmds.txt | while read c k v; do redis-cli SET $k $v >/dev/null; done)

5.84s user 3.11s system 77% cpu 11.480 total

One redis-cli process reading all 100,000 commands from stdin. It sends one command, waits for the reply, then sends the next:

time (redis-cli < cmds.txt > /dev/null)

0.33s user 0.65s system 11% cpu 8.192 total

--pipe, which streams the commands without waiting for replies. It needs input already encoded as RESP:

import sys
for i in range(100000):
    parts = [b"SET", f"product:{i}".encode(), str(i * 3).encode()]
    sys.stdout.buffer.write(b"*%d\r\n" % len(parts) +
        b"".join(b"$%d\r\n%s\r\n" % (len(p), p) for p in parts))

python3 gen_resp.py > cmds.resp
time (redis-cli --pipe < cmds.resp)

All data transferred. Waiting for the last reply...
Last reply received from server.
errors: 0, replies: 100000
0.02s user 0.02s system 59% cpu 0.079 total

That's 8.2 seconds versus 0.079 seconds for the same 100,000 writes, roughly a hundredfold, and the server did identical work in both cases. The difference is the time spent waiting: one network round trip per command versus a continuous stream. On a real network, where a round trip is often 0.5–1 ms rather than tens of microseconds over loopback, the gap is larger. (Starting a process per command is slower still: 11.5 s for just 2,000 keys.) Every client library supports pipelining. Use it whenever you have more than a handful of independent commands to send.

docs.title: Watching and inspecting a live server
docs.text:
MONITOR streams every command the server executes. Here it captures a short redis-py session:

redis-cli MONITOR

OK
1791854878.277435 [0 [::1]:60703] "HELLO" "3"
1791854878.277941 [0 [::1]:60703] "CLIENT" "SETINFO" "LIB-NAME" "redis-py"
1791854878.278115 [0 [::1]:60703] "CLIENT" "SETINFO" "LIB-VER" "8.1.0"
1791854878.278321 [0 [::1]:60703] "SET" "session:9" "x" "EX" "60"
1791854878.278565 [0 [::1]:60703] "GET" "product:7"
1791854878.278817 [0 [::1]:60703] "INCRBY" "a" "1"
1791854878.278823 [0 [::1]:60703] "INCRBY" "b" "1"

There are three useful findings in seven lines. The library opened with HELLO 3, so it negotiated RESP3. It labelled itself with CLIENT SETINFO, which makes it identifiable in CLIENT LIST. And its incr() method actually sends INCRBY key 1. The last two INCRBY calls were pipelined, 6 µs apart. MONITOR is a debugging tool, though. It costs the server real throughput, and it shows every argument, passwords and personal data included. Don't leave it running in production.

--bigkeys scans the keyspace (with SCAN, so it doesn't block like KEYS) and reports the largest key of each type:

redis-cli --bigkeys

-------- summary -------

Sampled 100003 keys in the keyspace!
Total key length in bytes is 1288901 (avg len 12.89)

Biggest string found "product:80350" has 6 bytes

0 lists with 0 items (00.00% of keys, avg size 0.00)
0 hashs with 0 fields (00.00% of keys, avg size 0.00)
0 streams with 0 entries (00.00% of keys, avg size 0.00)
100003 strings with 562963 bytes (100.00% of keys, avg size 5.63)
0 sets with 0 members (00.00% of keys, avg size 0.00)
0 zsets with 0 members (00.00% of keys, avg size 0.00)

--memkeys does the same ranked by MEMORY USAGE, --stat prints a rolling one-line summary every second, and --latency measures PING round trips continuously. Level 4 · 08 uses all of them for troubleshooting.

docs.title: How It Actually Works
docs.text:
Server-side, every connection has a query buffer. The event loop reads whatever bytes the socket has into that buffer, and the parser pulls out as many complete commands as it can, leaving any partial command in place until more bytes arrive. Then it executes those commands back to back and appends each reply to the client's output buffer. That's why pipelining works without any special server mode. Redis never needed the first reply to be read before it processed the second command; the client was simply choosing to wait. --pipe and library pipelines stop waiting.

The prefix-and-length design is what makes the parser fast. To read a bulk string, the server reads the $<len> line and then copies exactly len bytes. It never scans the payload for a terminator and never unescapes anything. Replies work the same way on the client side.

RESP3 doesn't change command semantics. The server keeps a per-connection protocol version (set by HELLO) and serializes the same internal result differently: a hash reply becomes a % map instead of a * array, a score becomes a , double instead of a $ string. Push messages (>) are tagged so that a client can pull them out of the reply stream and route them to a callback. That's what lets one RESP3 connection receive Pub/Sub messages and invalidation notices while still running ordinary commands. RESP2 needs a dedicated connection for that.

MONITOR works by registering the connection as a monitor. After each command executes, the server formats it and appends it to every monitor's output buffer. With many monitors or a busy server, that formatting work happens on the one command thread, which is why it's expensive.

docs.title: Common mistakes
docs.text:
• One round trip per command in a loop. It's the most common reason for "Redis is slow". The server is idle and the client is waiting. Pipeline the loop, or use a multi-key command like MSET.
  • Parsing raw redis-cli output in scripts and treating an empty line as "missing". Raw mode can't tell (nil) from "". Use EXISTS, --no-raw or --json.
  • Building --pipe input as inline text with values that contain spaces or newlines. Generate real RESP, as shown above.
  • Leaving MONITOR attached to a production server, or pasting its output, which contains every value and any AUTH arguments, into a ticket.
  • Using numbered databases for tenant isolation. They share everything, and Cluster only has database 0.
  • Assuming the reply type. A score is a string in RESP2 and a double in RESP3. Check what your client negotiated (CLIENT LIST shows resp=2 or resp=3).

docs.title: Exercise
docs.text:
1. With nc 127.0.0.1 6379 (or the Python socket script), send SET bin "a\r\nb" as a properly framed RESP array, then STRLEN bin. Why does the length come back as 4?
  2. Send HELLO 3 followed by HGETALL user:1 and SISMEMBER s x, and identify every RESP3 type prefix in the raw reply.
  3. Regenerate cmds.resp with 1,000,000 commands and time --pipe. Then time the same load with redis-py, once with a plain loop of r.set() and once with a pipeline that sends batches of 1,000. Work out the commands per second for each.
  4. Run MONITOR in one terminal and a script that uses your favourite client library in another. What does the library send when it connects? Does it send HELLO, CLIENT SETINFO or SELECT?

docs.title: 03 · Strings, Counters & Expiry
docs.text: The Redis string is the simplest type and the one you'll use most. A string is any sequence of bytes up to 512 MB: text, a JSON blob, a serialized protobuf, an image thumbnail, or an integer that Redis knows how to increment. Most of what makes strings useful lies in the options on SET and in a handful of atomic operations, and almost every key in a real deployment also has an expiry.

docs.title: SET and its options
docs.text:
127.0.0.1:6379> SET page:home "<h1>Home</h1>"
OK
127.0.0.1:6379> GET page:home
"<h1>Home</h1>"

SET overwrites unconditionally. Its options turn it into several different operations:

127.0.0.1:6379> SET page:home "<h1>Welcome</h1>" NX
(nil)
127.0.0.1:6379> SET page:about "<h1>About</h1>" XX
(nil)
127.0.0.1:6379> GET page:about
(nil)
  • NX — set only if the key does not exist. It returned (nil) because page:home was already there. This is "create once", the basis of idempotency keys and locks.
  • XX — set only if the key does exist. page:about didn't exist, so nothing was written.

GET returns the old value in the same step, which is useful when you need to know what you replaced:

127.0.0.1:6379> SET config:mode blue GET
(nil)
127.0.0.1:6379> SET config:mode green GET
"blue"

Since Redis 8.4, SET can also compare before writing. IFEQ writes only if the current value equals the one you give, which makes it an atomic compare-and-set:

127.0.0.1:6379> SET lock owner-1
OK
127.0.0.1:6379> SET lock owner-2 IFEQ owner-9
(nil)
127.0.0.1:6379> SET lock owner-2 IFEQ owner-1
OK
127.0.0.1:6379> GET lock
"owner-2"

Its partner DELEX (also 8.4) deletes only if the value matches, which is exactly what releasing a lock needs:

127.0.0.1:6379> DELEX lock IFEQ owner-1
(integer) 0
127.0.0.1:6379> DELEX lock IFEQ owner-2
(integer) 1

IFNE means "if not equal". IFDEQ and IFDNE compare against a digest of the value (the DIGEST command returns it), so you don't have to send a large value back just to compare it. On older servers, check HELP SET before relying on these. Valkey 9.1.2 accepted SET … IFEQ but has no DELEX or DIGEST (Level 4 · 09). Level 2 · 09 shows the Lua-script equivalent that works everywhere.

docs.title: Many keys at once
docs.text:
127.0.0.1:6379> MSET a 1 b 2 c 3
OK
127.0.0.1:6379> MGET a b nope c
1) "1"
2) "2"
3) (nil)
4) "3"
127.0.0.1:6379> MSETNX c 30 d 40
(integer) 0
127.0.0.1:6379> MGET c d
1) "3"
2) (nil)

MGET returns one slot per requested key, with (nil) holding the place of missing ones, so results line up with your input. MSETNX is all-or-nothing: because c existed, neither key was written, including d. Multi-key commands save round trips, but in Redis Cluster every key in one command has to live in the same hash slot (Level 4 · 05).

docs.title: Partial updates
docs.text:
127.0.0.1:6379> APPEND log "line1;"
(integer) 6
127.0.0.1:6379> APPEND log "line2;"
(integer) 12
127.0.0.1:6379> GETRANGE log 0 4
"line1"
127.0.0.1:6379> STRLEN log
(integer) 12
127.0.0.1:6379> SETRANGE log 0 LINE1
(integer) 12
127.0.0.1:6379> GET log
"LINE1;line2;"

APPEND creates the key if it's missing and returns the new length. GETRANGE and SETRANGE work on byte offsets, not characters, so be careful with UTF-8 text. These commands are handy for fixed-layout binary records, but if you're appending log lines you probably want a list or a stream (Level 1 · 06, Level 2 · 05).

docs.title: Counters
docs.text:
A string holding a decimal integer can be changed in place:

127.0.0.1:6379> SET visits 0
OK
127.0.0.1:6379> INCR visits
(integer) 1
127.0.0.1:6379> INCRBY visits 10
(integer) 11
127.0.0.1:6379> DECRBY visits 3
(integer) 8
127.0.0.1:6379> GET visits
"8"

INCR on a missing key treats it as 0, so you don't have to initialize counters. The reason to use INCR rather than reading the value and writing back value + 1 shows up under concurrency. This script has 16 threads that each add one like 5,000 times, both ways:

from concurrent.futures import ThreadPoolExecutor
import redis

r = redis.Redis(decode_responses=True)
r.mset({"likes:rmw": 0, "likes:incr": 0})

def rmw(_):
    n = int(r.get("likes:rmw"))
    r.set("likes:rmw", n + 1)

def incr(_):
    r.incr("likes:incr")

with ThreadPoolExecutor(16) as pool:
    list(pool.map(rmw, range(5000)))
    list(pool.map(incr, range(5000)))

print(r.mget("likes:rmw", "likes:incr"))

['570', '5000']

A second run printed ['556', '5000']. With read-modify-write, close to 89% of the likes vanished: many threads read the same number and wrote back the same "+1". INCR was exact both times because the whole read-add-write happens inside one command on Redis's single command thread. If you remember one thing from this lesson, make it this: push the change to Redis instead of the result.

Counters are 64-bit signed integers and refuse to wrap around:

127.0.0.1:6379> SET big 9223372036854775807
OK
127.0.0.1:6379> INCR big
(error) ERR increment or decrement would overflow

docs.title: Floats
docs.text:
INCRBYFLOAT exists, but read its output carefully:

127.0.0.1:6379> INCRBYFLOAT price 0.1
"0.10000000000000001"
127.0.0.1:6379> INCRBYFLOAT price 0.2
"0.30000000000000004"

Redis does the arithmetic in binary floating point and stores the result as a string. On this version, the string shows the full 17-significant-digit representation, so the binary rounding error that some other tools hide is plainly visible. Never keep money in floats. Store integer cents with INCRBY, and format at the edge of your application.

docs.title: Expiry
docs.text:
Any key can be given a time to live. When it runs out, the key disappears as if it had been deleted.

127.0.0.1:6379> SET token abc123 EX 30
OK
127.0.0.1:6379> TTL token
(integer) 30
127.0.0.1:6379> PTTL token
(integer) 29884

EX sets the TTL in seconds and PX in milliseconds. EXAT and PXAT take an absolute Unix time. TTL and PTTL report what's left, and they have two special answers:

127.0.0.1:6379> PERSIST token
(integer) 1
127.0.0.1:6379> TTL token
(integer) -1
127.0.0.1:6379> TTL nosuchkey
(integer) -2

-1 means the key exists with no expiry. -2 means there's no such key.

docs.title: The overwrite trap
docs.text:
This catches everyone at least once:

127.0.0.1:6379> SET token abc123 EX 30
OK
127.0.0.1:6379> SET token xyz789
OK
127.0.0.1:6379> TTL token
(integer) -1

A plain SET removes the TTL. A session that was supposed to expire in 30 minutes now lives forever, and because "forever" in a cache means "until memory runs out", the leak is slow and quiet. If you mean to change the value and keep the expiry, say so:

127.0.0.1:6379> SET token abc123 EX 30
OK
127.0.0.1:6379> SET token xyz789 KEEPTTL
OK
127.0.0.1:6379> TTL token
(integer) 30

INCR, APPEND, SETRANGE and the other in-place modifiers keep the TTL. Only commands that replace the value (SET, GETSET, MSET) reset it.

docs.title: Conditional and absolute expiry
docs.text:
EXPIRE takes the flags NX (only if the key has no TTL), XX (only if it has one), GT (only if the new TTL is longer) and LT (only if it's shorter):

127.0.0.1:6379> EXPIRE token 10 GT
(integer) 0
127.0.0.1:6379> EXPIRE token 100 GT
(integer) 1
127.0.0.1:6379> TTL token
(integer) 100

GT lets many writers each extend a deadline without any of them accidentally shortening it. EXPIRETIME returns the absolute Unix time of expiry, which is useful when you copy a key's deadline elsewhere:

127.0.0.1:6379> EXPIRE visits 60
(integer) 1
127.0.0.1:6379> EXPIRETIME visits
(integer) 1791855038

docs.title: Read and change expiry in one step
docs.text:
127.0.0.1:6379> GETEX visits PERSIST
"8"
127.0.0.1:6379> TTL visits
(integer) -1
127.0.0.1:6379> GETDEL config:mode
"green"
127.0.0.1:6379> EXISTS config:mode
(integer) 0

GETEX key EX 1800 is the "sliding session" pattern: read the session and push its expiry forward, atomically. GETDEL reads and removes, which suits single-use values like a one-time login code.

docs.title: How It Actually Works
docs.text:
A string value is stored in one of three encodings, which you can see with OBJECT ENCODING:

127.0.0.1:6379> OBJECT ENCODING visits
"int"
127.0.0.1:6379> OBJECT ENCODING page:home
"embstr"
127.0.0.1:6379> SET long "aaaa…(87 characters)…aaa"
OK
127.0.0.1:6379> OBJECT ENCODING long
"raw"
127.0.0.1:6379> SET n 12345
OK
127.0.0.1:6379> OBJECT ENCODING n
"int"
127.0.0.1:6379> APPEND n 6
(integer) 6
127.0.0.1:6379> OBJECT ENCODING n
"raw"
  • int — a value that parses as a 64-bit integer is stored as the integer itself, inside the object header, with no separate string allocation. This is why INCR is cheap: it adds to a machine word.
  • embstr — short strings (up to 44 bytes on 64-bit builds) are allocated in a single block together with the object header. That's one allocation and good cache locality, but the block can't be resized.
  • raw — longer strings, or any string that has been modified in place, get a separately allocated SDS buffer that can grow. APPEND n 6 had to turn the integer into real text and then extend it, so the encoding changed for good.

The encoding is invisible to clients (GET always returns bytes) but it affects memory and speed.

Expiry is kept in a second hash table, the expires dictionary, that maps keys to an absolute expiry time in milliseconds. TTL subtracts the current time from that entry, and PERSIST deletes it. Expired keys are removed in two ways. Lazily, any command that touches a key first checks whether it has expired and deletes it if so, so you can never read an expired value. Actively, a background cycle samples keys from the expires table several times a second and deletes the expired ones it finds, keeping its CPU use bounded. So an expired key that nobody reads can stay in memory for a while after its deadline. Level 3 · 02 measures this.

Because an absolute time is stored, a replica or a reloaded snapshot computes the same deadline. Expiry depends on the server's clock, so a clock jump on the server changes when keys expire.

docs.title: Common mistakes
docs.text:
• Read-modify-write counters. The race above lost about 89% of increments. Use INCR/INCRBY, or a transaction or script for anything more complex (Level 2 · 08–09).
  • Plain SET on a key that should expire. It silently removes the TTL. Use SET … EX again or SET … KEEPTTL.
  • Floats for money. INCRBYFLOAT shows binary rounding error. Use integer minor units.
  • Huge strings. A single 100 MB value is read, copied and sent on the one command thread. Split large blobs, or keep them in object storage and store only a pointer in Redis.
  • Forgetting that MSETNX is all-or-nothing. One existing key blocks the whole write.
  • Assuming GETRANGE counts characters. It counts bytes, and a multibyte UTF-8 character can be cut in half.

docs.title: Exercise
docs.text:
1. Build an idempotency check. A payment request carries an ID. SET idem:<id> processing NX EX 86400 succeeds only for the first attempt. Simulate three retries of the same ID and show that only one "processes". What should you store in the key once processing finishes, and why?
  2. Make the race script lose updates with INCRBYFLOAT and an integer counter at the same time. Then fix both with server-side operations.
  3. Write a sliding session: SET session:<id> <json> EX 30, then in a loop every 10 seconds call GETEX … EX 30 and print the TTL. Stop the loop and confirm the key disappears about 30 seconds later.
  4. Find the exact length at which OBJECT ENCODING switches from embstr to raw on your server by setting strings of increasing length.

docs.title: 04 · The Keyspace: Naming, SCAN & Safe Deletes
docs.text: Redis has no tables, schemas or folders. There's one flat namespace of keys per database, and the only structure is whatever you put in the names. That makes key design the closest thing Redis has to schema design. It also means operational tasks like "find all the cache keys", "delete this tenant" or "what's using the memory?" all come down to walking that flat namespace, and walking it the wrong way blocks the server.

docs.title: Naming keys
docs.text:
The near-universal convention is colon-separated segments, from general to specific:

user:1042:profile        a string or hash for one user
user:1042:sessions       a set of that user's session ids
session:9f3c2a           one session
cache:api:v2:/products?page=3
rate:login:203.0.113.7
leaderboard:2026-10

Some guidelines that pay off later:

  • Lead with the object type. Then SCAN MATCH cache:* finds all cache entries, and memory reports can be grouped by prefix.
  • Put the variable part where a pattern can match it. cache:api:* is easy to match. A key that buries the type in the middle is not.
  • Add a version segment to cached data (cache:api:v2:…). When the format changes you bump it, old keys simply age out through their TTLs, and you never have to mass-delete.
  • Keep keys reasonably short. Every key is stored in full, once per key. With 100 million keys, 30 extra bytes per name is 3 GB. Don't shorten names until they're unreadable, though; u:1:p costs more in debugging time than it saves.
  • Plan for Cluster now. In Redis Cluster, keys are spread over nodes by a hash of the name, and multi-key commands only work when all their keys hash to the same slot. Braces mark the part that gets hashed: user:{1042}:profile and user:{1042}:sessions always land together (Level 4 · 05).

docs.title: Inspecting keys
docs.text:
127.0.0.1:6379> DBSIZE
(integer) 43
127.0.0.1:6379> TYPE user:1:prefs
hash
127.0.0.1:6379> TYPE queue:emails
list
127.0.0.1:6379> TYPE nope
none
127.0.0.1:6379> EXISTS user:1:profile user:2:profile nope
(integer) 2

EXISTS with several keys returns how many of them exist, not a yes/no answer. OBJECT IDLETIME key says how many seconds have passed since the key was last read or written, which helps you spot data nobody uses.

Renaming and copying:

127.0.0.1:6379> RENAME session:1 session:one
OK
127.0.0.1:6379> RENAMENX session:2 session:one
(integer) 0
127.0.0.1:6379> COPY user:1:prefs user:2:prefs
(integer) 1
127.0.0.1:6379> HGETALL user:2:prefs
1) "theme"
2) "dark"

RENAME silently overwrites an existing destination; RENAMENX refuses to. COPY duplicates a value of any type, and it also refuses to overwrite unless you add REPLACE.

docs.title: Why not KEYS?
docs.text: KEYS pattern returns every matching key in a single reply. To do that it has to visit every key in the database, whatever the pattern, and it does it in one command on the one command thread. Lesson 01 measured a KEYS * on a million keys holding up an unrelated PING for 149 ms. KEYS is fine on your laptop, but it doesn't belong in application code. Many production setups rename or block it with ACLs (Level 4 · 07).

docs.title: SCAN: iterate in small steps
docs.text:
SCAN returns a small batch of keys plus a cursor. You pass the cursor back to get the next batch, and you start and stop at cursor 0:

127.0.0.1:6379> SCAN 0
1) "18"
2)  1) "user:15:profile"
    2) "session:5"
    3) "session:7"
    4) "user:9:profile"
    5) "session:11"
    6) "session:14"
    7) "user:3:profile"
    8) "user:5:profile"
    9) "user:1:profile"
   10) "session:2"

The next call would be SCAN 18. When a call returns cursor "0", the iteration is complete. Each call does a bounded amount of work, so other clients get served between calls.

The options:

127.0.0.1:6379> SCAN 0 MATCH user:* COUNT 100
1) "0"
2)  1) "user:15:profile"
    2) "user:9:profile"
    ...
   21) "user:14:profile"
127.0.0.1:6379> SCAN 0 TYPE hash COUNT 100
1) "0"
2) 1) "user:1:prefs"

COUNT is a hint for how much of the table to examine per call (default 10), not how many results you get back. MATCH and TYPE filter after the examining is done. With a pattern that matches little, you get pages that are empty even though the iteration isn't finished:

127.0.0.1:6379> SCAN 0 MATCH session:* COUNT 5
1) "40"
2) 1) "session:5"
   2) "session:7"
   3) "session:11"
127.0.0.1:6379> SCAN 0 MATCH nomatch:* COUNT 5
1) "40"
2) (empty array)

An empty page with a non-zero cursor means "keep going". A loop that stops at the first empty page is a classic bug. Only cursor 0 means done.

What SCAN guarantees:

  • A key that exists for the whole iteration will be returned at least once.
  • A key might be returned more than once (de-duplicate if that matters).
  • Keys added or removed during the iteration may or may not appear.

The same cursor interface exists inside collections: HSCAN, SSCAN and ZSCAN iterate one big hash, set or sorted set without blocking.

docs.title: Big keys: DEL vs UNLINK
docs.text:
Freeing a value with millions of elements means freeing millions of allocations. DEL does that on the command thread. UNLINK removes the key from the keyspace immediately and hands the freeing to a background thread. This script builds a 2-million-field hash, deletes it each way, and pings from another connection the whole time:

import redis, time, threading
r = redis.Redis()

def build(key, n):
    p = r.pipeline(transaction=False)
    for i in range(n):
        p.hset(key, f"f{i}", "v" * 20)
        if i % 10000 == 0: p.execute()
    p.execute()

for cmd in ("DEL", "UNLINK"):
    build("big:hash", 2_000_000)
    worst = 0.0; stop = threading.Event()
    def pinger():
        global worst
        c = redis.Redis(); c.ping()
        while not stop.is_set():
            t = time.perf_counter(); c.ping()
            worst = max(worst, time.perf_counter() - t); time.sleep(0.0005)
    th = threading.Thread(target=pinger); th.start(); time.sleep(0.2); worst = 0.0
    t = time.perf_counter(); r.execute_command(cmd, "big:hash"); el = time.perf_counter() - t
    time.sleep(0.5); stop.set(); th.join()
    print(f"{cmd:6} returned after {el*1000:7.1f} ms; worst PING meanwhile {worst*1000:6.1f} ms")

DEL    returned after   281.1 ms; worst PING meanwhile  280.2 ms
UNLINK returned after     0.5 ms; worst PING meanwhile    3.7 ms

DEL froze the server for 281 ms. UNLINK returned in half a millisecond and the server stayed responsive. Afterwards INFO memory shows the background work:

lazyfree_pending_objects:0
lazyfreed_objects:1

On this Redis 8.10 build, the lazyfree-* settings that would make DEL, eviction, expiry and FLUSHALL behave like UNLINK automatically are all no:

lazyfree-lazy-user-del      no
lazyfree-lazy-user-flush    no
lazyfree-lazy-expire        no
lazyfree-lazy-eviction      no
lazyfree-lazy-server-del    no

So use UNLINK explicitly, and FLUSHALL ASYNC / FLUSHDB ASYNC for whole databases, or turn those settings on in your config. (Defaults differ between projects and versions. Level 4 · 09 compares Valkey's. Always check with CONFIG GET lazyfree*.)

docs.title: Many keys: SCAN + UNLINK in batches
docs.text:
To delete every key matching a pattern without blocking, scan in pages and unlink in batches:

def delete_matching(pattern, batch=500):
    deleted, buf = 0, []
    for key in r.scan_iter(match=pattern, count=1000):
        buf.append(key)
        if len(buf) >= batch:
            deleted += r.unlink(*buf); buf.clear()
    if buf:
        deleted += r.unlink(*buf)
    return deleted

On a database with 500,000 user:* and 500,000 cache:* keys:

deleted 500000 keys in 0.81s; worst PING meanwhile 1.2 ms
remaining: 500000

It's slower overall than a single blocking command would be, but the worst latency any other client saw was 1.2 ms. That's the trade you want on a live server. scan_iter hides the cursor loop, and it correctly keeps going through empty pages.

If you control the design, you can avoid mass deletes altogether. Give data that will need bulk removal a TTL, use a version segment in the key name, or keep such data in its own logical structure (a hash per tenant, for example) so that one UNLINK removes all of it.

docs.title: How It Actually Works
docs.text:
The keyspace is a hash table whose size is a power of two. A key's bucket is hash(key) & (size - 1). When the table fills up, Redis allocates a larger one and rehashes incrementally: each command and a periodic timer move a few buckets from the old table to the new one, so growing a table with millions of keys never causes one long pause. During a rehash, both tables are live.

SCAN's cursor is a bucket position, but it isn't incremented normally. Redis increments the cursor's reversed bits, so the scan visits buckets in an order where every bucket of a smaller table corresponds to a contiguous group of buckets in a larger one. That's what lets SCAN keep its "every key present for the whole time is returned" guarantee even when the table grows or shrinks mid-iteration. It's also why it sometimes returns duplicates: after a shrink, two old buckets may map to one new bucket that gets visited again. The cursor holds no server-side state at all. Redis doesn't remember your iteration, so abandoning one costs nothing, and many clients can scan at once.

COUNT controls how many buckets one call visits, roughly. MATCH is applied to the keys in those buckets afterwards, which is why a rare pattern gives empty pages.

UNLINK takes the value out of the dictionary (instantly, from the point of view of every client) and, if freeing it would be expensive, puts the object on a queue for a background "bio" lazy-free thread. Freeing small values in the background would cost more than it saves, so small ones are still freed inline. The lazyfree_pending_objects metric is that queue's length.

docs.title: Common mistakes
docs.text:
• KEYS in application code. It's O(total keys) and blocks everyone. Use SCAN, or better, maintain an index set of the keys you'll need to find.
  • Stopping a SCAN loop on an empty page. Only cursor 0 ends the iteration.
  • Assuming SCAN returns each key once. De-duplicate when the operation isn't idempotent.
  • DEL on huge collections. Use UNLINK, or turn on lazyfree-lazy-user-del.
  • FLUSHALL without ASYNC on a big instance. It blocks for as long as freeing everything takes.
  • RENAME over an existing key by accident. It silently overwrites. Use RENAMENX when that matters.
  • Mixing tenants or environments in numbered databases. Use prefixes or separate instances.

docs.title: Exercise
docs.text:
1. Populate 200,000 keys and write a SCAN loop with COUNT 10 and MATCH user:1*. Count how many calls return an empty page before the cursor reaches 0. Repeat with COUNT 1000.
  2. Start a SCAN iteration, add 300,000 more keys halfway through (forcing a rehash), and finish it. Record how many keys came back and how many were duplicates.
  3. Build a 1-million-member sorted set and compare DEL with UNLINK using the ping-latency script. Then set lazyfree-lazy-user-del yes and measure DEL again.
  4. Design key names for a multi-tenant SaaS: tenants, users, sessions, a per-tenant rate limit and a cached report. Show the SCAN pattern that finds all keys of one tenant, and explain how you'd delete a tenant without scanning at all.

docs.title: 05 · Hashes & Per-Field Expiry
docs.text: A hash is a key whose value is a small map from field names to string values. It's the natural shape for an object, such as a user profile, a product, a shopping cart or a feature-flag set. You can read or change one field without touching the rest, and since Redis 7.4 each field can even have its own expiry.

docs.title: The basics
docs.text:
127.0.0.1:6379> HSET user:1042 name "Ana Lima" email ana@example.com plan free logins 0
(integer) 4
127.0.0.1:6379> HGET user:1042 email
"ana@example.com"
127.0.0.1:6379> HMGET user:1042 name plan missing
1) "Ana Lima"
2) "free"
3) (nil)
127.0.0.1:6379> HGETALL user:1042
1) "name"
2) "Ana Lima"
3) "email"
4) "ana@example.com"
5) "plan"
6) "free"
7) "logins"
8) "0"

HSET takes any number of field/value pairs and returns how many new fields it created. The old HMSET is just a deprecated alias. In RESP2, HGETALL returns a flat list of alternating fields and values (RESP3 returns a real map; see Level 1 · 02). The field order you see is not something you can rely on.

Updating:

127.0.0.1:6379> HINCRBY user:1042 logins 1
(integer) 1
127.0.0.1:6379> HSET user:1042 plan pro
(integer) 0
127.0.0.1:6379> HSETNX user:1042 plan enterprise
(integer) 0
127.0.0.1:6379> HSETNX user:1042 created 2026-10-13
(integer) 1

HSET … plan pro returned 0 because it updated an existing field rather than creating one. HSETNX writes a field only if it's absent, which is handy for "first seen" timestamps. HINCRBY and HINCRBYFLOAT are the per-field versions of the counters from Level 1 · 03, with the same atomicity.

Inspecting and removing:

127.0.0.1:6379> HLEN user:1042
(integer) 5
127.0.0.1:6379> HEXISTS user:1042 phone
(integer) 0
127.0.0.1:6379> HDEL user:1042 created phone
(integer) 1
127.0.0.1:6379> HSTRLEN user:1042 email
(integer) 15
127.0.0.1:6379> HKEYS user:1042
1) "name"
2) "email"
3) "plan"
4) "logins"
127.0.0.1:6379> HRANDFIELD user:1042 2 WITHVALUES
1) "email"
2) "ana@example.com"
3) "logins"
4) "1"

When the last field is removed, the key itself disappears. Redis never keeps empty collections around.

docs.title: Expiry: the whole key or single fields
docs.text:
EXPIRE works on a hash like any other key, and changing fields doesn't reset it:

127.0.0.1:6379> EXPIRE user:1042 60
(integer) 1
127.0.0.1:6379> HSET user:1042 plan team
(integer) 0
127.0.0.1:6379> TTL user:1042
(integer) 60

That differs from strings, where a plain SET clears the TTL, because HSET modifies the hash in place.

Per-field expiry arrived in Redis 7.4. HEXPIRE gives one or more fields a TTL in seconds (HPEXPIRE uses milliseconds). HTTL reads it back, with the same -1 for "no TTL" and -2 for "no such field":

127.0.0.1:6379> HSET cart:7 sku:pen 2 sku:ink 1 sku:pad 4
(integer) 3
127.0.0.1:6379> HEXPIRE cart:7 60 FIELDS 1 sku:ink
1) (integer) 1
127.0.0.1:6379> HTTL cart:7 FIELDS 3 sku:pen sku:ink sku:nope
1) (integer) -1
2) (integer) 60
3) (integer) -2
127.0.0.1:6379> HPERSIST cart:7 FIELDS 1 sku:ink
1) (integer) 1
127.0.0.1:6379> HTTL cart:7 FIELDS 1 sku:ink
1) (integer) -1

The FIELDS <count> part is required, and replies come back as an array with one result per field.

Redis 8.0 added commands that combine reading or writing with expiry, the same way GETEX and GETDEL do for strings:

127.0.0.1:6379> HSETEX otp:ana EX 300 FIELDS 1 code 482913
(integer) 1
127.0.0.1:6379> HTTL otp:ana FIELDS 1 code
1) (integer) 300
127.0.0.1:6379> HGETDEL otp:ana FIELDS 1 code
1) "482913"
127.0.0.1:6379> EXISTS otp:ana
(integer) 0
127.0.0.1:6379> HSET prefs:9 theme dark
(integer) 1
127.0.0.1:6379> HGETEX prefs:9 EX 3600 FIELDS 1 theme
1) "dark"
127.0.0.1:6379> HTTL prefs:9 FIELDS 1 theme
1) (integer) 3600
127.0.0.1:6379> TTL prefs:9
(integer) -1

HGETDEL reads a one-time code and removes it in one step, and because that was the only field, the key is gone. HGETEX slides one field's expiry forward while the key as a whole stays persistent (TTL is -1).

When a field expires, it disappears from the hash. When the last field expires, the key goes with it:

redis-cli HSET c a 1 b 2
redis-cli HPEXPIRE c 1500 FIELDS 1 a
sleep 2; redis-cli HGETALL c
redis-cli HPEXPIRE c 500 FIELDS 1 b
sleep 1; redis-cli EXISTS c

2
1
b
2
1
0

Where this helps: a hash of a user's active device tokens where each device expires on its own, a cart whose line items hold a reservation for 15 minutes, or a per-user rate-limit hash with one field per window. Before 7.4, each of those needed one key per field, or a cleanup job. On older servers and on other forks, check that the commands exist before designing around them.

docs.title: Hash or separate keys or a JSON string?
docs.text:
There are three common ways to store a user with five attributes:

  1. Five string keys: user:42:name, user:42:email, …
  2. One string containing JSON.
  3. One hash with five fields.

This script stores 100,000 users each way and measures used_memory per user:

import redis, json
r = redis.Redis()
N = 100_000
fields = lambda i: {"name": f"User {i}", "email": f"user{i}@example.com",
                    "plan": "free", "logins": str(i % 50), "country": "PT"}

def measure(label, write):
    r.flushall(); base = r.info("memory")["used_memory"]
    p = r.pipeline(transaction=False)
    for i in range(N):
        write(p, i)
        if i % 5000 == 0: p.execute()
    p.execute()
    per = (r.info("memory")["used_memory"] - base) / N
    print(f"{label:34} {per:6.0f} bytes/user  keys={r.dbsize()}")

measure("5 string keys per user", lambda p, i: p.mset({f"user:{i}:{k}": v for k, v in fields(i).items()}))
measure("1 JSON string per user", lambda p, i: p.set(f"user:{i}", json.dumps(fields(i))))
measure("1 hash per user (listpack)", lambda p, i: p.hset(f"user:{i}", mapping=fields(i)))
r.config_set("hash-max-listpack-entries", 0)      # force the big-hash encoding
measure("1 hash per user (hashtable)", lambda p, i: p.hset(f"user:{i}", mapping=fields(i)))
r.config_set("hash-max-listpack-entries", 512)

5 string keys per user                327 bytes/user  keys=500000
1 JSON string per user                160 bytes/user  keys=100000
1 hash per user (listpack)            143 bytes/user  keys=100000
1 hash per user (hashtable)           319 bytes/user  keys=100000

A small hash was the most compact option, smaller even than JSON (which repeats quotes and braces), and less than half the size of five separate keys. The last row shows where that saving comes from: force the same hash into its general-purpose encoding and it costs almost as much as separate keys.

Beyond memory, the trade-offs look like this:

Separate keys JSON string Hash Read one attribute GET fetch and parse all of it HGET Update one attribute atomically SET needs a script or WATCH HSET / HINCRBY TTL granularity per attribute whole object whole key, or per field (7.4+) Nested data no yes no (one level, values are strings)

A hash is the default for flat objects. Use a JSON string, or the JSON type from Level 3 · 08, when the data is nested and you always read it whole.

docs.title: How It Actually Works
docs.text:
A hash has two internal encodings:

127.0.0.1:6379> OBJECT ENCODING user:1042
"listpack"

redis-cli CONFIG GET 'hash-max-listpack*'

hash-max-listpack-entries
512
hash-max-listpack-value
64

While a hash has at most hash-max-listpack-entries fields and every field and value is at most hash-max-listpack-value bytes, Redis stores it as a listpack: one contiguous block of memory with fields and values laid out one after another, each with a tiny length header. There are no pointers, no per-entry allocations and no hash table. Lookup is a linear scan, which is fast for a few hundred short entries that sit in one or two CPU cache lines. Once either limit is exceeded, Redis converts the hash to a real hash table (hashtable encoding). The conversion is one-way: deleting fields later doesn't shrink it back. On this 8.10 build the entries limit defaults to 512; older releases used 128, so check yours.

Per-field TTLs need extra metadata. As soon as a field gets an expiry, a small hash switches to a listpackex encoding that stores expiry times alongside the entries:

listpack      (before HPEXPIRE)
listpackex    (after)

Expired fields are removed the same two ways expired keys are: lazily, when the hash is accessed, and actively, by the background expiry cycle, which tracks hashes that contain fields with TTLs.

The separate-keys layout costs more because every key pays for an entry in the global keyspace table, a key string, a value object and allocator rounding. That's the ~100 bytes of overhead from Level 1 · 01, paid five times per user instead of once.

docs.title: Common mistakes
docs.text:
• One giant hash for everything (HSET users <id> <json> for ten million users). You lose per-object expiry (unless you use field TTLs), the hash outgrows listpack, HGETALL becomes a blocking O(N) call, and in Cluster the whole thing lives on one node. Use one hash per object.
  • HGETALL on big hashes in hot paths. Read the fields you need with HMGET, or iterate with HSCAN.
  • Expecting nested values. Field values are strings. HSET user:1 address "{…}" stores JSON text you'll have to parse yourself.
  • Assuming HSET resets the key's TTL the way SET does on strings. It doesn't, and a hash that should expire on every write needs an explicit EXPIRE.
  • Raising the listpack limits blindly. Bigger listpacks save memory but make every access a longer linear scan. Measure with your real field counts.
  • Using HEXPIRE without the FIELDS n count, or forgetting that it returns an array of per-field results.

docs.title: Exercise
docs.text:
1. Model a product with name, price in cents, stock and a "views" counter. Write the commands for: show the product, record a view, and reserve 2 units, where the last one must fail if stock would go below zero. Which of these can a plain hash command do atomically, and which needs something more (Level 2 · 08–09)?
  2. Store a user's logged-in devices in one hash (devices:<user>, field = device id, value = last-seen time). Give each device a 30-day field TTL that's refreshed on every request with HGETEX. Demonstrate with 2-second TTLs that devices drop off independently.
  3. Rerun the memory script with 20 fields per user, then 600 fields per user. Where does the hash stop being the smallest option, and why?
  4. Use OBJECT ENCODING to show a hash converting from listpack to hashtable when one value exceeds 64 bytes. Delete that field. Does the encoding change back?

docs.title: 06 · Lists: Queues, Stacks & Blocking Pops
docs.text: A Redis list is an ordered sequence of strings that you can push onto and pop from at either end. Those end operations are cheap no matter how long the list is, which makes lists a natural fit for queues, stacks and "most recent N" logs. Lists also have a feature that plain data structures don't: a client can block on an empty list and wake up the instant something is pushed. That's what makes a list a working message queue.

docs.title: Push, range, pop
docs.text:
127.0.0.1:6379> RPUSH jobs j1 j2 j3
(integer) 3
127.0.0.1:6379> LPUSH jobs j0
(integer) 4
127.0.0.1:6379> LRANGE jobs 0 -1
1) "j0"
2) "j1"
3) "j2"
4) "j3"
127.0.0.1:6379> LLEN jobs
(integer) 4

L and R mean left (head) and right (tail). Pushes return the new length. LRANGE takes inclusive indexes, and negative indexes count from the end, so 0 -1 means "everything". Popping:

127.0.0.1:6379> LPOP jobs
"j0"
127.0.0.1:6379> RPOP jobs
"j3"
127.0.0.1:6379> LPOP jobs 5
1) "j1"
2) "j2"
127.0.0.1:6379> LPOP jobs
(nil)
127.0.0.1:6379> EXISTS jobs
(integer) 0

LPOP key count pops up to count items at once (Redis 6.2+). Once the last item is popped, the key no longer exists.

The two ends give you two disciplines:

  • Queue (FIFO): RPUSH to enqueue, LPOP to dequeue (or LPUSH + RPOP).
  • Stack (LIFO): LPUSH and LPOP on the same end.

docs.title: Capped lists: "the last N things"
docs.text:
Activity feeds, recent searches and recent log lines all want the newest N items and nothing older. Push, then trim:

127.0.0.1:6379> LPUSH recent:ana a1 a2 a3 a4 a5 a6
(integer) 6
127.0.0.1:6379> LTRIM recent:ana 0 2
OK
127.0.0.1:6379> LRANGE recent:ana 0 -1
1) "a6"
2) "a5"
3) "a4"

LPUSH with several values pushes them one at a time from left to right, so the last argument ends up at the head. LTRIM 0 2 keeps only indexes 0 to 2. In an application you'd send LPUSH and LTRIM together in a pipeline or transaction on every write. The list then never grows beyond N, and trimming one extra element each time is cheap.

docs.title: Working in the middle (carefully)
docs.text:
127.0.0.1:6379> LINDEX recent:ana -1
"a4"
127.0.0.1:6379> LPOS recent:ana a5
(integer) 1
127.0.0.1:6379> LINSERT recent:ana BEFORE a5 x
(integer) 4
127.0.0.1:6379> LSET recent:ana 0 a6!
OK
127.0.0.1:6379> LRANGE recent:ana 0 -1
1) "a6!"
2) "x"
3) "a5"
4) "a4"
127.0.0.1:6379> LREM recent:ana 0 x
(integer) 1

These commands work, but they all have to find a position. LREM key count value removes up to count occurrences (0 means all of them), and it has to scan the list to find them. How much does that matter? This script builds a 2-million-item list and times reads at different positions:

import redis, time
r = redis.Redis()
p = r.pipeline(transaction=False)
for i in range(0, 2_000_000, 1000):
    p.rpush("big:list", *[f"item-{j}" for j in range(i, i + 1000)])
p.execute()
print("LLEN", r.llen("big:list"), "encoding", r.object("encoding", "big:list"))
for idx in (0, -1, 1_000_000):
    t = time.perf_counter()
    for _ in range(200): r.lindex("big:list", idx)
    print(f"LINDEX {idx:>9}: {(time.perf_counter()-t)/200*1e6:7.1f} us per call")
t = time.perf_counter()
for _ in range(200): r.lpos("big:list", "item-1999999")
print(f"LPOS last item:   {(time.perf_counter()-t)/200*1e6:7.1f} us per call")

LLEN 2000000 encoding b'quicklist'
LINDEX         0:   115.1 us per call
LINDEX        -1:   111.3 us per call
LINDEX   1000000:   114.8 us per call
LPOS last item:   23403.8 us per call

Two lessons are in those numbers. First, LINDEX in the middle of 2 million items was no slower than at the ends. Each call was dominated by the client round trip, because the list is stored in chunks that know their own size and the server skips whole chunks to reach an index (see below). The documentation calls LINDEX O(N), and it is, but N here is effectively the number of chunks. Second, LPOS had to compare every element. It took 23 ms, and the server could do nothing else during that time. Searching a list by value is a linear scan. If you need "is X in here?" or "remove X" on large collections, you want a set or a sorted set.

docs.title: Blocking pops: a real work queue
docs.text:
A worker that polls an empty queue in a loop with LPOP either burns CPU and network or adds latency by sleeping. BLPOP and BRPOP solve that by blocking until there's something to pop, or until a timeout runs out:

127.0.0.1:6379> BLPOP q:nothing 1
(nil)
(1.06s)

With a timeout of 1 second and nothing pushed, it returned (nil) after a second. Here are three workers blocked on the same queue while a producer pushes six tasks, 100 ms apart:

import redis, threading, time
r = redis.Redis(decode_responses=True)
got = []

def worker(name):
    c = redis.Redis(decode_responses=True)       # one connection per blocked worker
    while True:
        item = c.blpop(["tasks"], timeout=2)
        if item is None: return
        _, payload = item
        task, sent = payload.split("|")
        got.append((name, task, (time.time() - float(sent)) * 1000))

ws = [threading.Thread(target=worker, args=(f"w{i}",)) for i in range(3)]
for w in ws: w.start()
time.sleep(0.3)
for i in range(6):
    r.rpush("tasks", f"task{i}|{time.time()}"); time.sleep(0.1)
for w in ws: w.join()
for name, task, ms in got: print(f"{task} -> {name}  waited {ms:.2f} ms")

task0 -> w2  waited 2.04 ms
task1 -> w1  waited 2.08 ms
task2 -> w0  waited 1.00 ms
task3 -> w2  waited 1.31 ms
task4 -> w1  waited 1.27 ms
task5 -> w0  waited 1.40 ms

Each task went to exactly one worker, about a millisecond after it was pushed (most of that is Python thread scheduling in this test). The workers took turns: Redis serves blocked clients in the order they started waiting, and a worker that just finished a task rejoins the back of the line.

A few rules for blocking commands:

  • A blocked connection can't be used for anything else. Give each blocking worker its own connection, not one shared from a pool that other code also uses.
  • BLPOP accepts several keys and pops from the first non-empty one in the order listed, which gives you simple priority queues: BLPOP q:high q:normal q:low 5.
  • Use a finite timeout and loop, so a worker notices shutdown signals and dead connections.
  • LMPOP / BLMPOP (Redis 7.0+) pop several items from the first non-empty of several lists:
127.0.0.1:6379> LMPOP 2 q:empty q:pending LEFT COUNT 2
1) "q:pending"
2) 1) "t2"
   2) "t3"

docs.title: The problem with pop: what if the worker dies?
docs.text:
BLPOP removes the task from Redis the moment it's delivered. If the worker crashes before finishing, the task is gone. Nobody will ever retry it. LMOVE (and its blocking twin BLMOVE) pops from one list and pushes to another atomically, so a task is never "in flight" without being stored somewhere:

127.0.0.1:6379> RPUSH q:pending t1 t2 t3
(integer) 3
127.0.0.1:6379> LMOVE q:pending q:processing LEFT RIGHT
"t1"
127.0.0.1:6379> LRANGE q:processing 0 -1
1) "t1"
127.0.0.1:6379> LREM q:processing 1 t1
(integer) 1

The worker moves a task into q:processing, does the work, then removes it with LREM. If the worker dies, the task is still sitting in q:processing, where a reaper process can find it and push it back. Level 3 · 07 builds that reliable queue properly (one processing list per worker, visibility timeouts, retries, dead letters) and compares it with Redis Streams, which have acknowledgement built in.

docs.title: How It Actually Works
docs.text:
Lists use an encoding called quicklist for anything but the smallest lists: a doubly linked list of nodes, each holding a listpack, which is a compact block of several elements. Small lists are a single listpack with no linked list at all. (q:pending printed (nil) for its encoding above only because the key had already been emptied and deleted.)

redis-cli CONFIG GET 'list-*'

list-max-ziplist-size
-2
list-max-listpack-size
-2
list-compress-depth
0

(list-max-ziplist-size is the older name of the same setting, kept as an alias.) A negative list-max-listpack-size limits each node by bytes: -2 means 8 KB per node. list-compress-depth can LZF-compress interior nodes and leave depth nodes uncompressed at each end, which helps for long lists where you only touch the ends. It's off (0) by default.

This layout is why push and pop at the ends are O(1): they touch only the head or tail node. It's also why LINDEX in the middle was fast. Each node records how many elements it holds, so the server walks node by node, skipping hundreds of short elements at a time, and then scans within one node.
