LPOS and LREM have to compare values, though, so they visit every element.

Blocking works without any thread waiting. When BLPOP finds all its keys empty, Redis marks the client as blocked, records which keys it's waiting for in a dictionary (key → queue of blocked clients), and simply stops reading its commands. When a later command pushes to one of those keys, Redis notes that the key is "ready". After that command finishes, it serves the waiting clients in FIFO order, popping on their behalf and writing the replies. The timeout is checked by the periodic server cron. All of it happens on the same single command thread.

docs.title: Common mistakes
docs.text:
• Treating a list as a set. LPOS, LREM and "check before push" are O(N) scans and race-prone. Use a set or sorted set for membership.
  • Unbounded lists. A log or feed list with no LTRIM grows until memory runs out. Pair every push with a trim, or use a stream with MAXLEN (Level 2 · 05).
  • BLPOP on a shared pooled connection. It blocks that connection, and other code waiting for it stalls.
  • Timeout 0 (block forever) in workers you need to stop gracefully. Use a few seconds and loop.
  • Losing tasks on crash with plain BLPOP. Use BLMOVE into a processing list, or streams with consumer groups.
  • Reading a whole huge list with LRANGE 0 -1. Page through it with bounded ranges.

docs.title: Exercise
docs.text:
1. Build a "recent searches" feature: keep the last 10 distinct searches per user, newest first. Searching for something already in the list should move it to the front rather than duplicate it. Which commands do you need, and why should they run in one MULTI block?
  2. Write a priority worker that serves q:high before q:low with one BLPOP. Push 5 low and 5 high tasks before starting it, and show that all the high ones come out first.
  3. Kill a worker (Ctrl-C) between BLMOVE and LREM. Write a reaper that finds stranded tasks in the processing list and moves them back to pending. What goes wrong if the reaper runs while a healthy worker is still working on a task?
  4. Repeat the LPOS timing with lists of 100k, 1M and 4M items and plot the time against the length.

docs.title: 07 · Sets: Membership, Set Algebra & Random Picks
docs.text: A set is an unordered collection of unique strings. Adding a member that's already there does nothing, checking membership is O(1), and Redis can intersect, union and subtract sets on the server. That makes sets the right tool for tags, "who liked this", deduplicating events, matching skills to jobs, and anywhere you'd otherwise write "check if it's already in the list" by hand.

docs.title: Adding, checking, removing
docs.text:
127.0.0.1:6379> SADD post:1:tags redis database cache
(integer) 3
127.0.0.1:6379> SADD post:1:tags redis nosql
(integer) 1
127.0.0.1:6379> SMEMBERS post:1:tags
1) "redis"
2) "database"
3) "cache"
4) "nosql"
127.0.0.1:6379> SISMEMBER post:1:tags cache
(integer) 1
127.0.0.1:6379> SMISMEMBER post:1:tags cache sql nosql
1) (integer) 1
2) (integer) 0
3) (integer) 1
127.0.0.1:6379> SCARD post:1:tags
(integer) 4
127.0.0.1:6379> SREM post:1:tags nosql
(integer) 1

SADD returns how many members were new: the second call added only nosql because redis was already there. That return value is useful on its own. SADD seen:emails <message-id> returning 1 means "first time we've seen this message, process it", and 0 means "duplicate, skip it". It's an atomic dedupe check in a single command.

SMISMEMBER checks several candidates in one round trip. SCARD is O(1) because the count is stored, not computed.

docs.title: Set algebra on the server
docs.text:
Two candidates and a job:

127.0.0.1:6379> SADD user:ana:skills python redis sql docker
(integer) 4
127.0.0.1:6379> SADD user:ben:skills go redis kubernetes docker
(integer) 4
127.0.0.1:6379> SADD job:42:needs redis docker kubernetes
(integer) 3

What each candidate has in common with the job, and what Ana is missing:

127.0.0.1:6379> SINTER user:ana:skills job:42:needs
1) "redis"
2) "docker"
127.0.0.1:6379> SINTER user:ben:skills job:42:needs
1) "redis"
2) "docker"
3) "kubernetes"
127.0.0.1:6379> SDIFF job:42:needs user:ana:skills
1) "kubernetes"
127.0.0.1:6379> SUNION user:ana:skills user:ben:skills
1) "redis"
2) "sql"
3) "python"
4) "go"
5) "docker"
6) "kubernetes"

SDIFF A B means "in A but not in B", so the order of the arguments matters. When you only need a count, use SINTERCARD (Redis 7.0+), which doesn't build or send the members. Its LIMIT stops early once it has found enough:

127.0.0.1:6379> SINTERCARD 2 user:ben:skills job:42:needs
(integer) 3
127.0.0.1:6379> SINTERCARD 2 user:ben:skills job:42:needs LIMIT 2
(integer) 2

"Does this candidate match at least 2 of the requirements?" is a LIMIT 2 question. The *STORE variants write the result into a new key instead of returning it, which is useful for caching an expensive computation or for chaining operations:

127.0.0.1:6379> SUNIONSTORE team:skills user:ana:skills user:ben:skills
(integer) 6

docs.title: Random members
docs.text:
127.0.0.1:6379> SADD raffle alice bob carol dave erin
(integer) 5
127.0.0.1:6379> SRANDMEMBER raffle 2
1) "alice"
2) "dave"
127.0.0.1:6379> SRANDMEMBER raffle -4
1) "bob"
2) "bob"
3) "dave"
4) "alice"
127.0.0.1:6379> SPOP raffle
"erin"
127.0.0.1:6379> SCARD raffle
(integer) 4
127.0.0.1:6379> SMOVE raffle winners bob
(integer) 1
  • SRANDMEMBER key n with a positive n returns up to n distinct members and leaves the set alone.
  • With a negative n it returns exactly |n| members and may repeat (bob twice above), like sampling with replacement.
  • SPOP removes and returns random members. It's the atomic "draw a winner", and two clients can never draw the same one.
  • SMOVE moves a member from one set to another atomically.

Randomness here is good enough for picking samples or shuffling work. It isn't a cryptographic or audited lottery.

docs.title: How expensive is set algebra?
docs.text:
Two sets of a million visitor IDs each (half overlapping) and a 4-member vip set, timed from Python:

import redis, time
r = redis.Redis()
p = r.pipeline(transaction=False)
for i in range(0, 1_000_000, 5000):
    p.sadd("visitors:mon", *range(i, i + 5000))
    p.sadd("visitors:tue", *range(i + 500_000, i + 505_000))
p.execute()
r.sadd("vip", 7, 123456, 750000, 2_000_000)

def t(label, fn):
    s = time.perf_counter(); res = fn()
    print(f"{label:46} {(time.perf_counter()-s)*1000:8.2f} ms -> {res}")

t("SINTER vip visitors:mon visitors:tue (size)", lambda: len(r.sinter("vip", "visitors:mon", "visitors:tue")))
t("SINTER visitors:mon visitors:tue vip (size)", lambda: len(r.sinter("visitors:mon", "visitors:tue", "vip")))
t("SINTERCARD 2 visitors:mon visitors:tue", lambda: r.sintercard(2, ["visitors:mon", "visitors:tue"]))
t("SINTERSTORE both visitors:mon visitors:tue", lambda: r.sinterstore("both", ["visitors:mon", "visitors:tue"]))
t("SUNIONSTORE either visitors:mon visitors:tue", lambda: r.sunionstore("either", ["visitors:mon", "visitors:tue"]))
t("SISMEMBER visitors:mon 999999", lambda: r.sismember("visitors:mon", 999999))

SINTER vip visitors:mon visitors:tue (size)        0.23 ms -> 1
SINTER visitors:mon visitors:tue vip (size)        0.21 ms -> 1
SINTERCARD 2 visitors:mon visitors:tue           131.70 ms -> 500000
SINTERSTORE both visitors:mon visitors:tue       232.29 ms -> 500000
SUNIONSTORE either visitors:mon visitors:tue     337.91 ms -> 1500000
SISMEMBER visitors:mon 999999                      0.33 ms -> 1
  • An intersection that includes a small set is fast regardless of argument order (0.2 ms both ways): Redis sorts the inputs by size and iterates the smallest one, probing the others.
  • Intersecting two large sets costs time proportional to the smaller one. That's 132 ms just to count 500,000 common members, and the server was busy for all of it.
  • A union has to touch every member of every input. Storing 1.5 million members took 338 ms.

Those numbers are fine for an analytics job at 3 a.m. and a problem on a hot request path. For big sets, run the algebra rarely and cache the result with *STORE + EXPIRE, keep the sets smaller (per day rather than per year), or switch to an approximate structure. HyperLogLog (Level 2 · 03) counts unique visitors in 12 KB instead of the 32 MB that one of these sets occupies:

memory visitors:mon 32277585 bytes

docs.title: How It Actually Works
docs.text:
Sets have three encodings:

127.0.0.1:6379> SADD ids 1 2 3 1000
(integer) 4
127.0.0.1:6379> OBJECT ENCODING ids
"intset"
127.0.0.1:6379> SADD ids hello
(integer) 1
127.0.0.1:6379> OBJECT ENCODING ids
"listpack"
127.0.0.1:6379> OBJECT ENCODING user:ana:skills
"listpack"

The limits, from CONFIG GET 'set-max*' (shown as name and value pairs):

set-max-listpack-entries   128
set-max-listpack-value     64
set-max-intset-entries     512
  • intset — when every member is an integer and there are at most 512 of them, the set is a sorted array of integers using the smallest width that fits (16, 32 or 64 bits). Membership is a binary search. It's extremely compact: 500 integers took 1,032 bytes.
  • listpack — small sets of short strings (at most 128 members of at most 64 bytes each) are a flat listpack with linear search, as with small hashes.
  • hashtable — anything bigger is a hash table whose keys are the members and whose values are empty. That's O(1) membership, but every member pays for a table entry and its own string: 500 short strings took 15,567 bytes, fifteen times the intset.

Conversions go one way, towards the general encoding, as soon as a limit is crossed. Adding hello to an intset converted it on the spot.

SINTER sorts its inputs by cardinality, then for each member of the smallest set checks membership in each of the others, stopping at the first miss. That's why its cost depends on the smallest set. SUNION and SDIFF have to walk all of the inputs. SRANDMEMBER with a positive count picks distinct members with a strategy that depends on how large the count is relative to the set. For small counts it picks random buckets, so the distribution is close to uniform but not exactly uniform.

docs.title: Common mistakes
docs.text:
• SMEMBERS on a huge set. It's O(N) and sends everything. Use SSCAN to iterate, SCARD to count, SRANDMEMBER to sample.
  • Set algebra on million-member sets in request handlers. Precompute with *STORE and cache it, or use smaller per-period sets.
  • Using a set when order matters. Sets are unordered. If you need "most recent" or "top", use a sorted set (next lesson).
  • Expecting SDIFF to be symmetric. SDIFF A B ≠ SDIFF B A.
  • Counting unique events forever in a set. It grows without bound. Use a TTL per period, or HyperLogLog when an approximate count is enough.
  • Storing IDs as strings like "id42" when plain integers would let small sets use the intset encoding.

docs.title: Exercise
docs.text:
1. Build a tag system: posts have tag sets, and each tag has a set of post IDs. Write commands to add a tag to a post (both directions), find posts tagged both redis and python, and find posts tagged redis but not beginner. Why should the two-direction update run inside MULTI?
  2. Use SADD as a dedupe filter for a stream of 100,000 event IDs where 10% are repeats. Process each event only when SADD returns 1, and confirm the processed count. How would you stop the dedupe set from growing forever?
  3. Make the timing script's vip set 100,000 members and rerun the first SINTER. How does the time scale with the smallest set?
  4. Find the point where a set of integers switches from intset to hashtable on your server, and record MEMORY USAGE just before and just after.

docs.title: 08 · Sorted Sets: Rankings, Ranges & Time Windows
docs.text: A sorted set (zset) is a set where every member has a numeric score, and members are kept ordered by score. You can ask "what's Ana's rank?", "who are the top 10?", "which members score between X and Y?" and "remove everything older than five minutes", and each of these is a logarithmic-time operation on a structure with millions of members. If you learn one Redis type beyond strings and hashes, make it this one. Leaderboards, sliding-window rate limiters, delayed job schedulers, time-ordered indexes and priority queues are all sorted sets underneath.

docs.title: Scores and order
docs.text:
127.0.0.1:6379> ZADD lb:week41 1200 ana 980 ben 1500 caro 980 dan
(integer) 4
127.0.0.1:6379> ZRANGE lb:week41 0 -1 WITHSCORES
1) "ben"
2) "980"
3) "dan"
4) "980"
5) "ana"
6) "1200"
7) "caro"
8) "1500"

ZADD takes score first, then member. That's the opposite of most mental models, so expect to get it backwards once. Order is ascending by score, and ties (ben and dan at 980) are broken by comparing the member strings byte by byte. That tie-break is deterministic but probably not what your game wants ("whoever got there first"). There's a fix in the exercises.

For a leaderboard you want the top first:

127.0.0.1:6379> ZRANGE lb:week41 0 2 REV WITHSCORES
1) "caro"
2) "1500"
3) "ana"
4) "1200"
5) "dan"
6) "980"

Since Redis 6.2, ZRANGE with REV, BYSCORE, BYLEX and LIMIT replaces the older family of ZREVRANGE, ZRANGEBYSCORE and so on. Those still work, but you only need to learn one command.

docs.title: Changing scores, reading ranks
docs.text:
127.0.0.1:6379> ZINCRBY lb:week41 50 ben
"1030"
127.0.0.1:6379> ZSCORE lb:week41 ben
"1030"
127.0.0.1:6379> ZMSCORE lb:week41 ana nobody
1) "1200"
2) (nil)
127.0.0.1:6379> ZREVRANK lb:week41 ana
(integer) 1
127.0.0.1:6379> ZREVRANK lb:week41 ana WITHSCORE
1) (integer) 1
2) "1200"
127.0.0.1:6379> ZCARD lb:week41
(integer) 4

Ranks are 0-based: Ana is second place, rank 1. ZRANK counts from the lowest score, ZREVRANK from the highest. The WITHSCORE option (7.2+) returns rank and score together, which is exactly what a "your position" widget needs, in one round trip.

docs.title: ZADD's flags
docs.text:
ZADD has flags that turn it into conditional updates:

127.0.0.1:6379> ZADD lb:week41 GT 1100 ana
(integer) 0
127.0.0.1:6379> ZADD lb:week41 GT 1300 ana
(integer) 0
127.0.0.1:6379> ZADD lb:week41 GT CH 1400 ana
(integer) 1
127.0.0.1:6379> ZADD lb:week41 NX 9999 ana
(integer) 0
127.0.0.1:6379> ZADD lb:week41 LT 1 eve
(integer) 1
127.0.0.1:6379> ZADD lb:week41 INCR 10 eve
"11"

Read those return values carefully:

  • GT 1100 didn't change anything, because 1100 isn't greater than Ana's 1200.
  • GT 1300 did update Ana to 1300, yet it returned 0. By default ZADD returns the number of members added, not changed. Add CH to count changes too, as the third line shows.
  • NX only adds new members and never updates existing ones. XX only updates.
  • GT and LT don't stop new members from being added: eve didn't exist, so LT 1 added her.
  • INCR makes ZADD behave like ZINCRBY and return the new score.

ZADD … GT is the "personal best" operation. Submit every game score and the set keeps each player's maximum, atomically, with no read first.

docs.title: Range queries
docs.text:
By score, with ( meaning exclusive and -inf/+inf meaning unbounded:

127.0.0.1:6379> ZCOUNT lb:week41 1000 +inf
(integer) 3
127.0.0.1:6379> ZRANGE lb:week41 1000 1500 BYSCORE WITHSCORES
1) "ben"
2) "1030"
3) "ana"
4) "1200"
5) "caro"
6) "1500"
127.0.0.1:6379> ZRANGE lb:week41 (1200 +inf BYSCORE
1) "caro"
127.0.0.1:6379> ZRANGE lb:week41 +inf -inf BYSCORE REV LIMIT 0 2
1) "caro"
2) "ana"

With REV the range bounds are given high-to-low (+inf -inf). LIMIT offset count pages through a range.

By member name, when every score is equal (usually 0), the order is lexicographic, and BYLEX gives you prefix search:

127.0.0.1:6379> ZADD names 0 banana 0 apple 0 cherry 0 apricot
(integer) 4
127.0.0.1:6379> ZRANGE names [ap (b BYLEX
1) "apple"
2) "apricot"

[ means inclusive and ( means exclusive. [ap (b means "from ap up to but not including b", i.e. every member starting with ap. That's a simple autocomplete index.

docs.title: Time as the score
docs.text:
Scores are 64-bit floats, and a Unix timestamp fits comfortably. Using time as the score turns a sorted set into a time index.

Delayed jobs. Schedule a job for later by scoring it with its due time. A poller grabs whatever is due:

127.0.0.1:6379> ZADD jobs:delayed 1791856000 send-email:1 1791855000 resize-img:7 1791859999 report:3
(integer) 3
127.0.0.1:6379> ZRANGE jobs:delayed -inf 1791856500 BYSCORE
1) "resize-img:7"
2) "send-email:1"
127.0.0.1:6379> ZPOPMIN jobs:delayed
1) "resize-img:7"
2) "1791855000"

ZPOPMIN atomically removes the lowest-scored member, so two pollers can't both take the same job. (A poller should check that the popped score is actually due and put it back if not. A Lua script does both in one step, as Level 2 · 09 shows.) BZPOPMIN blocks like BLPOP does.

Sliding windows. "How many requests did this IP make in the last 60 seconds?" Add each event scored by its time, drop everything older than the window, and count:

ZADD   rate:ip:203.0.113.7  <now_ms> <unique-request-id>
ZREMRANGEBYSCORE rate:ip:203.0.113.7 -inf <now_ms - 60000>
ZCARD  rate:ip:203.0.113.7

With three requests at 0 s, 30 s and 55 s and "now" at 70 s, the window starts at 10 s:

127.0.0.1:6379> ZADD rate:ip:203.0.113.7 1791856000000 req-a 1791856030000 req-b 1791856055000 req-c
(integer) 3
127.0.0.1:6379> ZREMRANGEBYSCORE rate:ip:203.0.113.7 -inf (1791856010000
(integer) 1
127.0.0.1:6379> ZCARD rate:ip:203.0.113.7
(integer) 2

The request at 0 s fell out of the window, and two remain.

Level 3 · 04 builds a correct rate limiter from this pattern and compares it with cheaper approximations.

docs.title: Combining sorted sets
docs.text:
Monthly totals from weekly boards, best single week, and players present in both weeks:

127.0.0.1:6379> ZADD lb:week42 300 ana 900 fred
(integer) 2
127.0.0.1:6379> ZUNIONSTORE lb:month 2 lb:week41 lb:week42 AGGREGATE SUM
(integer) 6
127.0.0.1:6379> ZRANGE lb:month 0 -1 REV WITHSCORES
 1) "ana"
 2) "1700"
 3) "caro"
 4) "1500"
 5) "ben"
 6) "1030"
 7) "dan"
 8) "980"
 9) "fred"
10) "900"
11) "eve"
12) "11"
127.0.0.1:6379> ZUNIONSTORE lb:best 2 lb:week41 lb:week42 AGGREGATE MAX
(integer) 6
127.0.0.1:6379> ZRANGE lb:best 0 0 REV WITHSCORES
1) "caro"
2) "1500"
127.0.0.1:6379> ZINTERSTORE lb:both 2 lb:week41 lb:week42 WEIGHTS 1 2
(integer) 1
127.0.0.1:6379> ZRANGE lb:both 0 -1 WITHSCORES
1) "ana"
2) "2000"

WEIGHTS multiplies each input's scores before aggregating: Ana's 1400 × 1 + 300 × 2 = 2000. AGGREGATE can be SUM (the default), MIN or MAX. ZRANGESTORE saves a slice, such as a cached top 3:

127.0.0.1:6379> ZRANGESTORE lb:top3 lb:month 0 2 REV
(integer) 3
127.0.0.1:6379> ZRANGE lb:top3 0 -1 WITHSCORES
1) "ben"
2) "1030"
3) "caro"
4) "1500"
5) "ana"
6) "1700"

The stored set is still ordered by score ascending, so read it back with REV for top-first.

docs.title: What it costs at a million members
docs.text:
import redis, time, random
r = redis.Redis()
random.seed(7)
p = r.pipeline(transaction=False)
for i in range(0, 1_000_000, 5000):
    p.zadd("lb:global", {f"player:{j}": random.randint(0, 1_000_000) for j in range(i, i + 5000)})
p.execute()
print("ZCARD", r.zcard("lb:global"), "encoding", r.object("encoding", "lb:global"),
      "memory", r.memory_usage("lb:global"))

def t(label, fn, n=500):
    s = time.perf_counter()
    for _ in range(n): res = fn()
    print(f"{label:40} {(time.perf_counter()-s)/n*1e6:8.1f} us  -> {str(res)[:60]}")

t("ZINCRBY (random player)", lambda: r.zincrby("lb:global", 5, f"player:{random.randrange(1_000_000)}"))
t("ZREVRANK player:4242", lambda: r.zrevrank("lb:global", "player:4242"))
t("ZRANGE top 10 REV", lambda: len(r.zrange("lb:global", 0, 9, desc=True)))
t("ZRANGE ranks 500000..500009", lambda: len(r.zrange("lb:global", 500000, 500009)))
t("ZCOUNT 400000..600000", lambda: r.zcount("lb:global", 400000, 600000))
t("ZRANGE BYSCORE 400000..600000 (all)", lambda: len(r.zrangebyscore("lb:global", 400000, 600000)), n=5)
t("echo baseline PING", lambda: r.ping())

ZCARD 1000000 encoding b'skiplist' memory 77722996
ZINCRBY (random player)                     137.5 us  -> 74390.0
ZREVRANK player:4242                        120.0 us  -> 954015
ZRANGE top 10 REV                           124.8 us  -> 10
ZRANGE ranks 500000..500009                 112.1 us  -> 10
ZCOUNT 400000..600000                       117.9 us  -> 200168
ZRANGE BYSCORE 400000..600000 (all)       27322.5 us  -> 200168
echo baseline PING                          110.3 us  -> True

Updating a score, getting a rank, reading ten entries from the middle and counting 200,000 members in a score range all cost about the same as a PING, so the server work is a few microseconds. Returning those 200,000 members took 27 ms, because that work is proportional to the output size. The rule for sorted sets: every lookup is O(log N), plus O(M) for the M members you return. Keep M small with LIMIT and paging.

The million-member set used 77.7 MB, about 78 bytes per member. That's more than a plain set, because each member is in two structures at once (see below).

docs.title: How It Actually Works
docs.text:
Small sorted sets (up to zset-max-listpack-entries, 128, members of up to 64 bytes) are a listpack of alternating member/score entries kept in score order, as lb:month showed. Inserting is a linear scan and a memmove, which is fast at that size and very compact.

Large sorted sets use two structures together:

  • a hash table from member to score, which makes ZSCORE and "does this member exist?" O(1);
  • a skip list ordered by (score, member). A skip list is a linked list where each node also has a random number of "express lane" pointers that skip ahead. Searching starts in the top lane and drops a level whenever the next hop would overshoot, which takes O(log N) steps on average.

Redis's skip list stores a span on every forward pointer, meaning how many nodes that pointer skips. Summing the spans along a search path gives a node's rank, which is how ZRANK is O(log N) rather than a count from the start, and how ZRANGE 500000 500009 jumps straight to rank 500,000. ZCOUNT finds the first and last node of the range and subtracts their ranks, so it never visits the 200,000 members in between.

ZINCRBY looks up the old score in the hash table, removes the node from the skip list, and reinserts it at its new position. If the new score keeps it in the same place, the node is updated in place.

Scores are IEEE-754 doubles, so integers are exact only up to 2^53. Millisecond timestamps are fine, but packing a big score and a timestamp into one number for tie-breaking can silently lose precision. Do the arithmetic before you rely on it.

docs.title: Common mistakes
docs.text:
• Swapping score and member in ZADD. It's ZADD key score member.
  • Reading ZADD's return value as "changed". Without CH it only counts additions.
  • Unbounded range reads (ZRANGE key 0 -1 on a million-member set). Use LIMIT, or count with ZCOUNT.
  • Ties resolved alphabetically when your product expects "first come first served". Encode a tie-breaker into the score, or keep a secondary structure.
  • Never trimming time-scored sets. Event windows need ZREMRANGEBYSCORE (or ZREMRANGEBYRANK) on every write.
  • Using float scores for money or exact counts beyond 2^53.
  • Forgetting that ZRANGESTORE output is ascending and then reading it back the wrong way round.

docs.title: Exercise
docs.text:
1. Build a game leaderboard where equal scores are ordered by who reached that score first. Hint: score = points × 10^10 + (10^10 − seconds since season start). Check the arithmetic stays below 2^53 for your maximum points.
  2. Implement "players near me": given a player, return the 5 above and 5 below them with ranks and scores, in two commands at most.
  3. Write a delayed-job poller with ZRANGE … BYSCORE LIMIT 0 10 followed by ZREM per job. Run two pollers at once and show that a job can be processed twice. Then fix it using ZREM's return value as the claim.
  4. Use a BYLEX sorted set to autocomplete 10,000 city names. Return the first 5 matches for a prefix, and make matching case-insensitive without losing the original spelling.

docs.title: 09 · Clients: redis-py & node-redis
docs.text:
Everything so far ran through redis-cli. Applications use a client library, and most production incidents blamed on "Redis" are really about how the client was configured: a new connection per request, a pool that's too small, a timeout that's too long, or an automatic retry that ran a write twice. This lesson uses the two most common libraries and measures each of those behaviours:

  • redis-py 8.1.0 (Python, with the optional hiredis parser 3.4.2): pip install redis hiredis
  • node-redis 6.3.0 (Node.js 26): npm install redis

(ioredis, at 6.0.0 on npm when this was written, is the other popular Node client. It wasn't used here.)

docs.title: redis-py: the basics
docs.text:
import redis

r = redis.Redis(host="127.0.0.1", port=6379, decode_responses=True)
print(r.hgetall("user:1"))
print(r.zrange("lb", 0, -1, withscores=True))

raw = redis.Redis()
print(raw.get("greeting"))

{'name': 'Ana', 'plan': 'pro', 'logins': '4'}
[('ana', 10.0), ('ben', 25.0)]
b'hello'

Without decode_responses=True you get bytes, which is correct for binary values but noisy for text. Decide per client; you can keep one decoding client and one raw client. Hash values come back as strings ('4') because Redis stores strings, while sorted-set scores come back as floats because the library knows that command returns numbers.

Errors from the server raise exceptions:

try:
    r.incr("user:1")
except redis.ResponseError as e:
    print("ResponseError:", e)

ResponseError: WRONGTYPE Operation against a key holding the wrong kind of value

docs.title: What redis-py 8 sends when it connects
docs.text:
MONITOR captured the session above:

"HELLO" "3"
"CLIENT" "SETINFO" "LIB-NAME" "redis-py"
"CLIENT" "SETINFO" "LIB-VER" "8.1.0"
"HGETALL" "user:1"
"ZRANGE" "lb" "0" "-1" "WITHSCORES"

redis-py 8 negotiates RESP3 by default. In the library source, DEFAULT_RESP_VERSION = 3, together with a legacy_responses=True default that converts results back to the shapes older code expects. That's why hgetall still gives a dict and zrange gives a list of tuples. If you upgrade from redis-py 5 or 6 and see different result types, or if you run against a proxy or an old server that doesn't support HELLO, the protocol=2 and legacy_responses arguments are where to look. Check your installed version's changelog. These defaults are recent and may change again.

docs.title: One client, many requests
docs.text:
Every redis.Redis() object owns a connection pool. The cost of getting that wrong:

import redis, time
N = 2000

t = time.perf_counter()
for i in range(N):
    c = redis.Redis(); c.get("greeting"); c.close()
print(f"new client per request : {(time.perf_counter()-t)/N*1e6:7.1f} us/request")

shared = redis.Redis()
t = time.perf_counter()
for i in range(N):
    shared.get("greeting")
print(f"one shared client      : {(time.perf_counter()-t)/N*1e6:7.1f} us/request")

new client per request :  1940.6 us/request
one shared client      :   122.9 us/request

A new client per request was 16 times slower on loopback. Each one opened a TCP connection, sent HELLO and CLIENT SETINFO, ran one GET and then tore everything down. Over a real network, and with TLS or AUTH added, the difference grows. It also churns connections on the server and in the OS. Create the client once per process (at module level or in your app's startup) and share it. The redis-py client is thread-safe: each command borrows a connection from the pool and returns it.

The pool's defaults, printed from that client (trimmed):

socket_timeout=5, socket_connect_timeout=5, retry=<redis.retry.Retry ...>, socket_keepalive=True,
protocol=None, legacy_responses=True, host=localhost, port=6379

docs.title: Timeouts and retries: what actually happens
docs.text:
With nothing listening on port 6411:

dead = redis.Redis(port=6411)
t = time.perf_counter()
try:
    dead.ping()
except redis.ConnectionError as e:
    print(f"ConnectionError after {time.perf_counter()-t:.2f}s: {str(e)[:70]}")

ConnectionError after 4.43s: Error 61 connecting to localhost:6411. Connection refused.

"Connection refused" is instant at the TCP level, yet the call took 4.4 seconds to fail. The client's default retry policy is behind that:

r0 = redis.Redis()
retry = r0.get_retry()
print(retry._retries, type(retry._backoff).__name__, retry._supported_errors)

10 ExponentialWithJitterBackoff (<class 'redis.exceptions.ConnectionError'>, <class 'redis.exceptions.TimeoutError'>, <class 'TimeoutError'>)

redis-py 8.1 retries 10 times with exponential backoff on connection errors and on timeouts. For reads that's convenient. For writes it's a hazard. This test blocks the server for 1 second from another connection (a stand-in for any slow command or a brief network stall), while a client with a 0.2 s socket timeout runs one INCR:

import redis, threading, time
r0 = redis.Redis(); r0.delete("k")
fast = redis.Redis(socket_timeout=0.2); fast.ping()

def block():
    redis.Redis().execute_command("DEBUG", "SLEEP", "1")   # lab server only

th = threading.Thread(target=block); th.start(); time.sleep(0.05)
print("INCR returned", fast.incr("k"))
th.join(); time.sleep(0.3)
print("k is now", r0.get("k"))

INCR returned 2
k is now b'2'

One INCR call, applied twice. The first INCR reached the server and sat in the queue behind the sleep. The client timed out, reconnected and sent INCR again. When the server woke up it executed both. Repeat with retries disabled:

noretry = redis.Redis(socket_timeout=0.2,
                      retry=redis.retry.Retry(redis.backoff.NoBackoff(), 0))

no-retry client: TimeoutError Timeout reading from socket
k is now b'1'

Now the caller gets an error, and the increment still happened. That's the fundamental ambiguity of a timeout: you don't know whether the command ran. Practical consequences:

  • Choose the retry policy deliberately. Retries are safe for idempotent commands (GET, SET with a fixed value, SADD, ZADD GT) and unsafe for INCR, LPUSH, RPOPLPUSH and the like.
  • Make important writes idempotent: SET payment:<id> … NX, SADD processed <id>, or a Lua script that checks a request ID before applying a change (Level 2 · 09).
  • Set socket_timeout from your latency budget. A 5-second default on a request path means a stalled Redis turns into 5-second page loads, before any retries.

docs.title: Pipelines and transactions in redis-py
docs.text:
pipe = r.pipeline()                       # transaction=True by default
pipe.incr("visits").expire("visits", 60).get("visits")
print(pipe.execute())

pipe = r.pipeline(transaction=False)
pipe.incr("visits").get("visits")
print(pipe.execute())

[1, True, '1']
[2, '2']

What went over the wire:

"MULTI"
"INCRBY" "visits" "1"
"EXPIRE" "visits" "60"
"GET" "visits"
"EXEC"
"INCRBY" "visits" "1"
"GET" "visits"

r.pipeline() wraps the batch in MULTI/EXEC by default, so it's a transaction as well as a pipeline. That's usually harmless, but it isn't free, and in Redis Cluster a transaction requires all keys to be in one slot. Use transaction=False when you just want fewer round trips. Level 2 · 08 explains what MULTI does and doesn't guarantee.

docs.title: asyncio
docs.text:
redis.asyncio has the same API with await:

import asyncio, time
import redis.asyncio as aredis

async def main():
    r = aredis.Redis(decode_responses=True)
    await r.set("greeting", "hello")
    t = time.perf_counter()
    for i in range(1000):
        await r.get("greeting")
    print(f"1000 awaited one by one : {(time.perf_counter()-t)*1000:5.0f} ms")
    try:
        await asyncio.gather(*(r.get("greeting") for _ in range(1000)))
    except Exception as e:
        print("gather of 1000 on default pool:", type(e).__name__, e)
    await r.aclose()

    pool = aredis.BlockingConnectionPool(max_connections=20, timeout=5)
    r = aredis.Redis(connection_pool=pool)
    t = time.perf_counter()
    await asyncio.gather(*(r.get("greeting") for _ in range(1000)))
    print(f"1000 gathered, 20 conns : {(time.perf_counter()-t)*1000:5.0f} ms")
    t = time.perf_counter()
    async with r.pipeline(transaction=False) as p:
        for _ in range(1000): p.get("greeting")
        await p.execute()
    print(f"1000 in one pipeline    : {(time.perf_counter()-t)*1000:5.0f} ms")
    await r.aclose()

asyncio.run(main())

1000 awaited one by one :   139 ms
gather of 1000 on default pool: MaxConnectionsError Too many connections
1000 gathered, 20 conns :    75 ms
1000 in one pipeline    :     6 ms

Firing 1,000 commands at once on the default pool failed. Each concurrent command needs its own connection, and the default pool caps out at 100 (max_connections = max_connections or 100 in the source) and raises rather than waits. A BlockingConnectionPool makes callers queue for a connection instead, and 20 connections handled the burst in 75 ms. The pipeline did the same work in 6 ms over one connection. Under load, pick a pool size on purpose and prefer pipelines for batches.

docs.title: node-redis 6
docs.text:
import { createClient } from 'redis';

const client = createClient({ url: 'redis://127.0.0.1:6379' });
client.on('error', (err) => console.error('redis error:', err.message));
await client.connect();

await client.set('greeting', 'hello', { EX: 60 });
console.log(await client.get('greeting'));
await client.hSet('user:1', { name: 'Ana', plan: 'pro', logins: 3 });
console.log(await client.hGetAll('user:1'));
console.log(await client.hIncrBy('user:1', 'logins', 1));
await client.zAdd('lb', [{ score: 10, value: 'ana' }, { score: 25, value: 'ben' }]);
console.log(await client.zRangeWithScores('lb', 0, -1, { REV: true }));
console.log(await client.get('nope'));

const replies = await client.multi()
  .incr('counter')
  .expire('counter', 60)
  .get('counter')
  .exec();
console.log('multi:', replies);

const [a, b, c] = await Promise.all([client.incr('x'), client.incr('x'), client.incr('x')]);
console.log('parallel incr:', a, b, c);

try { await client.incr('greeting'); }
catch (e) { console.log('error class:', e.constructor.name, '-', e.message); }

console.log(await client.sendCommand(['OBJECT', 'ENCODING', 'user:1']));
await client.close();

hello
{ name: 'Ana', plan: 'pro', logins: '3' }
4
[ { value: 'ben', score: 25 }, { value: 'ana', score: 10 } ]
null
multi: [ 1, 1, '1' ]
parallel incr: 1 2 3
error class: SimpleError - ERR value is not an integer or out of range
listpack

Things to notice:

  • Method names are camelCase versions of commands (hSet, zRangeWithScores), and options are objects ({ EX: 60 }). sendCommand runs anything the typed API doesn't cover.
  • Always attach an 'error' listener. In Node, an EventEmitter that emits 'error' with no listener crashes the process. A Redis restart would take your app down with it.
  • One client is one connection, and commands issued in the same tick are automatically pipelined. MONITOR showed the two INCRs of a Promise.all arriving 5 µs apart:
"HELLO" "3"
"CLIENT" "SETINFO" "LIB-VER" "6.3.0"
"CLIENT" "SETINFO" "LIB-NAME" "node-redis"
"INCR" "x"
"INCR" "y"

node-redis 6 also opened with HELLO 3. Both libraries now speak RESP3 by default and normalize the results for you. The RESP: 3 client option exposes the RESP3 types more directly; with it, zScore returned a JavaScript number.

Because a node-redis client is a single multiplexed connection, a blocking command (BLPOP, XREAD BLOCK) blocks every other command on that client. Use a separate client (client.duplicate()) for blocking work and for Pub/Sub subscribers.

docs.title: How It Actually Works
docs.text:
A client library is three layers. A connection layer opens a socket, performs the handshake (HELLO with protocol version and optional AUTH, CLIENT SETINFO, SELECT if you chose a database) and reconnects when the socket breaks. A protocol layer encodes commands into RESP and parses replies. That's pure-Python in redis-py unless hiredis is installed, in which case a C parser does it much faster for large replies. A command layer maps methods to commands and converts reply types into language types: bytes or str, dicts for maps, floats for scores.

Pools differ in where concurrency comes from. redis-py's sync client takes a connection from the pool for each command (or pipeline) and returns it afterwards, so N threads need up to N connections. The asyncio client does the same per concurrent coroutine, which is why gather over 1,000 coroutines asked for 1,000 connections. node-redis instead writes every command from the whole process into one socket and matches replies by order. That works because RESP replies always come back in request order on a connection, and it's also why a blocking command stalls everything behind it.

Retries live in the connection layer. When a read times out, the library can't know whether the server received the command, executed it, or never saw it. All it can do is close the socket (the stream may hold a half-read reply) and try again on a fresh connection. The server, meanwhile, still has the original command in its query buffer and executes it. Exactly-once execution over an unreliable network is not something a client library can give you. Idempotent operations are how you get it.

docs.title: Common mistakes
docs.text:
• A client per request (or per function call). Create one per process and share it.
  • Unbounded concurrency on a bounded pool. Use a blocking pool, a semaphore, or pipelines.
  • Default retries on non-idempotent writes. They can double-apply. Configure retries per client, or make the writes idempotent.
  • Assuming a timeout means "didn't happen". It means "don't know".
  • Forgetting the 'error' listener in node-redis. An unhandled error event crashes Node.
  • Running BLPOP/SUBSCRIBE on the shared client. Use a dedicated connection.
  • Mixing decode_responses=True with binary values. Decoding a JPEG as UTF-8 fails. Keep a raw client for binary data.

docs.title: Exercise
docs.text:
1. Write a small Flask or FastAPI endpoint that increments a page counter. Load-test it (ab -n 2000 -c 20) once with a module-level client and once creating a client inside the handler. Compare throughput and connected_clients in INFO clients during the test.
  2. Reproduce the double-INCR with your own retry settings, then make the operation idempotent: the caller sends a request ID, and the increment applies only if SET seen:<request-id> 1 NX EX 600 succeeds. Do both commands in one MULTI. Does that fully solve it? Why or why not?
  3. In node-redis, start a BLPOP with a 5-second timeout on a client and immediately GET a key on the same client. How long does the GET take? Fix it with client.duplicate().
  4. Find out which protocol your production client library negotiates (check CLIENT LIST for resp=), and what its default socket timeout and retry policy are.

docs.title: 10 · Project — URL Shortener with Click Analytics
docs.text:
This project pulls Level 1 together. You'll build a URL shortener whose only storage is Redis, with click analytics on top, and test it under concurrency. It uses every type from this level, and each choice of type is deliberate:

Need Structure Why this one Next numeric id string + INCR atomic, gap-tolerant counter A link's data hash short:link:<code> one object, per-field updates, HINCRBY clicks Claim a code or alias once HSETNX on the link hash first writer wins, atomically Same URL → same code string short:by-target:<sha256> + SET NX dedupe without scanning Last 20 clicks list + LPUSH/LTRIM capped, newest first Unique visitors per day set per code per day, with TTL SADD dedupes, SCARD counts Top links today sorted set per day ZINCRBY + ZRANGE … REV

The finished module is about 130 lines. It has 13 tests, and the first version had a real bug that one of the tests found. That story is below.

docs.title: Setup
docs.text:
python3 -m venv .venv && .venv/bin/pip install redis hiredis pytest
redis-server --port 6379 --save '' --daemonize yes   # or your lab server

The tests use database 15 and flush it before and after each test. Don't point them at a database you care about.

docs.title: The code
docs.text:
shortener.py:

"""A URL shortener backed only by Redis (Level 1 project)."""
import hashlib
import string
import time
from datetime import datetime, timezone

import redis

ALPHABET = string.digits + string.ascii_letters          # base62
RECENT_CLICKS = 20
DAY_TTL = 8 * 24 * 3600                                    # keep per-day keys for a week


def base62(n: int) -> str:
    if n == 0:
        return ALPHABET[0]
    out = []
    while n:
        n, rem = divmod(n, 62)
        out.append(ALPHABET[rem])
    return "".join(reversed(out))


class AliasTaken(Exception):
    pass


class Shortener:
    def __init__(self, r: redis.Redis, prefix: str = "short"):
        self.r = r
        self.p = prefix

    # key helpers -----------------------------------------------------------
    def _link(self, code):      return f"{self.p}:link:{code}"
    def _by_target(self, url):  return f"{self.p}:by-target:{hashlib.sha256(url.encode()).hexdigest()[:32]}"
    def _recent(self, code):    return f"{self.p}:recent:{code}"
    def _visitors(self, code, day): return f"{self.p}:visitors:{code}:{day}"
    def _top(self, day):        return f"{self.p}:top:{day}"

    @staticmethod
    def _today(now=None):
        return datetime.fromtimestamp(now or time.time(), tz=timezone.utc).strftime("%Y-%m-%d")

    # writes ----------------------------------------------------------------
    def shorten(self, url: str, owner: str = "anon", ttl: int | None = None) -> str:
        """Return a code for url. The same url (without ttl) always maps to the same code."""
        if not url.startswith(("http://", "https://")):
            raise ValueError("only http(s) URLs")
        if ttl is None:
            existing = self.r.get(self._by_target(url))
            if existing:
                return existing
        while True:                                   # skip codes already claimed as aliases
            code = base62(self.r.incr(f"{self.p}:next-id") + 100_000)   # skip the very short codes
            if self._create(code, url, owner, ttl):
                break
        if ttl is None:
            # first writer wins; a concurrent writer of the same URL reuses its code
            if not self.r.set(self._by_target(url), code, nx=True):
                winner = self.r.get(self._by_target(url))
                self.r.unlink(self._link(code))
                return winner
        return code

    def shorten_alias(self, alias: str, url: str, owner: str = "anon") -> str:
        if not alias.isalnum() or not 3 <= len(alias) <= 32:
            raise ValueError("alias must be 3-32 letters/digits")
        # HSETNX creates the hash only if the field is absent: an atomic "claim"
        if not self.r.hsetnx(self._link(alias), "target", url):
            raise AliasTaken(alias)
        self.r.hset(self._link(alias), mapping={"owner": owner, "created": int(time.time()), "clicks": 0})
        return alias

    def _create(self, code, url, owner, ttl) -> bool:
        # claim the code first: HSETNX fails if an alias (or anything) already owns it
        if not self.r.hsetnx(self._link(code), "target", url):
            return False
        pipe = self.r.pipeline(transaction=True)
        pipe.hset(self._link(code), mapping={"owner": owner, "created": int(time.time()), "clicks": 0})
        if ttl:
            pipe.expire(self._link(code), ttl)
        pipe.execute()
        return True

    # reads -----------------------------------------------------------------
    def resolve(self, code: str, visitor: str = "", referrer: str = "-", now: float | None = None) -> str | None:
        target = self.r.hget(self._link(code), "target")
        if target is None:
            return None
        day = self._today(now)
        pipe = self.r.pipeline(transaction=False)
        pipe.hincrby(self._link(code), "clicks", 1)
        pipe.lpush(self._recent(code), f"{int(now or time.time())}|{referrer}")
        pipe.ltrim(self._recent(code), 0, RECENT_CLICKS - 1)
        if visitor:
            pipe.sadd(self._visitors(code, day), visitor)
            pipe.expire(self._visitors(code, day), DAY_TTL)
        pipe.zincrby(self._top(day), 1, code)
        pipe.expire(self._top(day), DAY_TTL)
        pipe.execute()
        return target

    def stats(self, code: str, now: float | None = None) -> dict | None:
        day = self._today(now)
        pipe = self.r.pipeline(transaction=False)
        pipe.hgetall(self._link(code))
        pipe.ttl(self._link(code))
        pipe.scard(self._visitors(code, day))
        pipe.lrange(self._recent(code), 0, 4)
        link, ttl, uniques, recent = pipe.execute()
        if not link:
            return None
        return {"target": link["target"], "clicks": int(link["clicks"]), "ttl": ttl,
                "unique_today": uniques, "recent": recent}

    def top_today(self, n: int = 5, now: float | None = None):
        return self.r.zrange(self._top(self._today(now)), 0, n - 1, desc=True, withscores=True)

    def delete(self, code: str, owner: str) -> bool:
        link = self.r.hgetall(self._link(code))
        if not link or link.get("owner") != owner:
            return False
        pipe = self.r.pipeline(transaction=True)
        pipe.unlink(self._link(code), self._recent(code))
        if self.r.get(self._by_target(link["target"])) == code:
            pipe.unlink(self._by_target(link["target"]))
        pipe.execute()
        return True

docs.title: Design notes
docs.text:
Codes from a counter. INCR short:next-id hands out unique integers with no coordination between app servers. Adding 100,000 before base62-encoding keeps codes at three characters or more (the first is q0V), so nobody can guess the first few links by trying 1, 2, 3. Sequential codes are still enumerable, though. If links can be private, use random codes (secrets.token_urlsafe) claimed with the same HSETNX and retried on collision.

Claiming with HSETNX. A custom alias like launch must belong to whoever asked first. HSETNX link:launch target <url> creates the field only if it's absent, and creating the field creates the hash. So the check-and-create is a single atomic command, and twenty concurrent claims produce exactly one winner (see test_alias_race).

Same URL, same code. The reverse index key is a SHA-256 of the URL, which keeps keys short and avoids special characters. Two requests shortening the same new URL at the same moment can both miss the index and both create a code. The SET … NX decides which one wins, and the loser deletes its own code and returns the winner's. The race is resolved rather than prevented, and test_concurrent_same_url_single_code checks that 20 threads get one code.

Click recording is one round trip. resolve sends six or seven commands in one non-transactional pipeline: increment clicks, push and trim the recent list, add the visitor to today's set, bump today's top-links board, and refresh TTLs. None of them depends on another's result, so there's no need for MULTI. Each command is atomic by itself, which is all the click counter needs. (test_clicks_are_exact_under_concurrency: 8 threads × 250 clicks = exactly 2,000.)

Bounded memory. Recent clicks are trimmed to 20. Per-day sets and boards expire after 8 days. Only the link hashes live forever, unless created with a TTL.

docs.title: The tests
docs.text:
test_shortener.py:

import threading, time
import pytest, redis
from shortener import Shortener, AliasTaken, base62

@pytest.fixture
def s():
    r = redis.Redis(db=15, decode_responses=True)
    r.flushdb()
    yield Shortener(r)
    r.flushdb()

def test_base62():
    assert [base62(n) for n in (0, 61, 62, 100_001)] == ["0", "Z", "10", "q0V"]

def test_shorten_and_resolve(s):
    code = s.shorten("https://redis.io/docs/")
    assert s.resolve(code) == "https://redis.io/docs/"
    assert s.resolve("nope") is None

def test_same_url_same_code(s):
    assert s.shorten("https://example.com/a") == s.shorten("https://example.com/a")
    assert s.shorten("https://example.com/a") != s.shorten("https://example.com/b")

def test_rejects_non_http(s):
    with pytest.raises(ValueError):
        s.shorten("javascript:alert(1)")

def test_alias_claimed_once(s):
    assert s.shorten_alias("launch", "https://example.com/launch") == "launch"
    with pytest.raises(AliasTaken):
        s.shorten_alias("launch", "https://evil.example/")
    assert s.resolve("launch") == "https://example.com/launch"

def test_alias_race(s):
    wins, errors = [], []
    def claim(i):
        try:
            s.shorten_alias("promo", f"https://example.com/{i}"); wins.append(i)
        except AliasTaken:
            errors.append(i)
    ts = [threading.Thread(target=claim, args=(i,)) for i in range(20)]
    [t.start() for t in ts]; [t.join() for t in ts]
    assert len(wins) == 1 and len(errors) == 19
    assert s.resolve("promo") == f"https://example.com/{wins[0]}"

def test_concurrent_same_url_single_code(s):
    codes = []
    def go():
        codes.append(s.shorten("https://example.com/hot"))
    ts = [threading.Thread(target=go) for _ in range(20)]
    [t.start() for t in ts]; [t.join() for t in ts]
    assert len(set(codes)) == 1
    assert s.resolve(codes[0]) == "https://example.com/hot"

def test_clicks_are_exact_under_concurrency(s):
    code = s.shorten("https://example.com/popular")
    def hit():
        for _ in range(250): s.resolve(code, visitor="v")
    ts = [threading.Thread(target=hit) for _ in range(8)]
    [t.start() for t in ts]; [t.join() for t in ts]
    assert s.stats(code)["clicks"] == 2000

def test_stats_uniques_and_recent_capped(s):
    code = s.shorten("https://example.com/x")
    for i in range(30):
        s.resolve(code, visitor=f"user{i % 7}", referrer=f"ref{i}")
    st = s.stats(code)
    assert st["clicks"] == 30 and st["unique_today"] == 7
    assert len(st["recent"]) == 5 and st["recent"][0].endswith("|ref29")
    assert s.r.llen(s._recent(code)) == 20

def test_top_today(s):
    a = s.shorten("https://example.com/1"); b = s.shorten("https://example.com/2")
    for _ in range(3): s.resolve(a)
    for _ in range(5): s.resolve(b)
    assert s.top_today(2) == [(b, 5.0), (a, 3.0)]

def test_expiring_link(s):
    code = s.shorten("https://example.com/temp", ttl=1)
    assert s.resolve(code) == "https://example.com/temp"
    time.sleep(1.2)
    assert s.resolve(code) is None

def test_delete_only_by_owner(s):
    code = s.shorten("https://example.com/mine", owner="ana")
    assert s.delete(code, owner="ben") is False
    assert s.delete(code, owner="ana") is True
    assert s.resolve(code) is None
    assert s.shorten("https://example.com/mine") != code

def test_generated_code_never_overwrites_alias(s):
    s.shorten_alias("q0V", "https://example.com/alias-owner")      # the next generated code
    code = s.shorten("https://example.com/generated")
    assert s.resolve("q0V") == "https://example.com/alias-owner"
    assert code != "q0V" and s.resolve(code) == "https://example.com/generated"

docs.title: The bug the last test found
docs.text:
The first version of _create wrote the new link with a plain HSET in a pipeline:

def _create(self, code, url, owner, ttl):
    pipe = self.r.pipeline(transaction=True)
    pipe.hset(self._link(code), mapping={"target": url, "owner": owner,
                                         "created": int(time.time()), "clicks": 0})
    ...

Generated codes and custom aliases share one namespace, short:link:<code>. So what happens if someone claims the alias q0V before the counter reaches it? A test for exactly that:

def test_generated_code_never_overwrites_alias(s):
    s.shorten_alias("q0V", "https://example.com/alias-owner")      # the next generated code
    code = s.shorten("https://example.com/generated")
    assert s.resolve("q0V") == "https://example.com/alias-owner"
    assert code != "q0V" and s.resolve(code) == "https://example.com/generated"

>       assert s.resolve("q0V") == "https://example.com/alias-owner"
E       AssertionError: assert 'https://exam...com/generated' == 'https://exam...m/alias-owner'
1 failed, 12 passed in 1.64s

The generated link silently overwrote someone's alias, because HSET overwrites. The fix is the same idea used for aliases: claim with HSETNX first and take the next id if the claim fails. That's the while True loop in shorten and the bool return of _create in the code above. The broader lesson for Redis design is to ask, for every write, whether it can overwrite something it shouldn't. Redis will never complain about it.

(One more honest note: the first draft of test_base62 expected "q0T" for 100,001. The arithmetic was wrong, not the code. 100,001 = 26·62² + 0·62 + 57, and digit 57 in this alphabet is V. The test caught the test.)

docs.title: How It Actually Works
docs.text:
Each request touches only O(1) or O(log N) operations: HGET, HINCRBY, LPUSH/LTRIM (O(1) when trimming one element off a short list), SADD, ZINCRBY (O(log N) in today's board). So resolve latency stays flat as the number of links grows. The only O(N) operation is stats's LRANGE 0 4, and N is 5.

Correctness rests on one rule: every decision that must be unique happens inside a single Redis command. "Is this alias free?" and "take it" are one HSETNX. "Does this URL already have a code?" and "record mine" are one SET NX. "Add a click" is one HINCRBY. Because Redis runs commands one at a time, these can't interleave with other clients. The places where the code reads, decides in Python, then writes (delete checks the owner, then unlinks) are exactly the places that could race. For delete the worst case is harmless: deleting a link that was just deleted. Level 2 · 08–09 shows how to make read-decide-write atomic when it isn't harmless.

The daily keys use UTC dates, so "today" changes at midnight UTC for every server. Their 8-day TTL is refreshed on each click, so a key expires 8 days after its last activity. That's a few redundant EXPIRE calls in exchange for not needing a cleanup job.

docs.title: Common mistakes
docs.text:
• Read-then-write claims (EXISTS then HSET). Two clients both see "free". Claim in one command.
  • Overwrites across shared namespaces. Generated codes and aliases collided in the first version. Look for them whenever two code paths write the same key pattern.
  • Counting uniques in an ever-growing set. Use per-period keys with TTLs, or HyperLogLog (Level 2 · 03) for big sites.
  • Using KEYS for the "top links" page. Maintain the sorted set as you go instead.
  • Trusting user input as a redirect target. The http(s) check is the minimum; a real service also needs abuse and malware checks.

docs.title: Exercise
docs.text:
1. Add short:links:<owner> (a sorted set of codes scored by creation time) so a user can list their links, newest first, 10 per page. Keep it consistent in shorten, shorten_alias and delete.
  2. Replace sequential codes with 7-character random codes claimed via HSETNX. Write a test that forces a collision (by seeding the random generator, or by pre-claiming the code) and checks that the retry works.
  3. Add a per-link daily click histogram using a hash short:hourly:<code>:<date> with one field per hour, and expose it from stats.
  4. Benchmark resolve with 1,000,000 links and 100,000 resolves from 8 threads. Report requests per second and the server's used_memory per link.

docs.title: Level 2 · Data Structures in Depth
docs.text:
Level 1 used Redis's core types correctly. Level 2 goes underneath them and beyond them. You'll see why one extra sorted-set member made a key 12× larger, why a million small values fit in 7.9 MB instead of 46 MB, and how 10 million unique visitors fit in 12 KB. You'll also see why a stream reader that passes $ loses half its messages, why a slow subscriber gets cut off at 32 MB, and why a Lua script ran the same transfers 7× faster than WATCH.

Some results surprised us, and they're reported as found. On the Homebrew build of Redis 8.10.2 used here, BITCOUNT returned wrong totals above 2^21. Lesson 02 shows the evidence, the comparison with Valkey, and a workaround. Several commands used here are very recent (8.2's XACKDEL, 8.6's idempotent XADD, 8.8's XNACK), and each lesson says which version introduced them.

Prerequisites: Level 1, or equivalent experience with Redis's strings, hashes, lists, sets and sorted sets and a client library.

docs.title: Modules
docs.text:
1. Encodings & Memory — listpack, intset, skiplist and quicklist, the thresholds between them, hash bucketing, and reading fragmentation in INFO memory.
  2. Bitmaps & Bitfields — daily-active-user bitmaps, BITOP set algebra, packed counters with overflow control, the sparse-offset trap, and a BITCOUNT bug found.
  3. HyperLogLog, Bloom Filters & Other Sketches — approximate counting and membership with measured error rates: HyperLogLog, Bloom, Cuckoo, Count-Min and Top-K.
  4. Geospatial Indexes — GEOADD and GEOSEARCH, nearest-N on a million points, why ANY matters, and the spherical model's 0.2% error.
  5. Streams: An Append-Only Log — entry IDs, ranges, XREAD without losing messages, bounded trimming, and idempotent XADD.
  6. Stream Consumer Groups & Recovery — the pending entries list, XACK, recovering a crashed worker with XAUTOCLAIM, dead letters, XACKDEL and XNACK.
  7. Pub/Sub, Sharded Pub/Sub & Keyspace Notifications — broadcast messaging, slow-subscriber disconnects, sharded channels, and how late expiry events really are.
  8. Transactions: MULTI, EXEC & WATCH — what a Redis transaction guarantees (no rollback), and optimistic locking that took overdrafts from 2,815 to zero.
  9. Lua Scripts & Redis Functions — atomic server-side logic, conversion traps, BUSY scripts that can't be killed, and persistent function libraries.
  10. Project — Game Leaderboard & Activity Feed — a Functions-based weekly leaderboard with first-come tie-breaking, a trimmed activity stream and an idempotent badge worker.

docs.title: After Level 2
docs.text: You know what each structure costs and how to compose them atomically. Level 3 applies that to the jobs Redis is most often hired for: caching (and the stampedes, invalidation bugs and eviction surprises that come with it), rate limiting, distributed locks and their limits, sessions, reliable job queues, JSON documents, and the query engine's secondary and vector indexes.

docs.title: 01 · Encodings & Memory
docs.text: Level 1 kept running into OBJECT ENCODING: int and embstr strings, listpack hashes, intset sets, skiplist sorted sets. This lesson puts those pieces together. Every Redis type has a compact encoding for small values and a general one for large values, and the boundary between them is configurable. Knowing where the boundaries are, and designing around them, is the most effective memory optimization Redis offers. It can cut memory use several-fold with no change in behaviour.

docs.title: A survey of encodings
docs.text:
This script creates one small and one large value of each type and reports the encoding and MEMORY USAGE:

import redis
r = redis.Redis(decode_responses=True)
r.flushall()

def show(key):
    print(f"{key:16} {r.type(key):6} {r.object('encoding', key):11} {r.memory_usage(key):>8} bytes")

r.set("s:int", 123456); r.set("s:short", "hello"); r.set("s:long", "x" * 100)
r.rpush("l:small", *range(10)); r.rpush("l:big", *[f"item{i}" for i in range(10000)])
r.sadd("set:ints", *range(100)); r.sadd("set:small", *[f"m{i}" for i in range(100)])
r.sadd("set:big", *[f"m{i}" for i in range(1000)])
r.hset("h:small", mapping={f"f{i}": i for i in range(100)})
r.hset("h:big", mapping={f"f{i}": i for i in range(1000)})
r.zadd("z:small", {f"m{i}": i for i in range(100)}); r.zadd("z:big", {f"m{i}": i for i in range(1000)})
r.xadd("st", {"a": 1})
for k in ["s:int", "s:short", "s:long", "l:small", "l:big", "set:ints", "set:small", "set:big",
          "h:small", "h:big", "z:small", "z:big", "st"]:
    show(k)

s:int            string int               24 bytes
s:short          string embstr            48 bytes
s:long           string raw              137 bytes
l:small          list   listpack          53 bytes
l:big            list   quicklist      99677 bytes
set:ints         set    intset           235 bytes
set:small        set    listpack         525 bytes
set:big          set    hashtable      30164 bytes
h:small          hash   listpack         723 bytes
h:big            hash   hashtable      37052 bytes
z:small          zset   listpack         723 bytes
z:big            zset   skiplist       78352 bytes
st               stream stream           289 bytes

Compare the 100-member and 1,000-member versions of the same type. Ten times the members cost about 57× the memory for sets (525 → 30,164 bytes), 51× for hashes and 108× for sorted sets. The general encodings aren't just bigger in total. Each element costs far more.

Type Compact encoding General encoding Switch when (defaults on 8.10) string int, embstr (≤44 bytes) raw non-integer, longer, or modified in place list listpack quicklist (linked listpacks) list exceeds one listpack node (list-max-listpack-size, 8 KB) set intset, listpack hashtable >512 ints, >128 members, or a member >64 bytes hash listpack (listpackex with field TTLs) hashtable >512 fields or a value >64 bytes zset listpack skiplist + hash table >128 members or a member >64 bytes stream radix tree of listpacks (always) —

docs.title: The cliff at the threshold
docs.text:
Here are the costs either side of the default thresholds:

for n in (128, 129):
    r.delete("z"); r.zadd("z", {f"m{i}": i for i in range(n)})
    print(f"zset with {n} members: {r.object('encoding','z'):9} {r.memory_usage('z')} bytes")
for n in (512, 513):
    r.delete("h"); r.hset("h", mapping={f"f{i}": i for i in range(n)})
    print(f"hash with {n} fields : {r.object('encoding','h'):9} {r.memory_usage('h')} bytes")

zset with 128 members: listpack  941 bytes
zset with 129 members: skiplist  11692 bytes
hash with 512 fields : listpack  4397 bytes
hash with 513 fields : hashtable 22925 bytes

One extra member made the sorted set 12× bigger. One extra field made the hash 5× bigger. If your data naturally sits near a threshold, say leaderboards of about 150 members or hashes of about 600 fields, moving the threshold or reshaping the data changes your memory bill dramatically.

docs.title: Hash bucketing: storing a million small values
docs.text:
A classic case is a large mapping from IDs to small values, such as photo → owner, user → last-seen timestamp, or SKU → stock. The obvious design is one string key per ID. Here are four layouts for one million pairs:

import redis
r = redis.Redis()
N = 1_000_000

def run(label, write):
    r.flushall(); base = r.info("memory")["used_memory"]
    p = r.pipeline(transaction=False)
    for i in range(N):
        write(p, i)
        if i % 10000 == 9999: p.execute()
    p.execute()
    total = r.info("memory")["used_memory"] - base
    print(f"{label:44} {total/1e6:7.1f} MB  {total/N:6.1f} bytes/item  keys={r.dbsize()}")

run("1M string keys  photo:<id> -> owner id",
    lambda p, i: p.set(f"photo:{i}", i * 7 % 100000))
run("1M string keys  long name prefix",
    lambda p, i: p.set(f"application:media-service:photo-owner:{i}", i * 7 % 100000))
run("1000 hashes x 1000 fields (listpack limit 512)",
    lambda p, i: p.hset(f"photo:{i // 1000}", i % 1000, i * 7 % 100000))
run("2000 hashes x 500 fields (stays listpack)",
    lambda p, i: p.hset(f"photo:{i // 500}", i % 500, i * 7 % 100000))

1M string keys  photo:<id> -> owner id          46.1 MB    46.1 bytes/item  keys=1000000
1M string keys  long name prefix                92.5 MB    92.5 bytes/item  keys=1000000
1000 hashes x 1000 fields (listpack limit 512)    30.4 MB    30.4 bytes/item  keys=1000
2000 hashes x 500 fields (stays listpack)        7.9 MB     7.9 bytes/item  keys=2000
  • A verbose key prefix doubled memory for the same data, 46 → 92.5 MB.
  • Bucketing into hashes of 1,000 fields helped somewhat (30.4 MB), but those hashes had crossed the 512-field threshold into hashtable.
  • Buckets of 500 fields stayed listpack, and the same million pairs took 7.9 MB, about 6× less than the string-per-key layout.

The access pattern changes only slightly. GET photo:123456 becomes HGET photo:246 456 (bucket = id // 500, field = id % 500). What you give up: no per-item TTL (unless you use field TTLs, which switch the encoding to listpackex), and every lookup is a linear scan of up to 500 entries. That's measured in microseconds, but it isn't free, and raising the bucket size towards thousands makes it worse.

docs.title: Reading INFO memory
docs.text:
On a server holding 2 million 100-byte strings:

redis-cli INFO memory

used_memory:320135840
used_memory_rss:302366720
used_memory_peak:320136192
used_memory_overhead:82410032
used_memory_dataset:237725808
used_memory_dataset_perc:74.62%
allocator_frag_ratio:1.00
mem_fragmentation_ratio:0.94
mem_allocator:libc
  • used_memory — bytes Redis's allocator has handed out. This is what maxmemory is compared against.
  • used_memory_overhead — keyspace tables, client buffers, replication backlog and so on. used_memory_dataset is the rest, the data itself.
  • used_memory_rss — what the OS says the process holds in RAM. This is what your container limit or the OOM killer sees.
  • mem_fragmentation_ratio — RSS ÷ used_memory.
  • mem_allocator:libc — this Homebrew macOS build uses the system malloc. Official Linux builds and the official container image use jemalloc, which Redis is tuned for. Some of what follows depends on that.

Then delete every second key (1 million UNLINKs) and look again:

used_memory:170446768
used_memory_rss:361021440
mem_fragmentation_ratio:2.12

Redis now holds half the data, but the process's RSS didn't shrink. It actually grew, because the pipeline's client buffers needed memory too. Freed memory sits in the allocator's free lists, in pages that still contain some live allocations, so it can't go back to the OS. A ratio of 2.12 means half the RAM the process occupies is holes. MEMORY DOCTOR diagnoses it in plain words (its output, trimmed):

 * Peak memory: In the past this instance used more than 150% the memory that is currently using. The allocator
   is normally not able to release memory after a peak, so you can expect to see a big fragmentation ratio ...
 * High total RSS: This instance has a memory fragmentation and RSS overhead greater than 1.4 ... make sure you
   are using the Jemalloc allocator and not the default libc malloc. Note: The currently used allocator is "libc".

What you can do about fragmentation:

  • Active defragmentation (activedefrag yes) moves live allocations to compact pages while the server runs. It needs Redis's bundled jemalloc, and this build refused:
ERR CONFIG SET failed (possibly related to argument 'activedefrag') - Active defragmentation cannot be
enabled: it requires a Redis server compiled with a modified Jemalloc like the one shipped by default with
the Redis source distribution
  • MEMORY PURGE asks the allocator to return free pages to the OS. On this libc build it returned OK and RSS fell to 134 MB with a ratio of 0.79. A ratio below 1 on Linux usually means part of Redis has been swapped out, which is a serious latency problem. macOS also compresses idle memory, which can push RSS below used_memory without swapping. Read the ratio with your OS in mind.
  • Restart a replica after a big deletion and fail over to it. Loading from a snapshot packs memory tightly.

docs.title: How It Actually Works
docs.text:
A listpack is a single allocation: a 6-byte header (total bytes and element count), then entries, then an end marker. Each entry is an encoding byte or two that describes the type and length (small integers are stored in as little as one byte), the data, and a back-length so the list can be walked in both directions. There are no pointers and no per-element allocations, and a few hundred entries fit in a handful of cache lines. Lookup is a linear scan and insertion is a memmove, which is why the thresholds exist. Beyond a few hundred entries, the O(N) operations become noticeable, so Redis switches to structures with O(1) or O(log N) access and pays for them with pointers and headers per element.

The general encodings are where the per-element overhead comes from. A hashtable entry is a bucket pointer, an entry struct and separately allocated field and value strings. A sorted set at scale has a hash-table entry and a skip-list node per member, and each skip-list node has a variable number of level pointers plus spans. Each allocation is rounded up to the allocator's size class (jemalloc uses classes of 8, 16, 32, 48, 64, 80… bytes), so a 9-byte string costs 16.

Conversions happen inside the command that crosses a threshold. The ZADD that adds member 129 rebuilds the listpack as a skip list on the spot, which costs O(N) once. They go one way only, because converting back on every deletion would make workloads oscillate. A key that grew past a threshold and then shrank keeps its large encoding until it's rewritten (for example, by reloading from an RDB snapshot, which re-encodes compactly).

Fragmentation is an allocator property. Redis frees objects in an unpredictable order, so pages end up partially used. jemalloc exposes per-allocation hints that Redis's active defrag uses: it re-allocates a value into a better spot and fixes the one pointer to it, a little at a time within a CPU budget (active-defrag-cycle-min/max). A generic malloc offers no such hints, which is why the feature needs jemalloc.

docs.title: Common mistakes
docs.text:
• Sizing from one encoding and running in another. Test memory with realistic collection sizes. 128 versus 129 members was 941 versus 11,692 bytes.
  • Raising listpack thresholds into the thousands to save memory. Every access becomes a long linear scan, and a listpack bigger than a few KB defeats the cache-locality argument. Benchmark latency as well as memory.
  • Verbose key names on hundreds of millions of keys. The name is stored once per key and doubled memory here.
  • Watching only used_memory. The OOM killer looks at RSS. Monitor mem_fragmentation_ratio too.
  • Benchmarking memory on a laptop build and assuming production matches. This course's macOS build uses libc malloc, and Linux production almost always uses jemalloc. Check mem_allocator.
  • Bucketing data that needs per-item TTLs without planning for field TTLs (7.4+) or a separate expiry mechanism.

docs.title: Exercise
docs.text:
1. Store 1,000,000 user → "last seen" timestamps three ways: string keys, hash buckets of 100, and hash buckets of 1,000 with hash-max-listpack-entries raised to 1024. Record memory and the average HGET latency for each (time 10,000 random lookups).
  2. Find a sorted set size near the threshold in an application you know (or invent one). Measure MEMORY USAGE for 120, 128, 129 and 200 members, then set zset-max-listpack-entries 256 and repeat. How does ZRANK latency change?
  3. Grow a hash past 512 fields, delete back down to 10, and check its encoding. Then DEBUG RELOAD (lab only: saves and reloads the RDB) and check again.
  4. On a Linux machine or container with an official Redis build, repeat the "delete every second key" experiment with activedefrag yes and watch mem_fragmentation_ratio over a minute.

docs.title: 02 · Bitmaps & Bitfields
docs.text:
A Redis string is a byte array, and a set of commands treats it as an array of bits. That gives you a bitmap: one bit per user, per day, per feature flag. A bitmap for 10 million users fits in 1.25 MB, and bitwise AND/OR across days runs on the server. BITFIELD goes further and packs many small integers (8-bit counters, 4-bit ratings) into one string.

Bitmaps are not a separate type. TYPE reports string, and GET returns the raw bytes. They're a way of using strings.

docs.title: Setting and reading bits
docs.text:
Mark users 5, 9 and 42 active on one day, and 9, 42 and 77 the next:

127.0.0.1:6379> SETBIT active:2026-10-12 5 1
(integer) 0
127.0.0.1:6379> SETBIT active:2026-10-12 9 1
(integer) 0
127.0.0.1:6379> SETBIT active:2026-10-12 42 1
(integer) 0
127.0.0.1:6379> SETBIT active:2026-10-13 9 1
(integer) 0
127.0.0.1:6379> SETBIT active:2026-10-13 42 1
(integer) 0
127.0.0.1:6379> SETBIT active:2026-10-13 77 1
(integer) 0
127.0.0.1:6379> GETBIT active:2026-10-13 9
(integer) 1
127.0.0.1:6379> GETBIT active:2026-10-13 5
(integer) 0
127.0.0.1:6379> BITCOUNT active:2026-10-13
(integer) 3
127.0.0.1:6379> STRLEN active:2026-10-13
(integer) 10

SETBIT returns the bit's previous value. That's useful as "was this user already counted today?" in the same round trip. The string grows to cover the highest offset set: bit 77 needs 10 bytes, and new bytes are zero.

Bit 0 is the most significant bit of byte 0:

127.0.0.1:6379> SETBIT flags 0 1
(integer) 0
127.0.0.1:6379> SETBIT flags 7 1
(integer) 0
127.0.0.1:6379> GET flags
"\x81"

That's 1000 0001. This matters as soon as another program reads the bytes, for example when you GET a bitmap and decode it in Python.

docs.title: Bitwise operations across keys
docs.text:
BITOP combines bitmaps and stores the result:

127.0.0.1:6379> BITOP AND active:both active:2026-10-12 active:2026-10-13
(integer) 10
127.0.0.1:6379> BITCOUNT active:both
(integer) 2
127.0.0.1:6379> BITOP OR active:either active:2026-10-12 active:2026-10-13
(integer) 10
127.0.0.1:6379> BITCOUNT active:either
(integer) 4
127.0.0.1:6379> BITOP DIFF active:churned active:2026-10-12 active:2026-10-13
(integer) 10
127.0.0.1:6379> BITCOUNT active:churned
(integer) 1

Two users were active both days (9, 42), four on either day, and one (user 5) was active yesterday but not today. AND, OR, XOR and NOT have existed since Redis 2.6. DIFF (in the first key but none of the others), DIFF1, ANDOR and ONE (bits set in exactly one input) are recent Redis 8 additions. They ran on this 8.10.2 server, but older servers and other forks may reject them, so check HELP BITOP.

Weekly actives are an OR over seven daily keys, and "active every day this week" is an AND. Each costs O(size of the bitmaps), done in C on the server.

BITPOS finds the first set or clear bit:

127.0.0.1:6379> BITPOS active:2026-10-13 1
(integer) 9
127.0.0.1:6379> BITPOS active:2026-10-13 0
(integer) 0

BITPOS key 0 is a quick way to find the first free slot in an allocation bitmap. BITCOUNT and BITPOS take an optional range, in bytes by default or in bits with the BIT keyword:

127.0.0.1:6379> BITCOUNT active:2026-10-13 0 7 BIT
(integer) 0

docs.title: Bitmap vs set at scale
docs.text:
Here are 3 million active users out of 10 million, stored both as a bitmap and as a set:

import redis, random, time
r = redis.Redis()
random.seed(1)
active = random.sample(range(10_000_000), 3_000_000)
p = r.pipeline(transaction=False)
for i, uid in enumerate(active):
    p.setbit("dau:bitmap", uid, 1)
    if i % 20000 == 0: p.execute()
p.execute()
for i in range(0, len(active), 10000):
    r.sadd("dau:set", *active[i:i+10000])
print("bitmap:", r.memory_usage("dau:bitmap"), "bytes;", "set:", r.memory_usage("dau:set"), "bytes")

bitmap: 2244637 bytes; set: 124998402 bytes

The bitmap was 56× smaller: 2.2 MB versus 125 MB. (Its STRLEN is exactly 1,250,000 bytes. MEMORY USAGE is higher because the string grew in steps as SETBIT extended it, and the allocation kept spare capacity.) A bitmap's size depends on the highest ID, not on how many bits are set, so it suits dense integer IDs. A set's size depends on the count.

docs.title: The sparse-offset trap
docs.text:
What if IDs aren't dense? One SETBIT at a large offset:

t = time.perf_counter(); r.setbit("sparse", 2**31, 1); el = time.perf_counter() - t
print(f"SETBIT at offset 2^31 took {el*1000:.0f} ms; key is now {r.strlen('sparse')} bytes, "
      f"used_memory={r.info('memory')['used_memory_human']}")

SETBIT at offset 2^31 took 72 ms; key is now 268435457 bytes, used_memory=370.64M

One bit cost 256 MB and a 72 ms stall while Redis allocated and zeroed it. Using 64-bit IDs, hashed IDs or UUIDs as offsets is a memory bomb. The maximum offset is 2^32 − 1 (a 512 MB string). Map sparse IDs to a dense range first, or use a set, or a HyperLogLog if an approximate count will do (next lesson).

docs.title: A wrong answer from BITCOUNT on this build
docs.text:
Counting the 3-million-user bitmap gave a surprise:

t = time.perf_counter(); n = r.bitcount("dau:bitmap")
print(f"BITCOUNT -> {n} in {(time.perf_counter()-t)*1000:.2f} ms")

BITCOUNT -> 902848 in 0.24 ms

That should be 3,000,000. Counting the same bytes in Python agreed with the input, not with Redis:

b = r.get("dau:bitmap")
print("python popcount:", int.from_bytes(b, "big").bit_count(), "BITCOUNT:", r.bitcount("dau:bitmap"))

python popcount: 3000000 BITCOUNT: 902848

Testing strings of known content narrowed it down:

0x01 x 2,097,151 bytes:    2097151      (correct)
0x01 x 2,097,152 bytes:    2097152      (correct)
0x01 x 3,000,000 bytes:     902848      expected 3000000; 3000000 mod 2^21 = 902848
0xff x 262,151 bytes:           56      expected 2097208
0xff x 1,250,000 bytes:    1611392      expected 10000000; 10000000 mod 2^21 = 1611392

On this server (the Homebrew bottle of Redis 8.10.2 on Apple Silicon), every total above 2,097,152 (2^21) that we tried came back as the true count modulo 2^21, whole-key or with an explicit 0 -1 range. Smaller totals were exact. The same tests on Valkey 9.1.2 on the same machine returned the correct values. We couldn't determine whether this is specific to this build or affects other platforms. If you rely on BITCOUNT for large counts, test your own server with a known string, as above. Where it's wrong, a chunked count is correct, because each chunk stays far below the limit:

def bitcount_chunked(key, chunk=131072):          # 131,072 bytes = 1,048,576 bits per call
    n = r.strlen(key); total = 0
    for start in range(0, n, chunk):
        total += r.bitcount(key, start, min(start + chunk, n) - 1)
    return total

chunked: 10000000
dau chunked: 3000000

This is a good reminder that course numbers, benchmark numbers and database results are all worth a sanity check against an independent count.

docs.title: BITFIELD: packed integers
docs.text:
BITFIELD reads and writes integers of any width from 1 to 64 bits (u unsigned up to 63 bits, i signed) at any offset. #n means "the n-th field of this width", so u8 #1 is bits 8–15:

127.0.0.1:6379> BITFIELD counters SET u8 #0 250 GET u8 #0
1) (integer) 0
2) (integer) 250
127.0.0.1:6379> BITFIELD counters INCRBY u8 #0 10
1) (integer) 4

SET returns the old value. 250 + 10 in an unsigned 8-bit field wrapped to 4, which is the default overflow behaviour. You choose the behaviour per operation with OVERFLOW:

127.0.0.1:6379> BITFIELD counters OVERFLOW SAT INCRBY u8 #1 300
1) (integer) 255
127.0.0.1:6379> BITFIELD counters OVERFLOW FAIL INCRBY u8 #0 250
1) (integer) 254
127.0.0.1:6379> BITFIELD counters OVERFLOW FAIL INCRBY u8 #0 10
1) (nil)
127.0.0.1:6379> BITFIELD counters GET u8 #0
1) (integer) 254
127.0.0.1:6379> BITFIELD counters OVERFLOW WRAP INCRBY u8 #0 10
1) (integer) 8
  • SAT saturates at the type's limit (255).
  • FAIL refuses the increment and returns (nil), leaving the value unchanged (254 stays 254).
  • WRAP wraps around (254 + 10 = 264 → 8).

Field offsets with # are multiplied by the field width, so mixing widths over the same bytes gets confusing fast. i16 #1 is bits 16–31, not bits 8–23:

127.0.0.1:6379> BITFIELD counters INCRBY i16 #1 -5 GET i16 #1
1) (integer) -5
2) (integer) -5
127.0.0.1:6379> BITFIELD_RO counters GET u8 #0 GET u8 #1
1) (integer) 254
2) (integer) 255
127.0.0.1:6379> STRLEN counters
(integer) 4
