redis.call('INCRBY', KEYS[2], amt)
return 1
""")

def transfer_lua(c, src, dst, amt):
    return TRANSFER(keys=[src, dst], args=[amt], client=c) == 1

docs.title: The transfer benchmark, again
docs.text:
Same workload as Level 2 · 08 (16 threads, 2,000 random transfers each, 5 accounts of 100), timed with WATCH and with the script:

WATCH  12.08s  total=500 min=22 transfers=21874 retries=56784
Lua     1.70s  total=500 min=6 transfers=25179 retries=0

Both kept the total at 500 and never overdrew an account. The script was 7× faster, with zero retries and a single round trip per transfer. It also completed more transfers. Fewer were refused for insufficient funds, because each decision saw the current balance instead of a balance that was stale by the time EXEC ran. Under contention, scripts win. With rare conflicts and logic that needs client-side data, WATCH is fine.

docs.title: The cost of atomicity: a slow script blocks everyone
docs.text:
While a script runs, the server runs nothing else. Here's a script with an infinite loop, using a 1-second busy-reply-threshold (the default is 5000 ms) so the demo stays short:

r.config_set("busy-reply-threshold", 1000)
# thread 1: c.eval("local i = 0 while true do i = i + 1 end", 0)
# thread 2, 0.2 s later:
other.get("anything")

other client after 0.8s: BUSY Redis is busy running a script. You can only call SCRIPT KILL or SHUTDOWN NOSAVE.
SCRIPT KILL -> True
script client after 1.0s: Script killed by user with SCRIPT KILL... script: 3fcf51a9b854b8f66cb8685600b0d7df968f4398, on @user_script:1.

After the threshold, Redis starts answering other clients with BUSY and allows SCRIPT KILL. But if the script has already written anything, killing it would leave a half-applied change, so Redis refuses:

SCRIPT KILL on a script that wrote -> UNKILLABLE Sorry the script already executed write commands against the
dataset. You can either wait the script termination or kill the server in a hard way using the SHUTDOWN NOSAVE command.

That's not a figure of speech. The lab server had to be shut down with SHUTDOWN NOSAVE and restarted, losing everything since its last save. Keep scripts short and bounded: no unbounded loops, and no KEYS-style scans over large collections inside a script.

docs.title: Redis Functions: named, persistent libraries
docs.text:
Functions fix the script cache's weaknesses. A library is loaded once with FUNCTION LOAD, it's stored in the dataset (so it's persisted in RDB/AOF and replicated), and its functions are called by name with FCALL:

#!lua name=bank

local function transfer(keys, args)
  local amt = tonumber(args[1])
  if not amt or amt <= 0 then
    return redis.error_reply('ERR amount must be a positive number')
  end
  local bal = tonumber(redis.call('GET', keys[1]) or '0')
  if bal < amt then return 0 end
  redis.call('DECRBY', keys[1], amt)
  redis.call('INCRBY', keys[2], amt)
  return 1
end

local function balance(keys, args)
  return tonumber(redis.call('GET', keys[1]) or '0')
end

redis.register_function('transfer', transfer)
redis.register_function{function_name='balance', callback=balance, flags={'no-writes'}}

redis-cli -x FUNCTION LOAD < bank.lua

bank

127.0.0.1:6379> MSET acct:ana 100 acct:ben 0
OK
127.0.0.1:6379> FCALL transfer 2 acct:ana acct:ben 30
(integer) 1
127.0.0.1:6379> FCALL transfer 2 acct:ana acct:ben 500
(integer) 0
127.0.0.1:6379> FCALL transfer 2 acct:ana acct:ben -5
(error) ERR amount must be a positive number
127.0.0.1:6379> FCALL_RO balance 1 acct:ben
(integer) 30
127.0.0.1:6379> FCALL_RO transfer 2 acct:ana acct:ben 1
(error) ERR Can not execute a script with write flag using *_ro command.
  • The no-writes flag allows FCALL_RO, which can run on read-only replicas. The server refused to run the writing function in read-only mode.
  • Loading the same library again fails (ERR Library 'bank' already exists). Deploy new versions with FUNCTION LOAD REPLACE.
  • After the same save-and-restart that emptied the script cache, FUNCTION LIST still showed bank.

Treat function libraries like database migrations. Keep them in version control and load them with REPLACE as part of deployment. Every node, including replicas created later, gets them through replication and persistence.

docs.title: How It Actually Works
docs.text:
Redis embeds a Lua 5.1 interpreter. EVAL hashes the script body with SHA-1, compiles it into a function named after the hash (that's the f_<sha> the cache holds), and calls it with KEYS and ARGV set as globals. redis.call goes through the same command dispatcher a client uses, but within the same execution, so there's no event-loop iteration between calls and no other client runs. Scripts run in a sandbox: global variables can't be created, and libraries like os and io aren't available, which keeps scripts deterministic and safe.

Replication used to send the script itself to replicas, which required scripts to be deterministic. Since Redis 7.0, only effects replication is used: the write commands a script performed are wrapped in MULTI/EXEC and sent to replicas and the AOF. That's why a script can safely use TIME or random numbers, and also why its effects, not its logic, are what's replayed.

During a long script, the server periodically checks the elapsed time from a hook inside the Lua VM. After busy-reply-threshold, it starts processing other connections' input just enough to answer them with BUSY and to accept SCRIPT KILL/SHUTDOWN NOSAVE. SCRIPT KILL raises an error inside the VM, but only if the script hasn't written yet, because there's no undo log to roll a write back.

Functions use the same VM and dispatcher. The difference is lifecycle: the library code is stored in the server's function registry, which is serialized into RDB and AOF and replicated with FUNCTION LOAD. Flags declared at registration (no-writes, allow-oom, allow-stale, …) let the server decide before execution whether a call is allowed in the current context.

docs.title: Common mistakes
docs.text:
• Building key names inside the script instead of passing them in KEYS. It breaks Cluster routing and ACLs.
  • Returning floats and getting truncated integers. Return strings.
  • Writing first, validating later. Errors mid-script leave partial writes. Validate at the top.
  • Long or unbounded scripts. They block everything, and once they've written they can't be killed.
  • Relying on the script cache surviving. Handle NOSCRIPT, or use Functions.
  • Hot-reloading functions without REPLACE, or editing them by hand on one node in production.
  • Using Lua to "speed up" ordinary commands. Pipelining already removes round trips. Use scripts for atomic decisions.

docs.title: Exercise
docs.text:
1. Write the delayed-job claim from Level 1 · 08 as a script: atomically take up to N members of jobs:delayed whose score ≤ now, remove them, and push them onto jobs:ready. Run two pollers and prove no job is taken twice.
  2. Write an idempotent append that works on any Redis version: SET idem:<request-id> 1 NX EX 600 and XADD only if the SET succeeded, returning the previously stored stream ID on retries (store it in the idem key).
  3. Package exercises 1 and 2 as a Functions library jobs with sensible flags, load it, restart the server, and show it's still there.
  4. Measure the overhead of EVALSHA versus a plain INCR with redis-benchmark or a Python loop. When is the script overhead worth paying?

docs.title: 10 · Project — Game Leaderboard & Activity Feed
docs.text:
This project combines Level 2 into one feature set a real game backend needs:

  • a weekly leaderboard that keeps each player's best score, where ties go to whoever got there first;
  • "players around me" and top-N queries;
  • an activity stream of every submission, trimmed automatically;
  • an approximate count of distinct players this week;
  • a Pub/Sub announcement when someone enters the top 10;
  • a badge worker that reads the stream through a consumer group and never double-awards, even after a crash.

The write path, a score submission, touches four structures. It has to be atomic and decide things ("did this beat your best?", "what's your rank now?") based on current data. That's a job for a Redis Function.

docs.title: The score encoding
docs.text:
Sorted sets break ties alphabetically (Level 1 · 08). To make equal points rank by submission time, pack both into one score:

score = points × 2^20 + (2^20 − 1 − seconds_since_week_start)

A week is 604,800 seconds, which is less than 2^20 (1,048,576). So the time part never overflows into the points part. With equal points, an earlier submission leaves a larger remainder and ranks higher. Doubles hold integers exactly up to 2^53, so points can go up to 2^33 (about 8.6 billion) before precision is lost. ZADD GT keeps the higher composite, which gives "personal best" semantics. A later submission with equal points doesn't replace the earlier one, because its composite is smaller.

docs.title: The function library
docs.text:
leaderboard.lua:

#!lua name=leaderboard

-- score layout: points * 2^20 + (2^20 - 1 - seconds since week start)
-- a week is 604,800 s < 2^20, so equal points rank the EARLIER submission higher
local SHIFT = 1048576

local function submit(keys, args)
  local board, activity, players = keys[1], keys[2], keys[3]
  local player, points = args[1], tonumber(args[2])
  local now_ms, week_start_ms = tonumber(args[3]), tonumber(args[4])
  local maxlen = args[5]
  if not points or points < 0 or points ~= math.floor(points) then
    return redis.error_reply('ERR points must be a non-negative integer')
  end
  local secs = math.floor((now_ms - week_start_ms) / 1000)
  if secs < 0 or secs >= SHIFT then
    return redis.error_reply('ERR timestamp outside this week')
  end
  local composite = points * SHIFT + (SHIFT - 1 - secs)
  local improved = redis.call('ZADD', board, 'GT', 'CH', composite, player)
  local rank = redis.call('ZREVRANK', board, player)
  redis.call('PFADD', players, player)
  redis.call('XADD', activity, 'MAXLEN', '~', maxlen, '*',
             'player', player, 'points', points, 'best', tostring(improved == 1), 'rank', rank + 1)
  if improved == 1 and rank < 10 then
    redis.call('PUBLISH', board .. ':top10', player .. ' is now #' .. (rank + 1))
  end
  return {improved, rank + 1}
end

redis.register_function('lb_submit', submit)

Notes:

  • All three keys come in through KEYS and share the hash tag {<game>}, so in Cluster they live in one slot and the function can run there (Level 4 · 05).
  • Validation comes first, and the writes come after, so a bad input can't leave a partial update (Level 2 · 09).
  • ZADD GT CH returns 1 only if the score was changed, which is exactly "improved your best".
  • The activity entry records whether it was a best and the rank at the time. The stream is trimmed with MAXLEN ~, so it costs nothing extra to keep bounded.
  • PUBLISH inside a function is fine. Like any write, it's propagated as an effect.

docs.title: The Python side
docs.text:
game.py:

"""Weekly game leaderboard + activity feed (Level 2 project)."""
import datetime as dt
import time
from pathlib import Path

import redis

SHIFT = 1 << 20
LIB = Path(__file__).with_name("leaderboard.lua").read_text()


def week_start(now: float) -> dt.datetime:
    d = dt.datetime.fromtimestamp(now, tz=dt.timezone.utc)
    monday = d - dt.timedelta(days=d.weekday())
    return monday.replace(hour=0, minute=0, second=0, microsecond=0)


def decode(composite: float) -> int:
    return int(composite) // SHIFT


class Leaderboard:
    def __init__(self, r: redis.Redis, game: str = "arena", feed_len: int = 1000):
        self.r, self.game, self.feed_len = r, game, feed_len
        r.function_load(LIB, replace=True)

    def _keys(self, now):
        ws = week_start(now)
        tag = ws.strftime("%G-W%V")                      # ISO week, e.g. 2026-W42
        base = f"lb:{{{self.game}}}"                     # hash tag keeps all keys in one slot
        return ws, (f"{base}:board:{tag}", f"{base}:activity", f"{base}:players:{tag}")

    def submit(self, player: str, points: int, now: float | None = None):
        now = time.time() if now is None else now
        ws, keys = self._keys(now)
        improved, rank = self.r.fcall("lb_submit", 3, *keys, player, points,
                                      int(now * 1000), int(ws.timestamp() * 1000), self.feed_len)
        board = keys[0]
        self.r.expire(board, 35 * 24 * 3600, nx=True)    # keep ~5 weeks of boards
        self.r.expire(keys[2], 35 * 24 * 3600, nx=True)
        return bool(improved), rank

    def top(self, n=10, now=None):
        _, (board, _, _) = self._keys(time.time() if now is None else now)
        rows = self.r.zrange(board, 0, n - 1, desc=True, withscores=True)
        return [(i + 1, p, decode(s)) for i, (p, s) in enumerate(rows)]

    def around(self, player, k=2, now=None):
        _, (board, _, _) = self._keys(time.time() if now is None else now)
        rank = self.r.zrevrank(board, player)
        if rank is None:
            return []
        start = max(0, rank - k)
        rows = self.r.zrange(board, start, rank + k, desc=True, withscores=True)
        return [(start + i + 1, p, decode(s)) for i, (p, s) in enumerate(rows)]

    def players_this_week(self, now=None):
        _, (_, _, players) = self._keys(time.time() if now is None else now)
        return self.r.pfcount(players)

    def feed(self, n=5):
        _, (_, activity, _) = self._keys(time.time())
        return [f for _, f in self.r.xrevrange(activity, count=n)]

Boards are per ISO week (2026-W42), so a "weekly reset" is just a new key. Old boards keep a 35-day TTL, set once with EXPIRE … NX, so history is available for a few weeks and then disappears without a cleanup job.

achievements.py, the badge worker:

"""Consumer-group worker: awards badges from the activity stream, at-least-once, idempotently."""
import redis

BADGES = [(1000, "bronze"), (5000, "silver"), (10000, "gold")]


def ensure_group(r, stream, group="badges"):
    try:
        r.xgroup_create(stream, group, id="0", mkstream=True)
    except redis.ResponseError as e:
        if "BUSYGROUP" not in str(e):
            raise


def process_batch(r, stream, consumer, group="badges", count=50, min_idle_ms=30000):
    _, msgs, _ = r.xautoclaim(stream, group, consumer, min_idle_time=min_idle_ms, start_id="0-0", count=count)
    if not msgs:
        res = r.xreadgroup(group, consumer, {stream: ">"}, count=count, block=100)
        msgs = res[0][1] if res else []
    awarded = 0
    for msg_id, f in msgs:
        pts = int(f["points"])
        for threshold, badge in BADGES:
            if pts >= threshold:
                # SADD returns 1 only the first time: re-delivery never double-awards
                awarded += r.sadd(f"badges:{f['player']}", badge)
        r.xack(stream, group, msg_id)
    return len(msgs), awarded

The worker follows the recovery loop from Level 2 · 06: claim stale entries first, then read new ones. Badges are stored in a set, so SADD's return value tells you whether this delivery actually awarded anything new. A message delivered twice (after a crash) awards nothing the second time. At-least-once delivery plus an idempotent handler gives effectively-once results.

import threading, time
import pytest, redis
from game import Leaderboard, week_start
from achievements import ensure_group, process_batch

NOW = 1791856800.0          # a fixed instant (Tue 2026-10-13 UTC) so tests are deterministic

@pytest.fixture
def lb():
    r = redis.Redis(db=0, decode_responses=True)
    for k in r.scan_iter("lb:{test}*"): r.unlink(k)
    for k in r.scan_iter("badges:*"): r.unlink(k)

    for k in r.scan_iter("lb:{test}*"): r.unlink(k)

def test_personal_best_only_goes_up(lb):
    assert lb.submit("ana", 500, NOW) == (True, 1)
    assert lb.submit("ana", 300, NOW + 1) == (False, 1)
    assert lb.submit("ana", 900, NOW + 2) == (True, 1)
    assert lb.top(1, NOW) == [(1, "ana", 900)]

def test_ties_go_to_whoever_got_there_first(lb):

    lb.submit("early", 700, NOW + 10)
    lb.submit("ben", 650, NOW)
    assert [p for _, p, _ in lb.top(3, NOW)] == ["early", "late", "ben"]

def test_equal_score_later_does_not_replace_earlier(lb):
    lb.submit("ana", 700, NOW)
    improved, _ = lb.submit("ana", 700, NOW + 100)
    assert improved is False

def test_rejects_bad_points(lb):
    with pytest.raises(redis.ResponseError, match="non-negative integer"):
        lb.submit("ana", -5, NOW)

def test_around_me(lb):
    for i in range(20):
        lb.submit(f"p{i:02}", i * 10, NOW)
    around = lb.around("p10", k=2, now=NOW)
    assert [(rank, p) for rank, p, _ in around] == [(8, "p12"), (9, "p11"), (10, "p10"), (11, "p09"), (12, "p08")]
    assert lb.around("nobody", now=NOW) == []

def test_new_week_new_board(lb):
    lb.submit("ana", 100, NOW)
    next_week = week_start(NOW).timestamp() + 7 * 24 * 3600 + 5
    lb.submit("ben", 50, next_week)
    assert [p for _, p, _ in lb.top(5, NOW)] == ["ana"]
    assert [p for _, p, _ in lb.top(5, next_week)] == ["ben"]

def test_concurrent_submissions_keep_max(lb):
    def player(i):
        for s in range(0, 2000, 7):
            lb.submit(f"c{i}", s, NOW)
    ts = [threading.Thread(target=player, args=(i,)) for i in range(8)]
    [t.start() for t in ts]; [t.join() for t in ts]
    top = lb.top(8, NOW)
    assert all(score == 1995 for _, _, score in top) and len(top) == 8

def test_feed_and_uniques(lb):
    lb.submit("ana", 10, NOW); lb.submit("ben", 20, NOW); lb.submit("ana", 5, NOW)
    feed = lb.feed(3)
    assert [(f["player"], f["points"], f["best"]) for f in feed] == [("ana", "5", "false"), ("ben", "20", "true"), ("ana", "10", "true")]
    assert lb.players_this_week(NOW) == 2

def test_feed_is_trimmed(lb):
    for i in range(1000):
        lb.submit(f"x{i}", i, NOW)
    assert lb.r.xlen("lb:{test}:activity") < 1000

def test_top10_announcements(lb):
    p = lb.r.pubsub(); p.subscribe("lb:{test}:board:2026-W42:top10"); time.sleep(0.1)
    lb.submit("ana", 100, NOW)
    msgs = []
    end = time.time() + 1
    while time.time() < end:
        m = p.get_message(timeout=0.1)
        if m and m["type"] == "message": msgs.append(m["data"])
    assert msgs == ["ana is now #1"]

def test_badges_awarded_once_even_if_redelivered(lb):
    stream = "lb:{test}:activity"
    lb.submit("ana", 1200, NOW); lb.submit("ana", 6000, NOW + 1)
    ensure_group(lb.r, stream)
    # consumer "crashy" reads but never acks

    assert (n, awarded) == (2, 2) and awarded2 == 0
    assert lb.r.smembers("badges:ana") == {"bronze", "silver"}
    assert lb.r.xpending(stream, "badges")["pending"] == 0

import random, threading, time
import redis
from game import Leaderboard
r = redis.Redis(decode_responses=True)

random.seed(5)

t = time.perf_counter()

docs.title: How It Actually Works
docs.text:
Each submission is one FCALL, executed atomically on the server. Inside it: ZADD GT CH (O(log N)), ZREVRANK (O(log N), using the skip-list spans from Level 1 · 08), PFADD (O(1)), XADD with approximate trimming (amortized O(1)) and, rarely, a PUBLISH. No other client can see the board updated without the activity entry, or read a rank that doesn't match the score just written.

Ranks are read after the ZADD, inside the same function, so the rank in the activity entry and in the return value is exactly the rank the submission produced. A client doing ZADD and then ZREVRANK in two round trips could report a rank that someone else's submission had already changed.

The week tag is computed by the client from its clock, and the secs bound check in the function rejects timestamps outside the week. If app servers' clocks disagree near midnight on Sunday, a submission can land on the "wrong" week. Using the Redis server's time (redis.call('TIME')) inside the function would remove that dependency, at the cost of making tests harder to pin. That's a trade-off worth knowing you made.

docs.title: Common mistakes
docs.text:
• Separate ZADD and ZREVRANK round trips to report "your new rank". It's racy. Compute it in the same atomic unit.
  • Alphabetical tie-breaking by accident. Encode the tie-breaker into the score, and check the arithmetic against 2^53.
  • A forever-growing activity log. Trim on every XADD.
  • Non-idempotent consumers. A redelivered "award gold badge" must not award twice.
  • Weekly resets by deleting the board with a cron job. Rotate key names, and let TTLs clean up.
  • Keys without a shared hash tag in a multi-key function. It works on one node and fails in Cluster.

docs.title: Exercise
docs.text:
1. Add per-country boards (board:<week>:<country>) updated in the same FCALL, and a top_in_country method. What changes about the keys you pass, and what does that mean for Cluster?
  2. Move the two EXPIRE … NX calls into the function and measure the throughput change with demo.py.
  3. Use the server clock (redis.call('TIME')) inside the function instead of client timestamps. How do you keep the tests deterministic now?
  4. Add an all-time board that tracks the best score ever, updated with the same function. What's the size of the all-time board after a year if 2 million distinct players have played? Estimate it from this lesson's bytes-per-member, then measure it.

docs.title: Level 3 · Caching & Application Patterns
docs.text:
Level 3 is about the jobs Redis is hired for: caching, rate limiting, locking, sessions, job queues, documents and search. Each one looks like a few lines of code, and each has a failure mode that only shows up under concurrency or at the worst possible moment. That's why every lesson here reproduces the failure before fixing it:

  • a stale price cached for five minutes, whether the writer deletes the key or overwrites it;
  • 50 database calls for one expired key;
  • a fixed-window limiter that let through 20 requests in 20 ms against a limit of 10;
  • a correctly implemented lock that still let two clients write, until fencing tokens rejected the stale one;
  • kill -9 losing jobs from a BLPOP queue but none from a BLMOVE queue;
  • an HNSW vector index that found only 68% of the true nearest neighbours with default settings.

Everything was run on Redis 8.10.2 with redis-py 8.1.0, and the JSON, search and probabilistic modules loaded. The project uses FastAPI 0.143.0 under Uvicorn 0.54.0.

Prerequisites: Levels 1 and 2. In particular, Level 2 · 08–09 on transactions and Lua scripts, which almost every pattern here relies on.

docs.title: Modules
docs.text:
1. Caching Patterns: Cache-Aside to Write-Behind — a cache at 97.7% hits in front of SQLite, the stale-write race that defeats delete-on-write, a versioned fix, write-through and write-behind.
  2. maxmemory, Eviction & How Expiry Really Works — OOM errors under noeviction, the volatile-* trap, LFU vs LRU measured, and how expired keys are reclaimed.
  3. Cache Stampedes & Invalidation — rebuild locks, XFetch and stale-while-revalidate compared, TTL jitter, and invalidating groups of keys.
  4. Rate Limiting Algorithms — fixed window, sliding log, sliding window counter and token bucket as atomic scripts, with boundary bursts and memory measured.
  5. Distributed Locks & Their Limits — SET NX PX with tokens, safe release, the paused-holder failure, fencing tokens and the Redlock debate.
  6. Sessions & Client-Side Caching — secure session IDs, sliding and absolute expiry, rotation, logout-everywhere, and CLIENT TRACKING with redis-py's local cache.
  7. Reliable Job Queues — a kill -9 crash test, processing lists, heartbeats, reapers, retries, dead letters, delays, and lists vs streams.
  8. JSON Documents — JSONPath reads, atomic nested updates, merge semantics, and when the JSON type is worth twice the memory.
  9. Query Engine: Secondary Indexes & Vector Search — TEXT/TAG/NUMERIC/GEO indexes, aggregations, a negation trap, FLAT vs HNSW recall, and vector sets.
  10. Project — Caching & Rate-Limiting Layer for an API — a tested FastAPI service with per-client limits, stampede-proof caching and stale-while-revalidate, plus the race its tests caught.

docs.title: After Level 3
docs.text: Your application logic is correct. Level 4 makes the server it depends on survive: RDB snapshots and the AOF, replication and failover with Sentinel, Redis Cluster and resharding, ACLs and TLS, monitoring and troubleshooting, versions and licensing (including Valkey), and a capstone that builds a secured, persistent cluster, fails it over under load, and measures exactly what was lost.

docs.title: 01 · Caching Patterns: Cache-Aside to Write-Behind
docs.text: Caching is the job Redis is hired for most often, and the one most often done subtly wrong. Putting values in Redis is easy. The hard parts are deciding who writes the cache, when it's invalidated, and what happens when reads and writes race. This lesson builds a cache in front of a real database (SQLite, with 5 ms of artificial latency so it behaves like a database across a network), measures what it buys you, and then reproduces the race that makes the textbook pattern serve stale data for minutes.

docs.title: Cache-aside (lazy loading)
docs.text:
The application checks the cache first. On a miss it reads the database and stores the result with a TTL:

import json, random, sqlite3, statistics, time
import redis

r = redis.Redis(decode_responses=True)
db = sqlite3.connect("shop.db", check_same_thread=False)
# ... table `products` with 10,000 rows ...

DB_LATENCY = 0.005          # pretend the real database is 5 ms away

def db_get_product(pid):
    time.sleep(DB_LATENCY)
    row = db.execute("SELECT id, name, price_cents, stock FROM products WHERE id=?", (pid,)).fetchone()
    return None if row is None else dict(zip(("id", "name", "price_cents", "stock"), row))

def get_product(pid, ttl=300):
    key = f"cache:v1:product:{pid}"
    cached = r.get(key)
    if cached is not None:
        return json.loads(cached)                    # hit (may be the cached "null")
    product = db_get_product(pid)                    # miss: go to the source of truth
    r.set(key, json.dumps(product), ex=ttl if product else 30)   # cache misses briefly too
    return product

Run 5,000 requests with long-tailed popularity (a few products are very popular, most rarely requested), first straight to the database and then through the cache. The hit ratio comes from the server's keyspace_hits and keyspace_misses counters:

no cache    : mean  7.06 ms  p50  7.10 ms  p99 10.46 ms
cache-aside : mean  0.33 ms  p50  0.12 ms  p99  8.04 ms  hit ratio 97.7%
cached keys: 113
  • With a 97.7% hit ratio, the mean latency fell from 7.06 ms to 0.33 ms, about 20×.
  • The p99 barely moved (10.5 → 8.0 ms). The slowest 1% are the misses, which still pay for the database plus a Redis round trip. Caches improve averages far more than tails. If your SLO is on p99, the cold path still matters.
  • Only 113 products were ever requested, so a cache sized for a fraction of the catalogue served nearly everything. This is why caching works at all: real access patterns are skewed.

Details in that small function that matter in production:

  • A version segment in the key (v1). When the cached format changes, deploy v2. Old entries are simply never read again and expire on their own.
  • A TTL on everything. It's the safety net for every invalidation bug below.
  • Negative caching. A product that doesn't exist is cached as null for 30 s. Otherwise a flood of requests for a missing ID (a bot, or a broken link) goes straight to the database every time.
  • JSON, not pickle. Never unpickle data from a shared cache. Anyone who can write the key can then run code in your process.

docs.title: The race that serves stale data
docs.text:
The standard advice is "on update, write the database, then delete the cache key". Here are two requests, interleaved with thread events so the interleaving is deterministic:

  1. A reader misses the cache and reads the price from the database: 1000.
  2. A writer updates the price to 1500 and invalidates the cache.
  3. The reader, which was slow (GC pause, network hiccup), now writes what it read, 1000, into the cache.
def scenario(writer_strategy):
    db_set_price(1000); r.delete(KEY)
    read_db_done, writer_done = threading.Event(), threading.Event()
    def reader():                       # a cache miss that is slow to write back
        price = db_price()              # reads OLD price 1000
        read_db_done.set(); writer_done.wait()
        r.set(KEY, json.dumps({"price_cents": price}), ex=300)
    def writer():
        read_db_done.wait()
        db_set_price(1500)              # the update
        writer_strategy()
        writer_done.set()
    ...

print("update DB, then DEL cache   -> db=%s cache=%s ttl=%s" % scenario(lambda: r.delete(KEY)))
print("update DB, then SET cache   -> db=%s cache=%s ttl=%s" %
      scenario(lambda: r.set(KEY, json.dumps({"price_cents": 1500}), ex=300)))

update DB, then DEL cache   -> db=1500 cache=1000 ttl=300
update DB, then SET cache   -> db=1500 cache=1000 ttl=300

Both strategies end with the old price cached for the full 5 minutes. Deleting doesn't help, because the delete happens before the stale write-back. Writing the new value doesn't help either, because the stale write-back overwrites it. The window is small, but at thousands of requests per second it gets hit, and nothing ever corrects it except the TTL.

docs.title: A fix: versioned write-back
docs.text:
Make the write-back conditional. Writers bump a version counter after changing the database. A reader notes the version before reading the database, and only writes to the cache if it's still the same, checked atomically in a script:

VER = "cache:ver:product:7"
SET_IF_VERSION = r.register_script("""
if (redis.call('GET', KEYS[2]) or '0') == ARGV[1] then
  return redis.call('SET', KEYS[1], ARGV[2], 'EX', ARGV[3])
end
return false
""")

def reader():
    ver = r.get(VER) or "0"
    price = db_price()
    ...
    SET_IF_VERSION(keys=[KEY, VER], args=[ver, json.dumps({"price_cents": price}), 300])

def writer():
    db_set_price(1500); r.incr(VER); r.delete(KEY)

versioned write-back        -> db=1500 cache=None reader-wrote=None

The stale write-back was refused (reader-wrote=None) and the cache is empty, so the next read loads 1500. Other approaches exist: a short "do not cache" lease set by the writer, or a TTL short enough that occasional staleness is acceptable. What matters is that you choose one knowingly. For many caches (product descriptions, avatars) a few minutes of staleness is fine and the TTL is the whole strategy. For prices, permissions and balances it isn't.

docs.title: Write-through
docs.text:
In write-through, every write goes to the database and then the cache in the same code path, so the cache is always populated for recently written data:

def update_product(pid, **changes):
    db_update(pid, changes)                          # 1. source of truth first
    product = db_get_product(pid)                    # 2. read back what was committed
    r.set(f"cache:v1:product:{pid}", json.dumps(product), ex=300)   # 3. refresh the cache

It avoids the first-read miss after a write, but it doesn't remove the race above (a concurrent slow reader can still overwrite step 3), and it caches data that may never be read. It's often combined with cache-aside for reads. Never write the cache first: if the database write then fails, the cache holds a value that never existed.

docs.title: Write-behind (write-back)
docs.text:
In write-behind, the application writes to Redis and a background job writes to the database later in batches. It suits high-volume, loss-tolerant updates like view counters, "last seen" times and analytics. Here 100,000 page views are recorded with one HINCRBY each, and one flush moves them to SQLite:

def record_view(page):                     # hot path: one Redis command, no DB write
    r.hincrby("views:pending", page, 1)

def flush():                               # runs every few seconds in a background job
    p = r.pipeline(transaction=True)       # atomically take the pending counts and reset
    p.hgetall("views:pending"); p.delete("views:pending")
    pending, _ = p.execute()
    db.executemany("INSERT INTO page_views VALUES (?, ?) ON CONFLICT(page) DO UPDATE "
                   "SET views = views + excluded.views",
                   [(k, int(v)) for k, v in pending.items()])
    db.commit()
    return len(pending)

100,000 views recorded in 14.40s
flushed 50 rows in 6.6 ms
db total: (100000, 50)

The database received 50 row updates instead of 100,000, and the totals match. (The 14.4 s is 100,000 sequential round trips from one Python thread. Pipelining would cut it, as Level 1 · 02 showed.) The MULTI makes "read and reset" atomic, so views recorded between the two commands aren't lost. The risk is the window between flushes: if Redis loses data (no persistence, or a failover with replication lag, Level 4), those counts are gone. If the flush crashes after EXEC but before commit, they're gone too. Only use write-behind for data where that's acceptable, or make the hand-off durable (a stream with a consumer group instead of a hash).

docs.title: Choosing
docs.text: Pattern Who fills the cache Staleness risk Good for Cache-aside + TTL readers, on miss up to TTL after a write (race) most read-heavy data Cache-aside + versioned write-back readers, conditionally until next read data where stale is harmful Write-through writers race still possible read-after-write heavy data Write-behind app writes Redis, job writes DB DB lags; loss on Redis failure counters, analytics

docs.title: How It Actually Works
docs.text:
A cache is a second copy of data with no transaction spanning both copies. Every pattern above is a different answer to "in which order do the two copies change, and who is allowed to write the second one?". The stale-cache race exists because the cache write is based on a database read that happened earlier. By the time the write lands, it reflects a past state. Deletion-based invalidation can't stop it, because nothing ties the write-back to the version of the data that was read. The version counter supplies that tie: it's a logical clock for the row, and the script compares and sets atomically on the single Redis thread, so no writer's increment can slip between the comparison and the SET.

The hit ratio comes from INFO stats: every read command that finds a key increments keyspace_hits, and every one that doesn't increments keyspace_misses. Taking the difference before and after a run measures that run. In production, graph hits / (hits + misses) per instance. A sudden drop usually means a deploy changed key names, a flush happened, or the cache is evicting (next lesson).

docs.title: Common mistakes
docs.text:
• No TTL "because we invalidate on write". Every invalidation bug then becomes permanent.
  • Trusting delete-on-write to prevent staleness. The race above defeats it.
  • Writing the cache before the database. A failed DB write leaves a phantom value.
  • Caching per-user or per-request data under shared keys. One user sees another's data. Put the user in the key, or don't cache it.
  • Unbounded key cardinality (caching every search query string forever). Use TTLs and maxmemory with an eviction policy.
  • Pickle in a shared cache. It's a remote code execution risk.
  • Measuring averages only. Look at p99, where the misses live.

docs.title: Exercise
docs.text:
1. Add a stats() helper that reports the hit ratio for the last minute using INFO stats deltas, and run the benchmark with TTLs of 1 s, 10 s and 300 s. Plot hit ratio against TTL.
  2. Reproduce the stale-write race without thread events: run 20 reader threads and 1 writer that bumps the price every 10 ms for 10 s, and count how many times the cache disagrees with the database once the writer stops. Then apply the versioned write-back and count again.
  3. Change the write-behind counter to use a stream and a consumer group so a crash between EXEC and commit loses nothing. What does the flusher acknowledge, and when?
  4. Implement negative caching for a "user by email" lookup, and explain what goes wrong if the negative entry's TTL is 1 hour and the user signs up 5 minutes later.

docs.title: 02 · maxmemory, Eviction & How Expiry Really Works
docs.text: A cache has to forget things, and Redis forgets in two ways. Expiry removes keys whose TTL has passed. Eviction removes keys, TTL or not, when memory reaches the maxmemory limit. Both run quietly in the background, and both behave differently from what most people assume. This lesson measures them on a scratch server on port 6430.

docs.title: The default: no limit, no eviction
docs.text:
127.0.0.1:6430> CONFIG GET maxmemory
1) "maxmemory"
2) "0"
127.0.0.1:6430> CONFIG GET maxmemory-policy
1) "maxmemory-policy"
2) "noeviction"

maxmemory 0 means "no limit" on 64-bit builds. Redis grows until the operating system or a container limit stops it, and the OOM killer is a much worse eviction policy than any of Redis's. Always set maxmemory on a server that holds a cache, leaving headroom below the machine or container limit for fragmentation, client buffers and the copy-on-write memory of a snapshot (Level 4 · 01).

What happens at the limit depends on the policy. With the default noeviction, set a 20 MB limit and keep writing:

r.config_set("maxmemory", "20mb")
n = 0
try:
    while True:
        r.set(f"k:{n}", "v" * 64); n += 1
except redis.ResponseError as e:
    print(f"after {n} keys: {e}")
print("GET still works:", r.get("k:1")[:8], "| DEL works:", r.delete("k:1"))

after 152861 keys: command not allowed when used memory > 'maxmemory'.
used_memory_human: 20.00M
GET still works: b'vvvvvvvv' | DEL works: 1
INFO stats evicted_keys: 0

Writes that could add memory fail with an error. Reads and deletes keep working. That's the right behaviour for Redis used as a primary store, a queue or a lock service, where silently dropping data would be a bug. It's the wrong behaviour for a cache, where you want old entries to make room for new ones.

docs.title: The eviction policies
docs.text:
Policy Evicts from Chooses noeviction — refuses writes allkeys-lru all keys least recently used (approximate) allkeys-lfu all keys least frequently used (approximate) allkeys-random all keys random volatile-lru / volatile-lfu / volatile-random only keys with a TTL as above volatile-ttl only keys with a TTL shortest remaining TTL

The volatile-* policies are meant for a server that mixes cache entries (with TTLs) and data that must not be evicted (without TTLs). Their trap is that if no keys have a TTL, there is nothing they're allowed to evict:

volatile-lru, keys without TTL: failed after 66031 keys: command not allowed when used memory > 'maxmemory'.

That's the same OOM error as noeviction. If a code path forgets to set TTLs, a volatile-* server behaves like an un-evicting one. A cleaner design is to keep durable data and cache data on separate instances, each with the policy that suits it.

docs.title: LRU vs LFU, measured
docs.text:
This benchmark uses 200,000 items with Zipf-like popularity (item k requested with weight 1/k^0.9), a 12 MB limit that holds about 10,700 of the 1 KB values (about 5% of the items), and a one-off batch job in the middle that reads 30,000 cold keys once each, as a report or a crawler might. Each request is a cache-aside GET, followed by a SET on a miss:

N_ITEMS = 200_000
WEIGHTS = [1 / (k ** 0.9) for k in range(1, N_ITEMS + 1)]      # Zipf-like popularity
def workload(seed):
    rnd = random.Random(seed)
    hot = rnd.choices(range(1, N_ITEMS + 1), weights=WEIGHTS, k=270_000)
    # requests 100k..130k are a one-off batch job reading 30k distinct cold keys once each
    return ([f"item:{k}" for k in hot[:100_000]] + [f"cold:{i}" for i in range(30_000)]
            + [f"item:{k}" for k in hot[100_000:]])

for policy in ("allkeys-lru", "allkeys-lfu", "allkeys-random"):
    r.flushall(); r.config_set("maxmemory", "12mb"); r.config_set("maxmemory-policy", policy)
    ...   # MGET 500 keys at a time, SET the misses, count hits

allkeys-lru     overall hit  43.3%  just after the batch job  41.4%  evicted  157407  keys now 10762
allkeys-lfu     overall hit  51.1%  just after the batch job  56.5%  evicted  135662  keys now 10768
allkeys-random  overall hit  43.0%  just after the batch job  42.3%  evicted  158256  keys now 10747
  • LFU won clearly: 51.1% against 43.3% overall, and 56.5% against 41.4% in the 30,000 requests right after the batch job. LFU remembers that popular items are popular, so it didn't let 30,000 one-time reads push them out. LRU sees only "recently touched", and the batch job touched everything recently.
  • LRU did no better than random here. With a long-tailed workload and a cache holding 5% of items, recency alone is a weak signal, and Redis's LRU is an approximation (below).
  • On a less skewed workload, an earlier run of this script saw all three policies within 0.6 points of each other. Measure with your own access pattern before switching. INFO stats keyspace_hits/misses and evicted_keys are all you need.

docs.title: How expiry really works
docs.text:
A key whose TTL has passed is never returned. Any command that touches it first checks the deadline and deletes it (lazy expiry). Keys nobody touches are removed by the active expiry cycle, which samples keys that have TTLs several times a second. Here 500,000 keys get a 1-second TTL and are never read, while DBSIZE is polled every 0.5 s:

hz=10: (seconds after writing, keys still in memory) -> [(0.5, 119707), (1.0, 18234), (1.5, 0)]
hz=100: (seconds after writing, keys still in memory) -> [(0.5, 121322), (1.0, 41087), (1.5, 0)]

(Writing the keys took longer than a second, so the earliest ones had already expired at the first sample.) All 500,000 were gone within about half a second of the last deadline, at both hz settings. When the sampler finds a high share of expired keys, it keeps going instead of stopping at its normal time budget, so a mass expiry is cleaned up quickly. What hz didn't visibly change here, it changes in the opposite case: a few expired keys scattered among millions of live ones are found more slowly, which is why Level 2 · 07's expired notifications arrived 130–324 ms late. INFO stats reports expired_keys and expired_stale_perc (the sampler's estimate of how much of the keyspace is expired but not yet deleted).

Two consequences:

  • Memory isn't freed at the deadline. Expired keys still count towards used_memory until they're reclaimed. Under memory pressure, eviction may remove live keys while expired ones are still waiting.
  • Expiry is not a timer. Don't build "do X when this key expires" on it if X has to happen on time.

docs.title: How It Actually Works
docs.text:
Eviction runs before each command that might use memory. If used_memory is above maxmemory, Redis frees keys until it's below, or fails the command if the policy finds nothing to evict. It doesn't keep a global LRU list, because that would cost two pointers per key and a list update on every access. Instead, each object has a 24-bit clock field. For LRU it's a coarse "last accessed" timestamp. For LFU it's an 8-bit logarithmic counter plus a 16-bit decay time: the counter grows probabilistically (each hit is less likely to increment it as it gets higher, controlled by lfu-log-factor), and it decays over time (lfu-decay-time), so yesterday's hot keys cool off. OBJECT FREQ key shows a key's counter when an LFU policy is active.

To pick a victim, Redis samples maxmemory-samples keys (default 5) and adds the best candidates to a small eviction pool of 16 entries kept sorted by idle time or frequency, then evicts the worst key in the pool. The pool carries good candidates over from earlier samples, which makes the approximation surprisingly close to true LRU/LFU. Raising maxmemory-samples to 10 makes it closer still, at some CPU cost.

Active expiry runs from serverCron (hz times per second) and also in a fast cycle before the event loop sleeps. Each pass samples keys from the expires dictionary of each database, 20 at a time, deletes the expired ones, and repeats while more than 10% of a sample was expired, within a CPU-time budget. active-expire-effort (1–10) scales those numbers. Since Redis 6 the cycle also remembers where it stopped in each database's expires table, so it eventually visits everything instead of relying purely on luck. Deletions caused by expiry and eviction are synchronous unless lazyfree-lazy-expire / lazyfree-lazy-eviction are on (Level 1 · 04), so evicting huge keys can cause latency spikes.

On replicas, keys aren't expired independently. The primary sends a DEL when it expires a key, and in the meantime a replica hides logically expired keys from reads so clients don't see them.

docs.title: Common mistakes
docs.text:
• No maxmemory. The OS will "evict" the whole process.
  • noeviction on a cache. Writes start failing at the limit, which usually surfaces as application errors rather than a cache problem.
  • volatile-* with keys that lack TTLs. It behaves like noeviction once those keys fill memory.
  • Mixing a cache and durable data under allkeys-*. Your queue or lock keys can be evicted.
  • Assuming LRU is best. Measure. LFU handled one-off scans much better here.
  • Using expiry as a scheduler, or expecting memory to drop the instant TTLs pass.
  • maxmemory equal to the container limit. Fork-based persistence, buffers and fragmentation need headroom.

docs.title: Exercise
docs.text:
1. Rerun the policy benchmark with the cache sized at 1%, 5% and 20% of the items. At which size does the choice of policy stop mattering?
  2. With allkeys-lfu, request one key 1,000 times and another 10 times, then compare OBJECT FREQ. Wait a few minutes (or lower lfu-decay-time to 1) and check again.
  3. Fill a 50 MB server with 1-hour-TTL keys under volatile-ttl, then write keys with 10-second TTLs. Which keys get evicted first, and is that what a session store would want?
  4. Set 1,000 keys with a 1-second TTL among 2 million keys without TTLs. Measure how long until all 1,000 are gone with hz 10 and hz 100, without ever reading them.

docs.title: 03 · Cache Stampedes & Invalidation
docs.text:
A cache protects a slow backend only while it holds the answer. The moment a popular key expires, every request that arrives before someone rebuilds it misses at the same time, and each one runs the expensive query. That's a cache stampede (or thundering herd), and it tends to strike exactly when traffic is highest. A cache sized to cut database load 50× can, for a few hundred milliseconds, multiply it.

This lesson reproduces a stampede against a "report query" that takes 200 ms, then compares three defences.

docs.title: The experiment
docs.text:
import json, math, random, threading, time, uuid
import redis
r = redis.Redis(decode_responses=True)
db_calls = 0; lock = threading.Lock()

def expensive_query():
    global db_calls
    with lock: db_calls += 1
    time.sleep(0.2)                         # a 200 ms report query
    return {"total": 42, "at": time.time()}

# 1. naive cache-aside
def get_naive(key):
    v = r.get(key)
    if v: return json.loads(v)
    val = expensive_query(); r.set(key, json.dumps(val), ex=60); return val

# 2. one rebuilder at a time, everyone else waits for the result
def get_locked(key, ttl=60, lock_ms=5000):
    while True:
        v = r.get(key)
        if v: return json.loads(v)
        token = uuid.uuid4().hex
        if r.set(f"{key}:lock", token, nx=True, px=lock_ms):
            try:
                val = expensive_query(); r.set(key, json.dumps(val), ex=ttl); return val
            finally:
                r.eval("if redis.call('GET',KEYS[1])==ARGV[1] then return redis.call('DEL',KEYS[1]) end return 0",
                       1, f"{key}:lock", token)            # release only our own lock
        time.sleep(0.02)                    # someone else is rebuilding; poll

# 3. probabilistic early expiration (XFetch): recompute *before* expiry with rising probability
def get_xfetch(key, ttl=60, beta=1.0):
    p = r.pipeline(transaction=False); p.get(key); p.pttl(key)
    v, pttl = p.execute()
    if v:
        data = json.loads(v)
        delta = data["compute_s"]           # how long the last rebuild took
        if -delta * beta * math.log(random.random()) < pttl / 1000:
            return data["value"]            # not yet: serve cached
    t = time.perf_counter(); val = expensive_query()
    r.set(key, json.dumps({"value": val, "compute_s": time.perf_counter() - t}), ex=ttl)
    return val

# 4. stale-while-revalidate: a soft TTL inside the value, a longer hard TTL on the key
def get_swr(key, ttl=60, grace=300):
    v = r.get(key)
    if v:
        data = json.loads(v)
        if time.time() < data["fresh_until"]:
            return data["value"]
        # stale: one caller refreshes in the background, everyone returns the stale value now
        if r.set(f"{key}:lock", 1, nx=True, px=5000):
            def refresh():
                val = expensive_query()
                r.set(key, json.dumps({"value": val, "fresh_until": time.time() + ttl}), ex=ttl + grace)
                r.delete(f"{key}:lock")
            threading.Thread(target=refresh).start()
        return data["value"]
    return get_locked_swr(key, ttl, grace)       # cold start: fall back to the lock

def get_locked_swr(key, ttl, grace):
    while True:
        v = r.get(key)
        if v: return json.loads(v)["value"]
        if r.set(f"{key}:lock", 1, nx=True, px=5000):
            val = expensive_query()
            r.set(key, json.dumps({"value": val, "fresh_until": time.time() + ttl}), ex=ttl + grace)
            r.delete(f"{key}:lock"); return val
        time.sleep(0.02)

def herd(fn, key, n=50):
    global db_calls
    r.delete(key, f"{key}:lock"); db_calls = 0
    lat = []
    def one():
        t = time.perf_counter(); fn(key); lat.append(time.perf_counter() - t)
    ts = [threading.Thread(target=one) for _ in range(n)]
    [t.start() for t in ts]; [t.join() for t in ts]
    lat.sort()
    return db_calls, lat[len(lat)//2] * 1000, lat[-1] * 1000

print("50 concurrent requests for a key that just expired:")
print("  naive      : db calls %2d   p50 %4.0f ms  max %4.0f ms" % herd(get_naive, "report:naive"))
print("  lock       : db calls %2d   p50 %4.0f ms  max %4.0f ms" % herd(get_locked, "report:lock"))

# XFetch: simulate steady traffic around expiry with a short TTL
global_calls = 0
def steady(fn, key, ttl, seconds, rps=200):
    global db_calls
    r.delete(key, f"{key}:lock"); db_calls = 0
    end = time.time() + seconds; misses_blocking = 0
    def client():
        nonlocal misses_blocking
        while time.time() < end:
            t = time.perf_counter(); fn(key, ttl=ttl)
            if time.perf_counter() - t > 0.1: misses_blocking += 1
            time.sleep(threading.active_count() / rps)
    ts = [threading.Thread(target=client) for _ in range(20)]
    [t.start() for t in ts]; [t.join() for t in ts]
    return db_calls, misses_blocking
print("20 clients, 10 s, TTL 2 s:")
print("  lock       : db calls %2d   requests that waited >100 ms: %d" % steady(get_locked, "s:lock", 2, 10))
print("  xfetch     : db calls %2d   requests that waited >100 ms: %d" % steady(get_xfetch, "s:xf", 2, 10))
print("  swr        : db calls %2d   requests that waited >100 ms: %d" % steady(get_swr, "s:swr", 2, 10))

50 concurrent requests for a key that just expired:
  naive      : db calls 50   p50  222 ms  max  231 ms
  lock       : db calls  1   p50  209 ms  max  230 ms
20 clients, 10 s, TTL 2 s:
  lock       : db calls  5   requests that waited >100 ms: 100
  xfetch     : db calls 35   requests that waited >100 ms: 35
  swr        : db calls  5   requests that waited >100 ms: 20

docs.title: 1. The stampede
docs.text:
Fifty requests arrive for a key that has just expired:

  • Naive cache-aside: 50 database calls. Every request missed, and every one ran the 200 ms query. For a heavier query, or with hundreds of requests, this is how a database falls over the moment a cache entry expires.
  • With a rebuild lock: 1 database call. The first request takes SET key:lock <token> NX PX 5000 and rebuilds, and the other 49 poll every 20 ms until the value appears. Latency was about the same (p50 209 ms against 222 ms; the query itself takes 200 ms), but the database did one-fiftieth of the work.

The lock has three details that matter. It has an expiry (PX 5000), so a rebuilder that crashes doesn't block everyone forever. It holds a random token, and the release only deletes the lock if the token still matches, so a slow rebuilder whose lock already expired can't delete someone else's. And waiters re-check the cache in a loop rather than assuming the lock holder succeeded. Level 3 · 05 looks at locks in more depth.

docs.title: 2. Steady traffic: who waits?
docs.text:
The lock stops the herd, but someone still waits for every rebuild. With 20 clients making requests for 10 seconds against a 2-second TTL:

Strategy DB calls Requests that waited > 100 ms Lock 5 100 XFetch (probabilistic early expiry) 35 35 Stale-while-revalidate 5 20

Lock. Few rebuilds, but each expiry made every concurrent request wait for the query, 100 slow requests in all.

XFetch ("optimal probabilistic cache stampede prevention", Vattani, Chierichetti and Lowenstein, 2015). Each reader recomputes early, with a probability that rises as expiry approaches and as the rebuild cost (delta) grows: recompute if −delta · beta · ln(rand) ≥ remaining TTL. Requests spread the rebuilds out, so there's no synchronized miss, and only the reader that decides to recompute waits. Its weakness showed in the numbers: the run started with an empty cache, so all 20 clients missed at once and rebuilt together. With a 2-second TTL against a 200 ms rebuild it also recomputed often. XFetch shines with longer TTLs relative to rebuild time, and it should be combined with a lock for the cold start.

Stale-while-revalidate won on both counts. The value carries a soft expiry (fresh_until), and the key has a longer hard TTL (soft + grace). When a reader finds the value stale, it returns the stale value immediately, and one reader (the one that gets the lock) refreshes it in the background. The only slow requests were the 20 at cold start, when there was nothing stale to serve. Every later refresh was invisible to users.

The trade-off is explicit: SWR serves data that's up to ttl + refresh time old, and the grace period bounds how stale it can get if refreshing keeps failing. For dashboards, catalogues and recommendation lists that's an excellent deal. For anything where stale is harmful, it isn't, and Level 3 · 01's versioned write-back is the tool.

docs.title: 3. Synchronized expiry: add jitter
docs.text:
Stampedes also happen without a single hot key. A cache warmed by a batch job sets 100,000 keys in a minute, all with EX 3600, and an hour later they all expire within the same minute. Spread them out:

ttl = 3600 + random.randint(0, 600)    # 1 h plus up to 10 min of jitter
r.set(key, value, ex=ttl)

That costs nothing and turns one expiry cliff into a gentle slope.

docs.title: 4. Invalidating groups of keys
docs.text:
Invalidation often targets a group: "everything cached for tenant 42" or "all pages that show product 7". Three ways to do it, from best to worst:

  1. Version in the key name. Keep cache:ver:tenant:42 and build keys as cache:t42:v{ver}:.... Invalidation is INCR cache:ver:tenant:42. Old keys become unreachable and expire through their TTLs. It's O(1), with no scanning and no race, at the cost of a little memory until they expire.
  2. Tag sets. On each cache write, SADD tag:product:7 <cache key> (with a TTL on the tag set). To invalidate, read the set and UNLINK its members, then the set itself. This is precise, but the tag sets need maintenance and can grow large.
  3. SCAN MATCH + UNLINK. Fine for a one-off cleanup (Level 1 · 04), but too slow and too heavy for routine invalidation of large keyspaces.

docs.title: How It Actually Works
docs.text:
A stampede is a coordination problem. Many independent requests discover the same fact (the value is missing) at the same moment, and none of them knows the others exist. Every fix gives them a way to coordinate through Redis:

  • The lock uses SET NX, which atomically elects exactly one rebuilder.
  • XFetch coordinates statistically. Each reader makes an independent random decision, tuned so the expected number of early recomputations is small and they're spread over time before the deadline.
  • SWR separates "is there something to serve?" (yes, until the hard TTL) from "should it be refreshed?" (yes, after the soft TTL), and uses SET NX to elect one refresher.

All of them rely on Redis being a single, linearizable point of coordination. If the cache is a Cluster, the lock key and the data key should share a hash tag so they live on the same node (report:{q1} and report:{q1}:lock).

docs.title: Common mistakes
docs.text:
• No stampede protection on expensive keys. It works in testing and fails at peak.
  • Locks without expiry, or released without checking the token.
  • Waiters that block forever. Always loop with a deadline, then fall back to computing it yourself or returning an error.
  • Identical TTLs on keys written together. Add jitter.
  • Serving stale data where staleness is unacceptable (prices at checkout, permissions).
  • Invalidating by scanning on every write. Use key versions or tags.

docs.title: Exercise
docs.text:
1. Run the steady-traffic test with TTLs of 2, 10 and 60 seconds. How do XFetch's database-call count and waits change as the TTL grows relative to the 200 ms rebuild?
  2. Add a lock to XFetch's cold-start path and rerun. How many requests still wait?
  3. Make SWR's background refresh fail half the time (raise an exception). What do clients see during the grace period, and after it ends?
  4. Implement tenant-wide invalidation with a version counter and show that invalidating 100,000 cached entries takes a single INCR. How much memory do the orphaned entries hold until they expire?

docs.title: 04 · Rate Limiting Algorithms
docs.text: "At most 10 requests per second per client" sounds like one requirement, but there are several reasonable definitions of it, and they differ exactly where it matters: at bursts and window boundaries. Redis is the standard place to keep rate-limit state, because every app server sees the same counters, and because one script can check and update a limit atomically. This lesson implements four algorithms and runs the same traffic through all of them.

docs.title: The implementations
docs.text:
Each limiter is a Lua script, so "read the state, decide, update" can't interleave with another request. All four take the current time as an argument, which makes the tests deterministic. In production, either pass a time from the app servers (and keep their clocks in sync) or read redis.call('TIME') inside the script.

limiters.py:

"""Four rate limiters, each one atomic in Redis. All take an explicit now_ms so tests are deterministic."""
import redis

r = redis.Redis(decode_responses=True)

FIXED = r.register_script("""
-- KEYS[1] = prefix ; ARGV = limit, window_ms, now_ms
local window = math.floor(ARGV[3] / ARGV[2])
local key = KEYS[1] .. ':' .. window
local n = redis.call('INCR', key)
if n == 1 then redis.call('PEXPIRE', key, ARGV[2]) end
return n <= tonumber(ARGV[1]) and 1 or 0
""")

SLIDING_LOG = r.register_script("""
-- KEYS[1] = zset ; ARGV = limit, window_ms, now_ms, request_id
redis.call('ZREMRANGEBYSCORE', KEYS[1], '-inf', ARGV[3] - ARGV[2])
if redis.call('ZCARD', KEYS[1]) < tonumber(ARGV[1]) then
  redis.call('ZADD', KEYS[1], ARGV[3], ARGV[4])
  redis.call('PEXPIRE', KEYS[1], ARGV[2])
  return 1
end
return 0
""")

SLIDING_COUNTER = r.register_script("""
-- KEYS[1] = prefix ; ARGV = limit, window_ms, now_ms
local w = tonumber(ARGV[2]); local now = tonumber(ARGV[3])
local cur = math.floor(now / w)
local cur_key, prev_key = KEYS[1] .. ':' .. cur, KEYS[1] .. ':' .. (cur - 1)
local prev = tonumber(redis.call('GET', prev_key) or '0')
local count = tonumber(redis.call('GET', cur_key) or '0')
local weight = 1 - (now % w) / w                -- share of the previous window still inside the sliding window
if prev * weight + count >= tonumber(ARGV[1]) then return 0 end
redis.call('INCR', cur_key); redis.call('PEXPIRE', cur_key, w * 2)
return 1
""")

TOKEN_BUCKET = r.register_script("""
-- KEYS[1] = hash ; ARGV = capacity, refill_per_sec, now_ms, cost
local cap, rate = tonumber(ARGV[1]), tonumber(ARGV[2])
local now, cost = tonumber(ARGV[3]), tonumber(ARGV[4])
local b = redis.call('HMGET', KEYS[1], 'tokens', 'ts')
local tokens = tonumber(b[1]) or cap
local ts = tonumber(b[2]) or now
tokens = math.min(cap, tokens + (now - ts) / 1000 * rate)
local ok = 0
if tokens >= cost then tokens = tokens - cost; ok = 1 end
redis.call('HSET', KEYS[1], 'tokens', tostring(tokens), 'ts', now)
redis.call('PEXPIRE', KEYS[1], math.ceil(cap / rate * 1000) + 1000)
return ok
""")

def fixed(client, now_ms, limit=10, window_ms=1000):
    return FIXED(keys=[f"rl:fixed:{client}"], args=[limit, window_ms, now_ms]) == 1

def sliding_log(client, now_ms, req_id, limit=10, window_ms=1000):
    return SLIDING_LOG(keys=[f"rl:log:{client}"], args=[limit, window_ms, now_ms, req_id]) == 1

def sliding_counter(client, now_ms, limit=10, window_ms=1000):
    return SLIDING_COUNTER(keys=[f"rl:swc:{client}"], args=[limit, window_ms, now_ms]) == 1

def token_bucket(client, now_ms, capacity=10, per_sec=10, cost=1):
    return TOKEN_BUCKET(keys=[f"rl:tb:{client}"], args=[capacity, per_sec, now_ms, cost]) == 1

How each one decides:

  • Fixed window. One counter per client per window (rl:fixed:ana:1791860000). INCR, and allow if the result is ≤ limit. The cheapest and simplest.
  • Sliding log. A sorted set of request timestamps. Drop entries older than the window, count, and allow if under the limit. Exact, but it stores one entry per request.
  • Sliding window counter. Two fixed-window counters, the current and the previous one. Estimate the count over the last second as previous × (share of previous window still in range) + current. Nearly exact, with constant memory.
  • Token bucket. A bucket holds up to capacity tokens and refills at rate per second. Each request takes a token if one is available. It allows bursts up to the capacity, then a steady rate. Stored as two hash fields, and refill is computed lazily from the elapsed time, so there's no background job.

docs.title: The boundary burst
docs.text:
The limit is 10 requests per second. A client sends 15 requests at t = 0.990 s and 15 more at t = 1.010 s, which is 30 requests within 20 ms, straddling a one-second boundary:

from limiters import r, fixed, sliding_log, sliding_counter, token_bucket
T0 = 1_791_860_000_000                         # a window boundary (divisible by 1000)
for k in r.scan_iter("rl:*"): r.delete(k)
# limit: 10 requests per 1 s. Burst of 15 at t=0.990 s, then 15 more at t=1.010 s
times = [T0 + 990] * 15 + [T0 + 1010] * 15
def run(name, fn):
    allowed = [fn(t, i) for i, t in enumerate(times)]
    print(f"{name:16} allowed {sum(allowed[:15]):2} at 0.990s + {sum(allowed[15:]):2} at 1.010s = {sum(allowed):2} within 20 ms")
run("fixed window",    lambda t, i: fixed("ana", t))
run("sliding log",     lambda t, i: sliding_log("ana", t, f"req-{i}"))
run("sliding counter", lambda t, i: sliding_counter("ana", t))
run("token bucket",    lambda t, i: token_bucket("ana", t))

fixed window     allowed 10 at 0.990s + 10 at 1.010s = 20 within 20 ms
sliding log      allowed 10 at 0.990s +  0 at 1.010s = 10 within 20 ms
sliding counter  allowed 10 at 0.990s +  1 at 1.010s = 11 within 20 ms
token bucket     allowed 10 at 0.990s +  0 at 1.010s = 10 within 20 ms

The fixed window allowed 20 requests in 20 milliseconds, twice the limit, because the first burst counted against window 0 and the second against window 1, each of which was "under 10". A client that times bursts to window boundaries can always get double the limit. The sliding log held exactly at 10. The sliding counter allowed one extra: at 1.010 s it estimated 10 × 0.99 + 0 = 9.9, which is under 10. That's the approximation, and it's small. The token bucket allowed 10, because the bucket was empty after the first burst and only 20 ms worth of tokens (0.2) had dripped back in.

docs.title: Steady overload
docs.text:
A client sends 200 requests at random times over 10 seconds (about 20/s, double the limit). "Most in any 1-s span" slides a one-second window across the accepted requests in 5 ms steps:

import random
from limiters import r, fixed, sliding_log, sliding_counter, token_bucket
T0 = 1_791_860_000_000
for k in r.scan_iter("rl:*"): r.delete(k)
random.seed(4)
# one client sending ~20 req/s at random times for 10 s against a 10 req/s limit
times = sorted(T0 + random.randint(0, 9999) for _ in range(200))
def worst_1s(accepted):
    return max(sum(1 for t in accepted if s <= t < s + 1000) for s in range(T0, T0 + 9000, 5))
for name, fn in [("fixed window", lambda t, i: fixed("bob", t)),
                 ("sliding log", lambda t, i: sliding_log("bob", t, f"r{i}")),
                 ("sliding counter", lambda t, i: sliding_counter("bob", t)),
                 ("token bucket", lambda t, i: token_bucket("bob", t))]:
    acc = [t for i, t in enumerate(times) if fn(t, i)]
    print(f"{name:16} accepted {len(acc):3} of 200 in 10 s; most in any 1-s span: {worst_1s(acc)}")
# memory per client at the limit
for name, key in [("fixed window", "rl:fixed:bob:*"), ("sliding log", "rl:log:bob"), ("sliding counter", "rl:swc:bob:*"), ("token bucket", "rl:tb:bob")]:
    keys = list(r.scan_iter(key))
    print(f"{name:16} keys per client {len(keys)}, bytes {sum(r.memory_usage(k) or 0 for k in keys)}")

fixed window     accepted 100 of 200 in 10 s; most in any 1-s span: 17
sliding log      accepted  93 of 200 in 10 s; most in any 1-s span: 10
sliding counter  accepted  99 of 200 in 10 s; most in any 1-s span: 12
token bucket     accepted 108 of 200 in 10 s; most in any 1-s span: 19
fixed window     keys per client 10, bytes 500
sliding log      keys per client 1, bytes 204
sliding counter  keys per client 10, bytes 480
token bucket     keys per client 1, bytes 71
  • All four let through roughly the long-run rate of about 10/s (93–108 of 200).
  • The sliding log never exceeded 10 in any one-second span. It's the only exact one.
  • The sliding counter peaked at 12, a small overshoot from its weighting.
  • The fixed window peaked at 17 by straddling boundaries.
  • The token bucket peaked at 19, by design: a full bucket of 10 plus 10 more refilled during that second. If you choose a token bucket, choose its capacity as the burst you're willing to accept.

Memory per client (in this simulation the window keys hadn't expired yet, because the TTLs run on the real clock while the test uses simulated times; in real time a fixed-window or sliding-counter client holds one or two keys):

  • The token bucket was the smallest (one hash, 71 bytes), and its size is independent of the limit.
  • The sliding log costs one sorted-set member per allowed request in the window: 204 bytes at a limit of 10, but at a limit of 10,000 per hour it holds 10,000 members per client. That's the price of exactness.

docs.title: Which to use
docs.text:
Algorithm Exact? Bursts Memory per client Use for Fixed window no, up to 2× at boundaries uncontrolled tiny coarse quotas (per day), where 2× briefly is fine Sliding log yes none above limit O(limit) low limits that must be exact (login attempts) Sliding window counter nearly small overshoot tiny most API rate limits Token bucket to its definition up to capacity tiny APIs that should allow short bursts

The client-facing part matters too. Return HTTP 429 with a Retry-After header, and ideally RateLimit-Limit/RateLimit-Remaining. The scripts can return those numbers instead of a 0/1 flag (see the exercises).

docs.title: How It Actually Works
docs.text:
Correctness comes from atomicity. Without a script, a sliding log needs ZREMRANGEBYSCORE, ZCARD, then a conditional ZADD, and two requests running those concurrently can both see 9 and both be admitted. Inside a script on Redis's single command thread, the check and the update are one step, so the limit holds even with hundreds of app servers.

Each script touches only the client's own keys, so in Redis Cluster each client's limiter runs entirely on one node (the multi-key fixed and sliding-counter scripts build their key names from the KEYS[1] prefix; for strict Cluster compliance, pass both window keys in KEYS with a hash tag like rl:{ana}:...). Load spreads naturally across nodes by client.

Expiry keeps the state from accumulating. Fixed-window keys expire with their window, sliding-counter keys after two windows, the log after one window of inactivity, and the bucket after the time it takes to refill completely, after which a missing bucket is equivalent to a full one. A client that stops sending eventually costs nothing.

docs.title: Common mistakes
docs.text:
• INCR and EXPIRE as two separate client calls. A crash between them leaves a counter with no TTL that blocks the client forever. Do both in one script (or use SET … NX EX then INCR).
  • Check-then-act in the client (ZCARD, then ZADD). Concurrent requests overshoot. Use a script.
  • Fixed windows for security limits. An attacker gets double the attempts by timing bursts.
  • Sliding logs with large limits. Memory grows with the limit, per client.
  • Mixing clocks. Times from many app servers with clock skew make windows inconsistent. Use one time source.
  • Limiting by IP behind a proxy without trusting the right header, which limits everyone as one client, or none.

docs.title: Exercise
docs.text:
1. Change the sliding-counter script to return {allowed, remaining, retry_after_ms} and use it to set HTTP headers in a small Flask or FastAPI endpoint.
  2. Make the token bucket support a request cost (an expensive endpoint costs 5 tokens) and show a client spending its budget on 2 expensive calls.
  3. Use redis.call('TIME') instead of a passed-in now_ms. How do you test it deterministically now?
  4. Load-test the sliding log and the token bucket at 5,000 requests/s across 1,000 clients. Compare server CPU (INFO cpu) and memory. Which would you choose for a public API, and why?

docs.title: 05 · Distributed Locks & Their Limits
docs.text: A distributed lock makes sure only one process at a time does something: runs the nightly invoice job, rebuilds a cache entry, or processes a particular user's payment. Redis makes a lock look trivial, one SET … NX. It is easy to get the basic version right, and it's even easier to believe that version gives a guarantee it can't give. This lesson builds a correct lock, then breaks it with a paused process, which is the failure every lease-based lock shares, and fixes the damage with fencing tokens.

docs.title: A correct basic lock
docs.text:
import threading, time, uuid
import redis
r = redis.Redis(decode_responses=True)

RELEASE = r.register_script("""
if redis.call('GET', KEYS[1]) == ARGV[1] then return redis.call('DEL', KEYS[1]) end
return 0
""")
EXTEND = r.register_script("""
if redis.call('GET', KEYS[1]) == ARGV[1] then return redis.call('PEXPIRE', KEYS[1], ARGV[2]) end
return 0
""")

def acquire(name, ttl_ms, wait_s=5):
    token = uuid.uuid4().hex
    deadline = time.time() + wait_s
    while time.time() < deadline:
        if r.set(f"lock:{name}", token, nx=True, px=ttl_ms):
            fence = r.incr(f"fence:{name}")          # monotonically increasing fencing token
            return token, fence
        time.sleep(0.01)
    return None, None

def release(name, token):
    return RELEASE(keys=[f"lock:{name}"], args=[token]) == 1

Three properties make this the correct basic form:

  1. NX makes acquisition atomic: only one SET can create the key.
  2. PX ttl makes it a lease. If the holder crashes, the lock frees itself. Without a TTL, one crashed process deadlocks the job forever.
  3. A random token, checked on release. Releasing with a plain DEL is a classic bug:
r.set("lock:report", "token-A", nx=True, px=300)    # A takes the lock
time.sleep(0.4)                                      # ...A stalls; its lease expires
print("B acquires:", r.set("lock:report", "token-B", nx=True, px=5000))
r.delete("lock:report")                              # A finishes and "releases" with DEL
print("C acquires while B still works:", r.set("lock:report", "token-C", nx=True, px=5000))

B acquires: True
C acquires while B still works: True

A's DEL removed B's lock, so C walked in while B was still working. With the token check, A's release is a no-op. Since Redis 8.4, DELEX key IFEQ token does the same check without a script:

DELEX with wrong token: 0  with right token: 1

EXTEND (a token-checked PEXPIRE) lets a long job renew its lease periodically, a "watchdog". Renew well before expiry, and stop working if a renewal fails, because that means you've lost the lock.

Under contention it does what it should. Twenty threads each do 50 read-modify-write increments of a counter, protected by the lock:

20 threads x 50 locked increments -> balance 1000 in 0.76s

That's exactly 1,000, with no lost updates. (For a counter you'd just use INCR. The lock is standing in for work that can't be expressed as one Redis command.)

docs.title: How a correct lock still fails: the paused holder
docs.text:
A lease has a fundamental weakness. The lock expires on Redis's clock, but the holder decides it's safe to act on its own view of time. If the holder pauses (a long garbage-collection pause, the VM being descheduled, a slow network call, the laptop lid closing) for longer than the lease, then:

  1. The lease expires while A is paused.
  2. B acquires the lock and does its work.
  3. A wakes up, still believing it holds the lock, and does its work too.

This script reproduces it. Client A takes a 500 ms lease and stalls for 1 s. B arrives at 0.6 s, after A's lease expired. Both write to a "storage service":

storage = {"value": None, "max_fence": 0, "writes": []}
def storage_write(value, fence=None):
    if fence is not None:
        if fence < storage["max_fence"]:
            storage["writes"].append(("REJECTED", value, fence)); return False
        storage["max_fence"] = fence
    storage["value"] = value; storage["writes"].append(("ok", value, fence)); return True

def scenario(use_fencing):
    r.delete("lock:invoice", "fence:invoice")
    storage.update(value=None, max_fence=0, writes=[])
    def client(name, pause):
        token, fence = acquire("invoice", ttl_ms=500)
        time.sleep(pause)                              # e.g. a GC pause or a slow network call
        storage_write(f"written by {name}", fence if use_fencing else None)
        print(f"  {name}: release -> {release('invoice', token)}")
    a = threading.Thread(target=client, args=("A", 1.0))   # A stalls longer than its 500 ms lease
    a.start(); time.sleep(0.6)
    b = threading.Thread(target=client, args=("B", 0.1))   # B gets the lock after A's lease expired
    b.start(); a.join(); b.join()
    for w in storage["writes"]: print("  storage:", w)
    print("  final value:", storage["value"])

Without fencing:
  B: release -> True
  A: release -> False
  storage: ('ok', 'written by B', None)
  storage: ('ok', 'written by A', None)
  final value: written by A

Both clients wrote, and A, whose lock had expired, wrote last, overwriting B's newer result. A's release returned False, so the token check stopped A from deleting B's lock, but by then the damage was done. No choice of TTL removes this: a pause can always be longer than the lease.

docs.title: Fencing tokens
docs.text:
The fix has to live in the resource being protected, not in the lock. Every time the lock is granted, issue a number that only ever increases (here INCR fence:invoice). The holder sends it with every write, and the storage rejects any write carrying a token lower than one it has already seen:

With fencing tokens:
  B: release -> True
  A: release -> False
  storage: ('ok', 'written by B', 2)
  storage: ('REJECTED', 'written by A', 1)
  final value: written by B

A's stale write (token 1) arrived after B's (token 2) and was refused. The resource can do this with a version column (UPDATE … WHERE fence < :token), a conditional write in object storage, or the same check in a Lua script if the protected data is in Redis itself.

When you can't add fencing because the protected system doesn't support conditional writes (sending an email, charging a card through a third-party API), make the operation idempotent instead (an idempotency key on the charge), and treat the lock as an efficiency measure that usually prevents duplicate work, not as a correctness guarantee.

docs.title: Failover and Redlock
docs.text:
There's a second failure mode. Redis replication is asynchronous (Level 4 · 03). If the primary acknowledges your SET NX and crashes before the write reaches a replica, the promoted replica has no lock, and another client can acquire it.

Redlock, the algorithm described in the Redis documentation, addresses that by acquiring the lock on a majority of N independent Redis primaries (typically 5) within a time budget, with validity reduced by the elapsed acquisition time. It survives the loss of a minority of nodes. It's also the subject of a well-known disagreement. Martin Kleppmann's 2016 essay "How to do distributed locking" argued that Redlock depends on timing assumptions (bounded pauses, network delays and clock drift) that real systems violate, and that it provides no fencing tokens, so it's unsafe when correctness depends on the lock. Salvatore Sanfilippo (antirez) replied defending it under its stated assumptions. Both essays are worth reading in full. A fair summary for practice:

  • For efficiency (avoid doing the same work twice; occasional duplicates are harmless), a single-instance lock like the one above is enough, and Redlock adds little.
  • For correctness (duplicates corrupt data), no lease-based lock is sufficient by itself, including Redlock. Use fencing tokens or idempotency at the resource, or a coordination system built on consensus (etcd, ZooKeeper), which provides fencing via revision numbers.

Redlock wasn't run for this course. It needs several independent primaries and client-library support, and the point above holds regardless of the implementation.

docs.title: How It Actually Works
docs.text:
SET key token NX PX ttl is a single command, so the check "does the key exist?" and the creation can't be split by another client. The expiry is stored as an absolute time and enforced by Redis's own clock (Level 1 · 03), and the holder's clock isn't involved at all. That's the root of the paused-holder problem: Redis's notion of "lock held" and the client's notion diverge whenever the client stops observing time.

The token release is a compare-and-delete, which must be atomic. Hence the script, or DELEX IFEQ from 8.4. A GET, compare in the client, then DEL would have its own race, with the lease expiring between the GET and the DEL.

Fencing works because it moves the decision to the only place that sees writes in their actual order: the resource. INCR on the fence key gives a total order of lock grants. Even if two holders overlap in real time, the resource accepts their writes only in grant order, and it rejects the older holder once a newer one has written.

docs.title: Common mistakes
docs.text:
• No TTL on the lock. One crash deadlocks forever.
  • Releasing with plain DEL. You can free someone else's lock.
