  • A TTL shorter than the work, without a watchdog. The lock silently expires mid-job.
  • Believing the lock guarantees mutual exclusion. Pauses, failovers and clock jumps break it. Fence or make operations idempotent.
  • Locks for things Redis can do atomically. INCR, SET NX, ZADD GT or a script are simpler and faster.
  • Spinning acquisition without backoff or a deadline. Add jitter and give up eventually.

docs.title: Exercise
docs.text:
1. Add a watchdog thread that extends the lease every ttl/3 while work runs, and stops the work if an extension returns 0. Rerun the paused-holder scenario with A's pause inside the work loop. Does the watchdog help when the whole process is paused? Why not?
  2. Protect a row in SQLite with fencing: add a fence column and update with UPDATE … SET value=?, fence=? WHERE id=? AND fence < ?. Reproduce the stale-writer scenario against it.
  3. Compare a lock-protected read-modify-write with a single Lua script doing the same update, for 20 threads × 500 updates. Report the time for each.
  4. Read both sides of the Redlock debate and write a one-paragraph decision for a job scheduler in your own system: which lock, what TTL, and what protects correctness.

docs.title: 06 · Sessions & Client-Side Caching
docs.text: This lesson covers two patterns that both treat Redis as the shared memory of a fleet of app servers. Sessions keep per-user state that any server can read, so a user's next request can land anywhere. Client-side caching goes the other way: app servers keep copies of hot Redis keys in their own memory, and Redis tells them when a copy goes stale.

docs.title: A session store
docs.text:
Sessions are small, read on almost every request, written occasionally, and supposed to vanish after inactivity. Redis with TTLs fits that exactly. Here's a complete store:

import json, secrets, time
import redis

r = redis.Redis(decode_responses=True)
IDLE_TTL = 30 * 60            # sliding: 30 minutes of inactivity
ABSOLUTE_TTL = 12 * 3600      # hard cap: re-login after 12 hours no matter what

def create_session(user_id, data):
    sid = secrets.token_urlsafe(32)                       # 256 bits from the OS CSPRNG
    now = int(time.time())
    p = r.pipeline(transaction=True)
    p.set(f"sess:{sid}", json.dumps({"uid": user_id, "created": now, **data}), ex=IDLE_TTL)
    p.sadd(f"user:{user_id}:sessions", sid)
    p.expire(f"user:{user_id}:sessions", ABSOLUTE_TTL)
    p.execute()
    return sid

def get_session(sid):
    raw = r.getex(f"sess:{sid}", ex=IDLE_TTL)             # read + slide the idle timeout atomically
    if raw is None:
        return None
    s = json.loads(raw)
    if time.time() - s["created"] > ABSOLUTE_TTL:
        destroy_session(sid); return None
    return s

def rotate_session(sid):
    """Issue a new id for the same session (call on login / privilege change) to defeat fixation."""
    s = get_session(sid)
    if s is None: return None
    new = secrets.token_urlsafe(32)
    p = r.pipeline(transaction=True)
    p.rename(f"sess:{sid}", f"sess:{new}")
    p.srem(f"user:{s['uid']}:sessions", sid); p.sadd(f"user:{s['uid']}:sessions", new)
    p.execute()
    return new

def destroy_session(sid):
    raw = r.getdel(f"sess:{sid}")
    if raw: r.srem(f"user:{json.loads(raw)['uid']}:sessions", sid)

def logout_everywhere(user_id):
    sids = r.smembers(f"user:{user_id}:sessions")
    if sids: r.unlink(*[f"sess:{s}" for s in sids])
    r.unlink(f"user:{user_id}:sessions")
    return len(sids)

if __name__ == "__main__":
    a = create_session(42, {"role": "user"}); b = create_session(42, {"role": "user"})
    print("session id length:", len(a), " ttl:", r.ttl(f"sess:{a}"))
    print("get:", get_session(a))
    a2 = rotate_session(a)
    print("old id after rotate:", get_session(a), "| new id works:", get_session(a2) is not None)
    print("logout everywhere removed", logout_everywhere(42), "sessions; b now:", get_session(b))
    print("memory of one session:", r.memory_usage(f"sess:{create_session(7, {'role': 'admin', 'cart': [1, 2, 3]})}"), "bytes")

session id length: 43  ttl: 1800
get: {'uid': 42, 'created': 1791886636, 'role': 'user'}
old id after rotate: None | new id works: True
logout everywhere removed 2 sessions; b now: None
memory of one session: 157 bytes

The decisions that matter:

  • Session IDs come from secrets, which draws from the OS's cryptographic generator. 32 bytes is 256 bits of randomness, 43 characters in URL-safe base64. Anything guessable, such as sequential IDs, timestamps, uuid1, or random instead of secrets, lets an attacker hijack sessions.
  • Two expiries. The idle timeout slides forward on every request: GETEX … EX reads and extends in one atomic step. The absolute lifetime (12 hours here) is checked against the creation time stored in the session. Without it, an active stolen session lives forever.
  • Rotation on login and on privilege change. If an attacker can plant a session ID in a victim's browser before login (session fixation), rotating the ID at login makes the planted one useless. RENAME keeps the value and the TTL, and the old ID stops working, as the output shows.
  • A per-user index (user:42:sessions) makes "log out of all devices" and "show my active sessions" cheap. It's a small set per user with its own TTL. It can hold IDs of sessions that already expired, and that's harmless: the UNLINK of a missing key is a no-op.
  • Store little. 157 bytes per session here. Keep the source of truth for carts and profiles in your database, and put only identifiers and small flags in the session.

Should the session be a hash or a JSON string? A hash lets you update one field (HSET sess:… last_page /x) without rewriting the whole value, and since 7.4 fields can expire on their own (Level 1 · 05). A JSON string is simpler when the session is read and written whole. Either works. Pick one per application.

docs.title: Client-side caching
docs.text: Even a 0.1 ms round trip adds up when every request reads the same feature flags or config ten times. Client-side caching keeps those values in the application's own memory. The classic problem with local caches is invalidation: how does server 7 know that server 3 just changed a flag? Since Redis 6, the server tells it.

docs.title: What the server does: CLIENT TRACKING
docs.text:
A RESP3 connection turns on tracking. Redis then remembers which keys this connection has read, and when any client modifies one of them, it sends an invalidate push message. This is a raw-socket session:

send(b"HELLO 3
")
print(send(b"CLIENT TRACKING ON
"))
print(send(b"GET feature:flags
"))
# another client: SET feature:flags '{"new_checkout": false}'
print(s.recv(65536))

b'+OK
'
b'$22
{"new_checkout": true}
'
b'>2
$10
invalidate
*1
$13
feature:flags
'

The > prefix is a RESP3 push frame: ["invalidate", ["feature:flags"]]. When another client modified the key a second time, before this connection had read it again, nothing more arrived:

nothing received: tracking is one-shot until the key is read again

Tracking is one-shot. After an invalidation, the server forgets that this client cares about the key until the client reads it again. That keeps server memory bounded: Redis only tracks keys that clients actually hold.

docs.title: What the library does
docs.text:
redis-py 8 implements the client side. Pass protocol=3 and a CacheConfig, and GETs are served from a local cache that is invalidated by those push messages:

import time, redis
from redis.cache import CacheConfig
writer = redis.Redis(decode_responses=True)
writer.set("feature:flags", '{"new_checkout": false}')
cached = redis.Redis(protocol=3, decode_responses=True, cache_config=CacheConfig())
plain = redis.Redis(decode_responses=True)
N = 20000
for name, c in (("plain client", plain), ("client-side cache", cached)):
    c.get("feature:flags")
    t = time.perf_counter()
    for _ in range(N): c.get("feature:flags")
    print(f"{name:18}: {(time.perf_counter()-t)/N*1e6:6.1f} us per GET")
print("cached value     :", cached.get("feature:flags"))
writer.set("feature:flags", '{"new_checkout": true}')
time.sleep(0.05)
print("after another client's SET:", cached.get("feature:flags"))
print("tracking clients:", [c["flags"] for c in writer.client_list() if "t" in c["flags"]])
print("INFO tracking_total_keys:", writer.info("stats").get("tracking_total_keys"))

plain client      :  113.7 us per GET
client-side cache :   45.9 us per GET
cached value     : {"new_checkout": false}
after another client's SET: {"new_checkout": true}
tracking clients: ['t']
INFO tracking_total_keys: 1
  • Cached reads were about 2.5× faster than round trips over loopback. That's less than you might expect from a local dictionary lookup. In redis-py 8.1, each cached read still goes through the connection's send_command, which first processes any pending invalidation messages from the socket (_process_pending_invalidations in the source). Over a real network, where a round trip is 0.5 ms or more, the gain is much larger.
  • After another client changed the key, the next read returned the new value. The invalidation arrived and the local copy was dropped.
  • The server shows the tracking flag t on the connection and 1 tracked key.

docs.title: Caveats
docs.text:
• Staleness window. Between the write and the invalidation reaching the client, the client can serve the old value. Usually that's microseconds to milliseconds, but it's not zero, and a lost connection loses invalidations (libraries flush the cache on reconnect for this reason).
  • Memory. Every cached value lives in every app process. Cache small, hot, rarely changing keys (flags, config, rate-limit rules), not your whole dataset.
  • Server cost. Tracking needs a table of key → tracking clients. Broadcasting mode (CLIENT TRACKING ON BCAST PREFIX flags:) avoids per-key memory on the server by notifying every client about any change under a prefix. That's useful when many clients cache the same small set of keys.

docs.title: How It Actually Works
docs.text:
Sessions rely on nothing more exotic than per-key expiry and atomic multi-command operations. GETEX updates the expiry in the same command as the read, so a request can't see a session that expires between "read" and "extend". RENAME is atomic and moves the TTL with the key, so rotation never leaves a moment where neither ID works.

For tracking, Redis keeps a radix tree (the tracking table) that maps each key to the set of client IDs that read it while tracking was on. Every write goes through the same "key modified" hook that WATCH uses (Level 2 · 08). The hook looks the key up in the table, sends an invalidate push to each client, and removes the entry. That's why tracking is one-shot. tracking-table-max-keys caps the table, and when it's full, Redis evicts entries by sending invalidations early, so clients refetch. In BCAST mode there's no per-key table, just a list of prefixes and the clients subscribed to them, checked on every write.

In RESP2, invalidations can't share the data connection, so tracking uses REDIRECT <client-id> to send them to a separate connection subscribed to the __redis__:invalidate channel. RESP3's push frames are what make the single-connection design practical, and why redis-py requires protocol=3 for its cache.

docs.title: Common mistakes
docs.text:
• Guessable session IDs. Use a CSPRNG and at least 128 bits.
  • Only a sliding expiry. A stolen session that's used regularly never expires. Add an absolute lifetime.
  • Not rotating the ID at login. It leaves the door open to session fixation.
  • Storing large objects in sessions. Every request pays to fetch them.
  • Client-side caching large or fast-changing keys. It wastes memory everywhere, and invalidation traffic can exceed the savings.
  • Assuming the local cache is never stale. It's eventually consistent, with a small window.

docs.title: Exercise
docs.text:
1. Store sessions as hashes instead of JSON, with last_seen updated on each request (HSET + EXPIRE in one pipeline). Compare memory per session and the cost of a request.
  2. Add an "active sessions" page: list each of a user's sessions with its creation time and remaining idle TTL, and let them revoke one. Make sure expired IDs in the index are cleaned up.
  3. Run the client-side caching benchmark against a Redis server on another machine (or add 1 ms of latency with a proxy) and report the speedup.
  4. Turn on BCAST tracking for a flags: prefix with two cached clients, update five flags, and count the invalidation messages each client receives.

docs.title: 07 · Reliable Job Queues
docs.text: "Push a job, have a worker pop it" is ten lines of code and works perfectly until a worker dies mid-job. Then the question is whether that job is lost, retried, or retried forever. This lesson kills workers with SIGKILL while they process 2,000 jobs, and compares a naive list queue with a reliable one. Then it covers retries, dead letters, delayed jobs, and when to use streams or an existing library instead.

docs.title: Two queues
docs.text:
rq.py (no relation to the RQ library) has both designs:

"""Two list-based queues: naive (BLPOP) and reliable (BLMOVE + per-worker processing list + reaper)."""
import json, os, sys, time
import redis

r = redis.Redis(decode_responses=True)

def enqueue(q, job_id, payload):
    r.lpush(f"{q}:pending", json.dumps({"id": job_id, "payload": payload, "attempts": 0}))

def do_work(job):
    time.sleep(0.01)                                   # 10 ms of "work"
    r.sadd("done", job["id"])                          # the side effect (idempotent: a set)

def naive_worker(q):
    while True:
        item = r.brpop(f"{q}:pending", timeout=1)
        if item is None: return
        do_work(json.loads(item[1]))

def reliable_worker(q, name):
    proc = f"{q}:processing:{name}"
    r.hset(f"{q}:heartbeats", name, int(time.time()))
    while True:
        raw = r.blmove(f"{q}:pending", proc, timeout=1, src="RIGHT", dest="LEFT")
        if raw is None: return
        r.hset(f"{q}:heartbeats", name, int(time.time()))
        do_work(json.loads(raw))
        r.lrem(proc, 1, raw)                           # ack: remove exactly this item

REQUEUE = """
-- move everything from a dead worker's processing list back to pending (or to dead letters)
local moved, dead = 0, 0
while true do
  local raw = redis.call('RPOP', KEYS[1])
  if not raw then break end
  local job = cjson.decode(raw)
  job.attempts = job.attempts + 1
  if job.attempts > tonumber(ARGV[1]) then
    redis.call('LPUSH', KEYS[3], cjson.encode(job)); dead = dead + 1
  else
    redis.call('RPUSH', KEYS[2], cjson.encode(job)); moved = moved + 1   -- RPUSH: retried first
  end
end
return {moved, dead}
"""

def reap(q, stale_after=3, max_attempts=3):
    """Run periodically: requeue jobs held by workers whose heartbeat is older than stale_after seconds."""
    total = [0, 0]
    for name, beat in r.hgetall(f"{q}:heartbeats").items():
        if time.time() - int(beat) > stale_after:
            moved, dead = r.eval(REQUEUE, 3, f"{q}:processing:{name}", f"{q}:pending", f"{q}:dead", max_attempts)
            total[0] += moved; total[1] += dead
            r.hdel(f"{q}:heartbeats", name)
    return total

if __name__ == "__main__":
    kind, q = sys.argv[1], sys.argv[2]
    naive_worker(q) if kind == "naive" else reliable_worker(q, sys.argv[3])

Naive: BRPOP hands the job to the worker and removes it from Redis in the same step. If the worker dies before finishing, nothing records that the job existed.

Reliable: BLMOVE atomically moves the job from pending into this worker's own processing list (q:processing:w3), so at every moment the job is stored somewhere. After the work, LREM removes exactly that item (the ack). Each worker updates a heartbeat in a hash. A reaper finds workers whose heartbeat is stale and moves their processing list back to pending with a Lua script that also counts attempts and diverts jobs that exceeded the limit to a dead-letter list.

docs.title: The crash test
docs.text:
Four workers process 2,000 jobs of 10 ms each. Every half second, one worker is killed with SIGKILL (no cleanup, no finally, like an OOM kill or a lost machine) and a new one is started. That's five kills in all:

import subprocess, sys, time, signal
import redis
from rq import enqueue, reap
r = redis.Redis(decode_responses=True)
PY = sys.executable
def run(kind):
    q = f"q:{kind}"
    for k in r.scan_iter(f"{q}*"): r.delete(k)
    r.delete("done")
    for i in range(2000): enqueue(q, i, {"n": i})
    procs = [subprocess.Popen([PY, "rq.py", kind, q, f"w{i}"]) for i in range(4)]
    for round_ in range(5):                       # every 0.5 s, kill -9 one worker and start a new one
        time.sleep(0.5)
        victim = procs.pop(0); victim.send_signal(signal.SIGKILL); victim.wait()
        procs.append(subprocess.Popen([PY, "rq.py", kind, q, f"w{4 + round_}"]))
    for p in procs: p.wait()
    requeued = [0, 0]
    if kind == "reliable":
        time.sleep(3.2)
        requeued = reap(q, stale_after=3)
        p = subprocess.Popen([PY, "rq.py", kind, q, "cleanup"]); p.wait()
    print(f"{kind:8}: 2000 jobs, 5 workers SIGKILLed -> done {r.scard('done')}, "
          f"lost {2000 - r.scard('done')}, requeued by reaper {requeued[0]}, dead-lettered {requeued[1]}")
run("naive")
run("reliable")

naive   : 2000 jobs, 5 workers SIGKILLed -> done 1996, lost 4, requeued by reaper 0, dead-lettered 0
reliable: 2000 jobs, 5 workers SIGKILLed -> done 2000, lost 0, requeued by reaper 5, dead-lettered 0
  • Naive: 4 jobs lost (an earlier run of the same test lost 5). Almost every kill caught a worker holding a job that existed nowhere else. Nothing reported an error. The jobs just never happened.
  • Reliable: 0 lost. The reaper found 5 jobs stranded in dead workers' processing lists and requeued them. (In the earlier run it was 3, and the other kills landed between jobs, when the worker held nothing.)

There's a subtlety in the requeued count. A worker killed after do_work but before LREM had already applied the side effect, and its job ran again after requeueing. This is at-least-once delivery, exactly like stream consumer groups (Level 2 · 06). The handler here is idempotent (SADD done <id>), so the duplicate was harmless. Yours must be too: use an idempotency key, a unique constraint, or a check-before-act on the side effect.

docs.title: Retries, backoff and dead letters
docs.text:
The reaper's script increments attempts each time a job is recovered, and after max_attempts it moves the job to q:dead instead of back to pending. The same applies to jobs that fail with an exception rather than a crash. The worker should catch the error, remove the job from its processing list, and either re-enqueue it with attempts + 1 or dead-letter it. Without that limit, a poison job (one that always crashes the worker) gets reaped, retried and crashes the next worker, forever.

For backoff, don't push a failed job straight back to pending. Schedule it for later: put it in a delayed-jobs sorted set scored by the retry time, and move due jobs to pending with a script (Level 1 · 08, Level 2 · 09 exercise):

-- KEYS[1] = delayed zset, KEYS[2] = pending list, ARGV[1] = now, ARGV[2] = batch size
local due = redis.call('ZRANGE', KEYS[1], '-inf', ARGV[1], 'BYSCORE', 'LIMIT', 0, ARGV[2])
for _, job in ipairs(due) do
  redis.call('ZREM', KEYS[1], job)
  redis.call('LPUSH', KEYS[2], job)
end
return #due

Run that every second. A typical policy is exponential backoff with jitter: retry after 1 s, 4 s, 16 s… plus a random offset, so a burst of failures doesn't retry in lockstep.

docs.title: Lists or streams?
docs.text:
List + BLMOVE (this lesson) Stream + consumer group (Level 2 · 06) Crash recovery your reaper + heartbeats built in: PEL + XAUTOCLAIM Delivery count you track attempts in the payload built in (times_delivered) History / replay gone after ack kept until trimmed Several independent consumers of the same jobs no yes, one group each Ordering FIFO ID order Simplicity fewer concepts more concepts, less code

For new code, streams usually win: recovery and delivery counts come for free. List queues are still everywhere, and the reliable pattern above is how the mature list-based libraries work underneath.

docs.title: Don't build it if a library fits
docs.text: Mature libraries implement retries, scheduling, rate limits, priorities, dashboards and graceful shutdown on top of Redis. Versions published at the time of writing: RQ 2.12.0 and Celery 5.6.3 (Python; Celery can also use other brokers) and BullMQ 6.3.14 (Node.js). None of them was run for this course, so check their documentation for the delivery guarantees they actually give. Understanding the patterns in this lesson is what lets you read that documentation critically and debug them when jobs go missing.

docs.title: How It Actually Works
docs.text:
The reliability comes from never having a moment when a job exists only in a process's memory. BLMOVE is one command: the pop from pending and the push to processing happen together on Redis's single thread, so there's no point at which a crash could drop the job between them. The ack (LREM) is the only way a job leaves the processing list. A crash at any point leaves the job in Redis, either in pending or in a processing list.

What Redis can't know is whether a worker is dead or just slow. That's why the reaper needs heartbeats and a staleness threshold. Like the lock lease in Level 3 · 05, the threshold is a guess. Set it too low, and a slow, healthy worker has its job requeued and run twice. Set it too high, and jobs from crashed workers wait that long. Workers should update their heartbeat during long jobs, not just between them.

LREM key 1 raw removes by value, so it scans the processing list. That's why each worker gets its own processing list (usually holding one job) instead of sharing a big one. The requeue script does RPOP/RPUSH in a loop inside one atomic call, so a reaper and a recovering worker can't fight over the same items.

All of this is only as durable as Redis itself. A job acknowledged as "enqueued" can still be lost if Redis crashes before persisting it, or fails over before replicating it. Level 4 covers what appendfsync and replication give you.

docs.title: Common mistakes
docs.text:
• BLPOP/BRPOP for jobs that must not be lost. The test lost roughly one per crash.
  • Non-idempotent handlers. Every reliable queue redelivers sometimes.
  • No attempt limit. Poison jobs loop forever.
  • A shared processing list with LREM scanning thousands of items.
  • Heartbeats only between jobs. Long jobs look dead and get duplicated.
  • Immediate retries. Use delayed retries with backoff and jitter.
  • Reinventing a library you could have used. Know the patterns, then use the tool.

docs.title: Exercise
docs.text:
1. Make one job in 500 raise an exception in do_work. Extend the worker to catch it, track attempts, and dead-letter after 3 failures, using delayed retries with exponential backoff. Verify the counts at the end.
  2. Port the crash test to a stream with a consumer group and XAUTOCLAIM. Compare the amount of code and the number of duplicate executions.
  3. Add priorities: q:high:pending and q:low:pending. How do you get priority with BLMOVE, which takes a single source? (Hint: BLMPOP can't move atomically. Consider a non-blocking LMOVE on high, then a blocking one on low with a short timeout.)
  4. Measure throughput of the reliable queue with 8 workers and no-op jobs. Then batch: move up to 10 jobs per round trip with a script. What's the speedup?

docs.title: 08 · JSON Documents
docs.text: Level 1 stored objects as hashes (flat) or as JSON strings (nested, but opaque to Redis). The JSON type, shipped as a module with Redis 8 (load it with the lab config from Level 1 · 01), stores a parsed document tree. You can read and update parts of it by path, atomically, without fetching and rewriting the whole thing. It's also what the query engine in the next lesson indexes.

docs.title: Writing and reading by path
docs.text:
127.0.0.1:6379> JSON.SET order:1001 $ '{"id":1001,"customer":{"name":"Ana","tier":"gold"},"items":[{"sku":"pen","qty":2,"price_cents":150},{"sku":"ink","qty":1,"price_cents":400}],"status":"open","notes":null}'
OK
127.0.0.1:6379> JSON.GET order:1001 $.customer.name
"[\"Ana\"]"
127.0.0.1:6379> JSON.GET order:1001 $.items[*].sku
"[\"pen\",\"ink\"]"
127.0.0.1:6379> JSON.GET order:1001 $..price_cents
"[150,400]"
127.0.0.1:6379> JSON.GET order:1001 '$.items[?(@.qty>1)].sku'
"[\"pen\"]"

Paths starting with $ are JSONPath: .field, [*] for all elements, .. for recursive descent, and [?(...)] filters. A JSONPath can match many places, so results always come back as a JSON array of matches, even for a single value. A path that matches nothing returns an empty array, not an error:

127.0.0.1:6379> JSON.GET order:1001 $.nosuch
"[]"

The older "legacy" path syntax (no leading $) returns a single value instead. It still works, but use $ paths in new code:

127.0.0.1:6379> JSON.GET order:1001 .customer.name
"\"Ana\""

docs.title: Updating parts of a document
docs.text:
Each of these changes one part of the document in place, as a single atomic command:

127.0.0.1:6379> JSON.NUMINCRBY order:1001 '$.items[?(@.sku=="pen")].qty' 3
"[5]"
127.0.0.1:6379> JSON.ARRAPPEND order:1001 $.items '{"sku":"pad","qty":1,"price_cents":250}'
1) (integer) 3
127.0.0.1:6379> JSON.SET order:1001 $.status '"paid"'
OK
127.0.0.1:6379> JSON.SET order:1001 $.paid_at '"2026-10-13T09:00:00Z"' NX
OK
127.0.0.1:6379> JSON.SET order:1001 $.paid_at '"later"' NX
(nil)
127.0.0.1:6379> JSON.DEL order:1001 '$.items[?(@.sku=="ink")]'
(integer) 1
  • The value argument of JSON.SET is JSON, so a string needs its own quotes: '"paid"'.
  • NX/XX work per path. NX refused to overwrite paid_at, which makes a natural "set once" timestamp.
  • A filter in the path ([?(@.sku=="pen")]) lets you update an array element by content, not by index, which is safer when another client may have reordered or appended to the array.

JSON.MERGE applies an RFC 7386 merge patch. Objects merge recursively, and a null deletes a field:

127.0.0.1:6379> JSON.MERGE order:1001 $ '{"customer":{"tier":"platinum"},"notes":null}'
OK
127.0.0.1:6379> JSON.GET order:1001
"{\"id\":1001,\"customer\":{\"name\":\"Ana\",\"tier\":\"platinum\"},\"items\":[{\"sku\":\"pen\",\"qty\":5,\"price_cents\":150},{\"sku\":\"pad\",\"qty\":1,\"price_cents\":250}],\"status\":\"paid\",\"paid_at\":\"2026-10-13T09:00:00Z\"}"

Two behaviours to watch for, because neither is reported as an error:

127.0.0.1:6379> JSON.NUMINCRBY order:1001 $.status 1
"[null]"
127.0.0.1:6379> JSON.SET order:1001 $.a.b.c 1
(nil)

Incrementing a string field returned [null] for that match and changed nothing. Setting a path whose parents don't exist returned (nil) and created nothing: JSON.SET only creates the last segment of a path. Check replies.

docs.title: Why not just store a JSON string?
docs.text:
Here are 8 threads each incrementing a nested views counter 250 times, once by GET → json.loads → modify → SET on a string, and once with JSON.NUMINCRBY:

def via_string():
    for _ in range(250):
        d = json.loads(r.get("doc:str")); d["views"] += 1; r.set("doc:str", json.dumps(d))
def via_json():
    for _ in range(250):
        r.json().numincrby("doc:json", "$.views", 1)

8 threads x 250 increments -> string+json.loads: 397 | JSON.NUMINCRBY: 2000

The string version lost 80% of the updates. That's the read-modify-write race from Level 1 · 03, now on a nested field. The JSON type got exactly 2,000.

Reading one field from a large document (20,000 events, 945 KB of JSON text):

GET whole string + json.loads, read owner      7.976 ms
JSON.GET big $.owner                           0.178 ms

That's 45× faster, because only the matched value crosses the network and only it gets serialized.

The cost is memory. Here are 100,000 small order documents stored both ways:

JSON string (SET)               303 bytes/doc
JSON type (JSON.SET)            607 bytes/doc
size of big doc as text: 944927 bytes; MEMORY USAGE as JSON type: 1702264

The parsed tree took about twice the memory of the text, both for small documents and for the large one. Each node is a typed value with its own allocation and, for objects, a key table.

JSON string Hash JSON type Nested data yes no yes Atomic update of one nested field no (needs WATCH/Lua) top-level fields only yes Read one field of a big doc fetch everything HGET path Memory smallest small (listpack) about 2× the text here Indexable by the query engine no yes yes

Use the JSON type for nested documents that are updated partially or queried (next lesson). Keep JSON strings for blobs you always read and write whole, such as cached API responses.

docs.title: How It Actually Works
docs.text:
JSON.SET parses the text once and stores a tree of typed nodes (object, array, string, number, boolean, null) as the key's value. Object members are kept in insertion order, which is why JSON.OBJKEYS returned the keys in the order they were written. A JSONPath is compiled and evaluated against that tree, producing the list of matching nodes. Reads serialize only those nodes. Writes modify them in place. Because the whole command runs on Redis's single command thread, a NUMINCRBY or ARRAPPEND is atomic exactly like HINCRBY.

The tree is serialized into RDB and AOF in the module's own format, replicated by sending the command as an effect, and counted by MEMORY USAGE through a module callback. That callback is how the 1.7 MB figure for the big document was measured.

docs.title: Common mistakes
docs.text:
• Forgetting that $ paths return arrays. Unwrap [0] in client code, or use a single-value path deliberately.
  • Unquoted string values in JSON.SET (paid instead of '"paid"') are rejected as invalid JSON.
  • Assuming silent replies mean success. [null] and (nil) mean nothing happened.
  • Read-modify-write on JSON strings under concurrency. Use the JSON type's commands, or a script.
  • Storing huge documents (megabytes) that many clients update. Every command on the key runs on one thread. Split them.
  • Using the JSON type for write-once blobs. You pay double memory for features you don't use.

docs.title: Exercise
docs.text:
1. Model a shopping cart as a JSON document. Write the commands for adding an item (or incrementing its quantity if already present: try NUMINCRBY with a filter, then ARRAPPEND if it matched nothing), removing an item by SKU, and applying a coupon to $.discount only once (NX). Which steps need a script to be atomic together?
  2. Measure memory for 100,000 documents as a JSON string, a JSON type and a hash (flattening customer.name to customer_name). Include the listpack threshold from Level 2 · 01 in your reasoning.
  3. Time JSON.GET of one field against GET + parse for documents of 1 KB, 10 KB, 100 KB and 1 MB. Where does the JSON type start to pay off?
  4. Use JSON.MERGE with nested nulls to delete two fields in different sub-objects in one command, and verify the result.

docs.title: 09 · Query Engine: Secondary Indexes & Vector Search
docs.text:
Everything so far has been looked up by key. The query engine (the search module shipped with Redis 8, loaded by the lab config) adds secondary indexes over hashes and JSON documents: full-text search, exact-match tags, numeric and geo ranges, aggregations, and vector similarity search. You declare an index over a key prefix, and Redis keeps it up to date as documents are written.

This lesson indexes 50,000 synthetic product documents and 50,000 synthetic vectors. Synthetic data is fine for learning how the engine behaves. Relevance on real text and real embeddings depends on your data and model, which weren't part of this experiment.

docs.title: Creating an index
docs.text:
Products are JSON documents like {"name": "wireless wooden lamp", "category": "garden", "price": 42.5, "rating": 4.1, "in_stock": true, "store": "-9.14,38.72"} under keys product:0 … product:49999. The index declares which fields to index and how:

r.execute_command("FT.CREATE", "idx:products", "ON", "JSON", "PREFIX", "1", "product:", "SCHEMA",
    "$.name", "AS", "name", "TEXT",
    "$.category", "AS", "category", "TAG",
    "$.price", "AS", "price", "NUMERIC", "SORTABLE",
    "$.rating", "AS", "rating", "NUMERIC",
    "$.in_stock", "AS", "in_stock", "TAG",
    "$.store", "AS", "store", "GEO")

indexed 50000 docs in 6.98s (background indexing of existing keys)

Creating an index over existing data indexes it in the background. FT.INFO's indexing field stays true until it's done, and queries during that time see partial results. New writes to matching keys are indexed synchronously as part of the write. The index used about 10.7 MB (total_index_memory_sz_mb) on top of the documents.

Field types matter:

  • TEXT is tokenized, stemmed and ranked: "lamps" matches "lamp". Use it for human language.
  • TAG is exact-match, for categories, IDs, flags and status values. Query with {value}.
  • NUMERIC supports ranges. Add SORTABLE to sort by it cheaply.
  • GEO supports radius queries over "lon,lat" strings.

docs.title: Querying
docs.text:
127.0.0.1:6379> FT.SEARCH idx:products "wireless lamp" LIMIT 0 2 RETURN 2 name price
1) (integer) 1156
2) "product:13001"
3) 1) "name"
   2) "wireless wireless lamp"
   3) "price"
   4) "283.03"
...
127.0.0.1:6379> FT.SEARCH idx:products "@category:{garden} @price:[10 20]" SORTBY price ASC LIMIT 0 3 RETURN 2 name price
1) (integer) 217
2) "product:24624"
3) 1) "price"
   2) "10.05"
   3) "name"
   4) "ergonomic wireless drone"
...
127.0.0.1:6379> FT.SEARCH idx:products "@name:(tent|backpack) @in_stock:{true} @rating:[4.5 +inf]" LIMIT 0 0
1) (integer) 1087
127.0.0.1:6379> FT.SEARCH idx:products "@store:[-9.14 38.72 5 km] @category:{outdoor}" LIMIT 0 2 RETURN 2 name store
1) (integer) 2
2) "product:26644"
3) 1) "name"
   2) "waterproof wooden lamp"
   3) "store"
   4) "-9.11684,38.72966"
...

The first element of each reply is the total number of matches, followed by one page of documents. LIMIT 0 0 is a cheap way to just count. Terms separated by spaces are ANDed, | is OR, @field: scopes a term to a field, and [min max] is a numeric range (with ( for exclusive and +inf/-inf for open ends).

docs.title: A negation trap
docs.text:
This query is meant to be "kettles that aren't toys":

127.0.0.1:6379> FT.SEARCH idx:products "-@category:{toys} kettl*" LIMIT 0 1 RETURN 1 name
1) (integer) 48988
2) "product:2545"
3) 1) "name"
   2) "compact wireless tent"

It matched 48,988 documents, including a tent. FT.EXPLAIN shows how the query was parsed:

127.0.0.1:6379> FT.EXPLAIN idx:products "-@category:{toys} kettl*"
"NOT{\n  INTERSECT {\n    TAG:@category {\n      toys\n    }\n    PREFIX{kettl*}\n  }\n}\n"

The - applied to everything after it: NOT (toys AND kettle). That's every document except toy kettles. Putting the positive term first, or parenthesizing the negation, gives the intended result:

127.0.0.1:6379> FT.SEARCH idx:products "kettl* -@category:{toys}" LIMIT 0 1 RETURN 1 name
1) (integer) 4059
2) "product:46219"
3) 1) "name"
   2) "foldable wireless kettle"
127.0.0.1:6379> FT.SEARCH idx:products "(-@category:{toys}) kettl*" LIMIT 0 0
1) (integer) 4059

On this server FT.CONFIG GET DEFAULT_DIALECT returned 1, and adding DIALECT 2 to the original query still returned 48,988. When a query returns a surprising count, run FT.EXPLAIN before anything else.

docs.title: Aggregations
docs.text:
FT.AGGREGATE runs a pipeline over the matches: group, reduce, sort and apply expressions:

127.0.0.1:6379> FT.AGGREGATE idx:products "*" GROUPBY 1 @category REDUCE COUNT 0 AS n REDUCE AVG 1 @price AS avg_price SORTBY 2 @n DESC
1) (integer) 5
2) 1) "category"
   2) "outdoor"
   3) "n"
   4) "10071"
   5) "avg_price"
   6) "251.423819879"
...

docs.title: What the index buys you
docs.text:
The same question, "garden products priced 10–20", answered by the index and by scanning every document from Python:

FT.SEARCH: 217 matches in 12.4 ms | SCAN + JSON.GET + filter in Python: 217 matches in 6.6 s

The answers are the same, and the index is about 500× faster. That's the whole point of a secondary index.

docs.title: Vector search
docs.text:
A vector index answers "which stored vectors are most similar to this one?", the core of semantic search, recommendations and retrieval-augmented generation. Here 50,000 synthetic 64-dimensional vectors (50 clusters plus noise, L2-normalized) are stored as FLOAT32 bytes in hashes and indexed twice: FLAT (exact brute force) and HNSW (an approximate graph index):

import time, numpy as np, redis
from redis.commands.search.query import Query
r = redis.Redis()
DIM, N = 64, 50_000
rng = np.random.default_rng(1)
centers = rng.normal(size=(50, DIM))
vecs = centers[rng.integers(0, 50, N)] + 0.3 * rng.normal(size=(N, DIM))
vecs = (vecs / np.linalg.norm(vecs, axis=1, keepdims=True)).astype(np.float32)

p = r.pipeline(transaction=False)
for i, v in enumerate(vecs):
    p.hset(f"doc:{i}", mapping={"emb": v.tobytes(), "lang": "en" if i % 4 else "pt"})
    if i % 5000 == 4999: p.execute()
p.execute()

for name, algo, extra in (("idx:vec:flat", "FLAT", []),
                          ("idx:vec:hnsw", "HNSW", ["M", "16", "EF_CONSTRUCTION", "200"])):
    r.execute_command("FT.CREATE", name, "ON", "HASH", "PREFIX", "1", "doc:", "SCHEMA",
                      "lang", "TAG", "emb", "VECTOR", algo, 6 + len(extra),
                      "TYPE", "FLOAT32", "DIM", DIM, "DISTANCE_METRIC", "COSINE", *extra)

def knn(index, q, k=10, filt="*"):
    qry = (Query(f"({filt})=>[KNN {k} @emb $v AS score]")
           .sort_by("score").return_fields("score").dialect(2).paging(0, k))
    return [d.id for d in r.ft(index).search(qry, query_params={"v": q.astype(np.float32).tobytes()}).docs]

# The rest of the script waits for indexing to finish, then times knn() for 200 noisy query vectors on each
# index, computes recall@10 against the FLAT results, cross-checks FLAT against NumPy (vecs @ q), and runs
# 50 hybrid queries with filt="@lang:{pt}".

FLAT index built over 50000 vectors in 8.3s, vector index memory 14.9 MB
HNSW index built over 50000 vectors in 9.6s, vector index memory 27.7 MB
idx:vec:flat    1.03 ms/query  recall@10 vs exact 1.000
idx:vec:hnsw    0.33 ms/query  recall@10 vs exact 0.684
FLAT agrees with numpy brute force on 20 of 20 queries
hybrid (KNN within lang=pt): 0.45 ms/query, all results pt: True

FLAT was exact (it matched an independent NumPy brute-force search on 20 of 20 queries) at about 1 ms per query. HNSW was 3× faster, but with the default query settings it found only 68% of the true top 10. That's a quality problem you'd never notice without measuring against an exact baseline.

The knob is EF_RUNTIME, the size of the candidate list HNSW explores per query. It can be set per query (KNN 10 @emb $v EF_RUNTIME 100 AS score):

HNSW EF_RUNTIME=default  0.34 ms/query  recall@10 0.684
HNSW EF_RUNTIME=50       0.35 ms/query  recall@10 0.966
HNSW EF_RUNTIME=100      0.36 ms/query  recall@10 0.991
HNSW EF_RUNTIME=200      0.41 ms/query  recall@10 0.994
HNSW EF_RUNTIME=500      0.58 ms/query  recall@10 1.000

At 100, recall was 0.991 for almost the same latency. On this data, the default was simply too low for a top-10 query. Measure recall on your own vectors and set EF_RUNTIME (or the index default) deliberately. Also note the memory: HNSW's graph cost almost twice FLAT's raw vectors.

Hybrid queries combine a filter with KNN, such as (@lang:{pt})=>[KNN 10 …], and every result honoured the filter. At 50,000 vectors FLAT is perfectly usable. HNSW earns its memory and recall tuning at millions of vectors, where brute force grows linearly.

docs.title: Vector sets
docs.text:
Redis 8 also has a built-in vector set type (no module needed), a key that holds named vectors with an HNSW index of its own:

127.0.0.1:6379> VADD colors VALUES 3 1 0 0 red
(integer) 1
127.0.0.1:6379> VADD colors VALUES 3 0.9 0.1 0 orange
(integer) 1
127.0.0.1:6379> VADD colors VALUES 3 0 0 1 blue
(integer) 1
127.0.0.1:6379> VSIM colors VALUES 3 1 0.05 0 WITHSCORES COUNT 2
1) "red"
2) "0.9993762075901031"
3) "orange"
4) "0.9989067316055298"
127.0.0.1:6379> TYPE colors
vectorset

It's like a sorted set for similarity: simple, one key per collection, with no schema or document fields. Use the query engine when you need filters and other fields alongside the vectors.

docs.title: How It Actually Works
docs.text:
An index is built from keyspace notifications inside the server. The module registers for changes to keys under the declared prefixes, and each JSON.SET or HSET on product:* re-extracts the indexed fields and updates the index structures in the same command. That's why the index is consistent with the data immediately after each write, and also why indexing adds cost to every write.

TEXT fields go into an inverted index: for each (stemmed) term, a compressed list of document IDs with frequencies and positions, used for relevance ranking (the scoring function is selectable with SCORER). TAG fields are inverted indexes without tokenization or stemming. NUMERIC fields use a range tree, and GEO is stored as geohash-encoded numerics, like GEOADD. A query is parsed into a tree of operators (INTERSECT, UNION, NOT, PREFIX… as FT.EXPLAIN showed), and each node iterates document IDs in order, which is how intersections stay cheap.

HNSW builds a multi-layer proximity graph. Each vector links to about M neighbours per layer, and upper layers are sparse "highways". A search descends from the top layer greedily, then explores the bottom layer while keeping a candidate list of size EF_RUNTIME. A small list finishes fast but can miss true neighbours that aren't reachable greedily. That's the 0.684 recall. A bigger list explores more and converges on the exact answer. FLAT just computes the distance to every vector, which is exact and O(N).

In Redis Cluster, each shard indexes its own keys, and a coordinator fans queries out and merges results (in Redis's own distributions and managed offerings; check what your deployment supports).

docs.title: Common mistakes
docs.text:
• TEXT where you meant TAG. Status values get stemmed and tokenized, and @status:open matches "opening".
  • Negation precedence. -a b means NOT (a AND b). Check with FT.EXPLAIN.
  • Querying during initial indexing and trusting the counts.
  • Indexing every field "just in case". Each indexed field costs memory and slows every write.
  • Shipping HNSW with untuned EF_RUNTIME. Recall was 0.68 here. Measure against FLAT or brute force.
  • Mismatched vector bytes: wrong dtype (float64 sent to a FLOAT32 field), wrong dimension, or vectors that aren't normalized when the metric assumes it.
  • Using the query engine as the source of truth for counts in reports without understanding its tokenization.

docs.title: Exercise
docs.text:
1. Add a SORTABLE TAG field brand to the product index (with FT.ALTER), backfill it, and write a query for "in-stock garden items under 50, sorted by rating, page 2 of 10 results".
  2. Use FT.AGGREGATE to compute, per category, the number of products rated ≥ 4.5 and their median price (REDUCE QUANTILE).
  3. Rebuild the HNSW index with M 32 and EF_CONSTRUCTION 400. Record build time, memory and recall at EF_RUNTIME 10, 50 and 100.
  4. Generate real embeddings for 2,000 sentences with any embedding model you have access to, index them, and compare FLAT and HNSW recall on 100 queries. Is the default EF_RUNTIME adequate for your data?

docs.title: 10 · Project — Caching & Rate-Limiting Layer for an API
docs.text:
This project puts Level 3 in front of a real HTTP API. A small FastAPI service has a deliberately slow "database" (50 ms for a product, 300 ms for a report), and a reusable Guard class adds:

  • rate limiting per API key (sliding window counter, Level 3 · 04) with 429, Retry-After and RateLimit-Remaining headers;
  • cache-aside with a rebuild lock so a cold key costs one database call, not thirty (Level 3 · 03);
  • stale-while-revalidate for the expensive report;
  • versioned invalidation that can't be undone by a slow reader writing back stale data (Level 3 · 01).

Versions used: FastAPI 0.143.0, Starlette 1.8.0, Uvicorn 0.54.0, httpx 0.28.1, redis-py 8.1.0, Redis 8.10.2.

docs.title: The Guard
docs.text:
guard.py:

"""Redis-backed caching (cache-aside + stale-while-revalidate + versioned invalidation) and rate limiting."""
import json, threading, time, uuid
import redis

LIMIT_LUA = """
-- sliding window counter using the server clock
-- KEYS[1] = current window key, KEYS[2] = previous window key ; ARGV = limit, window_ms
local t = redis.call('TIME')
local now = t[1] * 1000 + math.floor(t[2] / 1000)
local w, limit = tonumber(ARGV[2]), tonumber(ARGV[1])
local prev = tonumber(redis.call('GET', KEYS[2]) or '0')
local cur = tonumber(redis.call('GET', KEYS[1]) or '0')
local weight = 1 - (now % w) / w
local used = prev * weight + cur
if used >= limit then
  return {0, 0, w - (now % w)}
end
redis.call('INCR', KEYS[1]); redis.call('PEXPIRE', KEYS[1], w * 2)
return {1, math.floor(limit - used - 1), 0}
"""

SET_IF_VERSION_LUA = """
if (redis.call('GET', KEYS[2]) or '0') == ARGV[1] then
  return redis.call('SET', KEYS[1], ARGV[2], 'EX', ARGV[3])
end
return false
"""


class Guard:
    def __init__(self, r: redis.Redis, prefix="api"):
        self.r, self.p = r, prefix
        self._limit = r.register_script(LIMIT_LUA)
        self._set_if_version = r.register_script(SET_IF_VERSION_LUA)

    # ---------------- rate limiting ----------------
    def allow(self, client: str, limit: int, window_ms: int = 1000, now_ms: int | None = None):
        """Returns (allowed, remaining, retry_after_ms). Window keys share a hash tag per client."""
        now_ms = now_ms or int(time.time() * 1000)            # only used to name the windows
        win = now_ms // window_ms
        cur, prev = f"{self.p}:rl:{{{client}}}:{win}", f"{self.p}:rl:{{{client}}}:{win - 1}"
        ok, remaining, retry = self._limit(keys=[cur, prev], args=[limit, window_ms])
        return bool(ok), int(remaining), int(retry)

    # ---------------- caching ----------------
    def _ver_key(self, tag):
        return f"{self.p}:ver:{tag}"

    def invalidate(self, tag):
        """Bump the tag's version: every cached entry built from the old version becomes unreachable."""
        self.r.incr(self._ver_key(tag))

    def cached(self, tag: str, name: str, loader, ttl: int, grace: int = 0, lock_ms: int = 5000):
        """Return (value, status) where status is HIT, MISS, STALE or WAIT."""
        ver = self.r.get(self._ver_key(tag)) or "0"
        key = f"{self.p}:cache:{tag}:v{ver}:{name}"
        lock = f"{key}:lock"
        raw = self.r.get(key)
        if raw is not None:
            entry = json.loads(raw)
            if entry["fresh_until"] > time.time():
                return entry["value"], "HIT"
            if grace and self.r.set(lock, 1, nx=True, px=lock_ms):  # stale: refresh in background
                threading.Thread(target=self._fill, args=(tag, ver, key, lock, loader, ttl, grace), daemon=True).start()
            return entry["value"], "STALE"
        # cold miss: one loader, everyone else waits for it
        deadline = time.time() + lock_ms / 1000
        while time.time() < deadline:
            if self.r.set(lock, 1, nx=True, px=lock_ms):
                raw = self.r.get(key)                         # re-check: the previous holder may have
                if raw is not None:                           # just filled it and released the lock
                    self.r.delete(lock)
                    return json.loads(raw)["value"], "WAIT"
                return self._fill(tag, ver, key, lock, loader, ttl, grace), "MISS"
            time.sleep(0.01)
            raw = self.r.get(key)
            if raw is not None:
                return json.loads(raw)["value"], "WAIT"
        return loader(), "MISS"                                   # lock holder died: degrade gracefully

    def _fill(self, tag, ver, key, lock, loader, ttl, grace):
        try:
            value = loader()
            entry = json.dumps({"value": value, "fresh_until": time.time() + ttl})
            # write back only if nobody invalidated the tag while we were loading
            self._set_if_version(keys=[key, self._ver_key(tag)], args=[ver, entry, ttl + grace])
            return value
        finally:
            self.r.delete(lock)

Design notes:

  • Rate limiting uses Redis's clock (TIME inside the script) for the sliding-window weight, so app servers with skewed clocks still agree on how full a window is. The window key names are computed by the caller, because scripts must receive their keys in KEYS. A caller whose clock is far off would pick a different window key. With NTP-synced servers that's a non-issue, but it's a trade-off worth knowing about. The client ID sits in a hash tag ({client}), so both window keys live in one Cluster slot.
  • Every cache key contains the tag's version (api:cache:product:7:v3:detail). invalidate() is a single INCR. Old entries become unreachable at once and expire on their own.
  • The write-back is conditional on the version that was current when loading started, so a load that overlaps an update can't plant stale data (test_write_during_refresh_is_not_cached).
  • X-Cache reports what happened: HIT, MISS (this request loaded it), WAIT (waited for another request's load) or STALE (served old data while a background refresh runs).

docs.title: The app
docs.text:
app.py:

"""A small API with a slow 'database', protected by Guard."""
import threading, time
import redis
from fastapi import FastAPI, HTTPException, Request, Response

r = redis.Redis(decode_responses=True)
from guard import Guard
guard = Guard(r)
app = FastAPI()

DB = {i: {"id": i, "name": f"Product {i}", "price_cents": 1000 + i} for i in range(1, 101)}
DB_CALLS = {"product": 0, "report": 0}
_lock = threading.Lock()

def db_product(pid):
    with _lock: DB_CALLS["product"] += 1
    time.sleep(0.05)                                    # 50 ms query
    return DB.get(pid)

def db_report():
    with _lock: DB_CALLS["report"] += 1
    time.sleep(0.3)                                     # 300 ms aggregate
    return {"top": sorted(DB.values(), key=lambda p: -p["price_cents"])[:3], "built_at": time.time()}

@app.middleware("http")
async def rate_limit(request: Request, call_next):
    client = request.headers.get("x-api-key", "anon")
    ok, remaining, retry_ms = guard.allow(client, limit=20, window_ms=1000)
    if not ok:
        return Response(status_code=429, headers={"Retry-After": str(max(1, -(-retry_ms // 1000))),
                                                  "RateLimit-Remaining": "0"})
    response = await call_next(request)
    response.headers["RateLimit-Remaining"] = str(remaining)
    return response

@app.get("/products/{pid}")
def get_product(pid: int, response: Response):
    value, status = guard.cached(f"product:{pid}", "detail", lambda: db_product(pid), ttl=60)
    if value is None:
        raise HTTPException(404)
    response.headers["X-Cache"] = status
    return value

@app.put("/products/{pid}")
def put_product(pid: int, body: dict):
    if pid not in DB: raise HTTPException(404)
    DB[pid] = {**DB[pid], **body}                       # 1. write the source of truth
    guard.invalidate(f"product:{pid}")                  # 2. then invalidate by version
    guard.invalidate("report")
    return DB[pid]

@app.get("/reports/top")
def top_report(response: Response):
    value, status = guard.cached("report", "top", db_report, ttl=2, grace=60)
    response.headers["X-Cache"] = status
    return value

The order in put_product matters: change the source of truth first, then invalidate. Invalidating first would let a concurrent read reload the old row and cache it under the new version.

docs.title: Tests
docs.text:
test_api.py uses FastAPI's TestClient and a distinct API key per test, so rate limits don't interfere:

import threading, time
import pytest
from fastapi.testclient import TestClient
import app as appmod

@pytest.fixture
def client():
    for k in appmod.r.scan_iter("api:*"): appmod.r.unlink(k)
    appmod.DB_CALLS.update(product=0, report=0)
    with TestClient(appmod.app) as c:
        yield c

def key(i):            # a distinct API key per test so rate limits don't interfere
    return {"x-api-key": f"test-{i}-{time.time_ns()}"}

def test_miss_then_hit(client):
    h = key(1)
    r1 = client.get("/products/7", headers=h); r2 = client.get("/products/7", headers=h)
    assert (r1.headers["x-cache"], r2.headers["x-cache"]) == ("MISS", "HIT")
    assert r2.json()["price_cents"] == 1007 and appmod.DB_CALLS["product"] == 1

def test_not_found_is_404(client):
    assert client.get("/products/999", headers=key(2)).status_code == 404

def test_update_invalidates(client):
    h = key(3)
    client.get("/products/5", headers=h)
    client.put("/products/5", json={"price_cents": 1}, headers=h)
    r = client.get("/products/5", headers=h)
    assert r.headers["x-cache"] == "MISS" and r.json()["price_cents"] == 1

def test_stampede_single_db_call(client):
    results = []
    def hit(i):
        results.append(client.get("/products/42", headers=key(100 + i)).headers["x-cache"])
    ts = [threading.Thread(target=hit, args=(i,)) for i in range(30)]
    [t.start() for t in ts]; [t.join() for t in ts]
    assert appmod.DB_CALLS["product"] == 1
    assert results.count("MISS") == 1 and set(results) <= {"MISS", "WAIT", "HIT"}

def test_stale_while_revalidate(client):
    h = key(4)
    assert client.get("/reports/top", headers=h).headers["x-cache"] == "MISS"
    time.sleep(2.1)                                         # past the 2 s soft TTL
    t = time.perf_counter(); r = client.get("/reports/top", headers=h); el = time.perf_counter() - t
    assert r.headers["x-cache"] == "STALE" and el < 0.1     # served instantly, not after 300 ms
    time.sleep(0.5)                                         # background refresh finishes
    assert client.get("/reports/top", headers=h).headers["x-cache"] == "HIT"
    assert appmod.DB_CALLS["report"] == 2

def test_write_during_refresh_is_not_cached(client):
    h = key(5)
    def slow_get():
        client.get("/products/9", headers=h)               # loader takes 50 ms
    t = threading.Thread(target=slow_get); t.start(); time.sleep(0.02)
    client.put("/products/9", json={"price_cents": 5}, headers=h)
    t.join()
    r = client.get("/products/9", headers=h)
    assert r.json()["price_cents"] == 5

def test_rate_limit_429(client):
    h = key(6)
    codes = [client.get("/products/1", headers=h).status_code for _ in range(30)]
    assert codes.count(200) <= 21 and codes.count(429) >= 9
    blocked = client.get("/products/1", headers=h)
    assert blocked.status_code == 429 and int(blocked.headers["retry-after"]) >= 1

def test_limit_is_per_client(client):
    a, b = key(7), key(8)
    for _ in range(25): client.get("/products/1", headers=a)
    assert client.get("/products/1", headers=b).status_code == 200

def test_remaining_header_counts_down(client):
    h = key(9)
    rem = [int(client.get("/products/2", headers=h).headers["ratelimit-remaining"]) for _ in range(3)]
    assert rem[0] > rem[1] > rem[2]

docs.title: The bug the stampede test caught
docs.text:
The first version of cached() passed every test except one:

>       assert appmod.DB_CALLS["product"] == 1
E       assert 2 == 1

FAILED test_api.py::test_stampede_single_db_call - assert 2 == 1
1 failed, 8 passed, 1 warning in 24.71s

Thirty concurrent requests produced two database calls. The waiter loop was:

try SET lock NX  ->  fail
sleep 10 ms
GET key          ->  still empty (loader not finished)
try SET lock NX  ->  succeeds, because the loader has meanwhile written the key AND released the lock
load again       ->  second database call

A waiter could acquire the lock in the instant between the first loader finishing and the waiter's next check. The fix is the classic double-check: after acquiring the lock, look at the cache once more before loading:

if self.r.set(lock, 1, nx=True, px=lock_ms):
    raw = self.r.get(key)                         # re-check: the previous holder may have
    if raw is not None:                           # just filled it and released the lock
        self.r.delete(lock)
        return json.loads(raw)["value"], "WAIT"
    return self._fill(tag, ver, key, lock, loader, ttl, grace), "MISS"

After the fix the suite passed three runs in a row. Concurrency bugs like this are invisible in single-request testing and only show up when you assert on the count of backend calls under real parallelism.

docs.title: Running it for real
docs.text:
Start the app under Uvicorn and send traffic with curl:

uvicorn app:app --port 8077

Twenty-five rapid requests with one API key against a limit of 20 per second:

25 rapid requests, one API key:
200 200 200 200 200 200 200 200 200 200 200 200 200 200 200 200 200 200 200 200 200 429 429 429 429
HTTP/1.1 429 Too Many Requests
retry-after: 1
ratelimit-remaining: 0

21 requests got through, one more than the limit. That's the sliding-window counter's approximation (Level 3 · 04): the requests straddled a window boundary, and the weighted estimate of the previous window let one extra through. If the limit must be exact, use a sliding log.

Twenty concurrent first requests for the 300 ms report, with the twenty X-Cache response headers tallied:

x-cache: WAIT    (×19)
x-cache: MISS    (×1)

One request loaded the report and nineteen waited for its result. That's one database query instead of twenty.

docs.title: How It Actually Works
docs.text:
Each request does a small, fixed number of Redis round trips: one EVALSHA for the rate limit, a GET for the version, a GET for the cache entry, and on a miss, a SET NX for the lock, a conditional SET via script and a DEL. Every decision that must be exclusive (who loads, whether the write-back is still valid, whether the client is over its limit) is a single atomic Redis operation. The Python code only orchestrates.

Stale-while-revalidate splits freshness from existence: the entry carries fresh_until (soft TTL) and the key has ttl + grace (hard TTL). Within the grace period, users never wait for the report. If the background refresh keeps failing, the entry eventually expires and the next request loads synchronously, so a broken backend can't keep serving stale data forever.

What this layer doesn't do: it doesn't make Redis durable (rate-limit counters and cache entries are disposable, so that's fine), and it doesn't protect against Redis being down. A production version should catch connection errors and decide, per endpoint, whether to fail open (serve from the database, skip rate limiting) or fail closed.

docs.title: Common mistakes
docs.text:
• No double-check after acquiring a rebuild lock. Two loads under load, as the test showed.
  • Invalidating before writing the database. A concurrent read caches the old row.
  • Rate limits in process memory. With N app servers, every client gets N× the limit. Shared state belongs in Redis.
  • One global limit key. Hot-spots one Redis node, and one noisy client throttles everyone. Key by client.
  • Missing Retry-After. Well-behaved clients can't back off properly without it.
  • Failing closed by accident when Redis is unreachable. Decide explicitly.

docs.title: Exercise
docs.text:
1. Add fail-open behaviour: if Redis raises a connection error, skip rate limiting and call the loader directly, and expose a counter of degraded requests. Test it by pointing the app at a stopped Redis.
  2. Give different API keys different limits (free 20/s, pro 200/s) stored in a Redis hash, cached in-process with client-side caching (Level 3 · 06) so the lookup costs nothing on the hot path.
  3. Replace the sliding window counter with a token bucket for /reports/top only (bursty but expensive), with a cost of 5 tokens per call.
  4. Load-test with ab -n 5000 -c 50 against /products/{random id} and report the hit ratio, p99 latency and the number of database calls. Then double the product catalogue so that it no longer fits under a maxmemory limit, and repeat with allkeys-lru and allkeys-lfu.

docs.title: Level 4 · Operations & Production
docs.text:
Level 4 is about the server your application depends on: what survives a crash, what a failover loses, how a cluster changes shape under load, who's allowed to do what, how to find the cause of a slowdown, and how to upgrade without breaking anything. Every claim in this level was tested by breaking something on purpose:

  • kill -9 after 5,000 writes on a snapshot-only server, which lost all 5,000;
  • appendfsync always cutting a single client to under 30 writes per second on this laptop's disk;
  • an acknowledged write lost when a partitioned primary died, while WAIT had warned it wasn't replicated;
  • a Sentinel failover with a 3.2-second write outage and every acknowledged write intact;
  • a cluster resharded under load with zero client errors, through 8.4's atomic slot migration;
  • Python 3.14 rejecting TLS certificates that redis-cli accepted;
  • Redis 8.10 and Valkey 9.1 unable to read each other's snapshots, replicate, or restore each other's DUMPs.

Servers used: Redis 8.10.2 (Homebrew, macOS, Apple Silicon) and Valkey 9.1.2 for the comparison lesson. Multi-server lessons run every node on one laptop, which demonstrates behaviour and procedures, but not real availability. Things that couldn't be tested here are stated where they come up: OS-crash and power-loss durability, copy-on-write measurement (Linux-only instrumentation), and Valkey's own modules.

Prerequisites: Levels 1–3, and comfort running several processes from a terminal.

docs.title: Modules
docs.text:
1. Persistence I: RDB Snapshots & fork() — SAVE vs BGSAVE, fork cost, copy-on-write headroom, what a crash loses, load times and redis-check-rdb.
  2. Persistence II: AOF, fsync & Hybrid Persistence — fsync policies measured, process crash vs machine crash, multi-part AOF, rewrites, and truncated vs corrupt files.
  3. Replication: PSYNC, the Backlog & Consistency — diskless full sync, partial resync, backlog overflow, WAIT, and losing an acknowledged write.
  4. High Availability with Sentinel — three Sentinels, a primary killed under load, the failover log step by step, and Sentinel-aware clients.
  5. Redis Cluster: Hash Slots, MOVED & ASK — 16,384 slots, creating a cluster, redirects, CROSSSLOT, hash tags and cluster clients.
  6. Cluster Operations: Resharding, Scaling & Failover — adding nodes, ASK during a manual slot move, atomic slot migration under load, killed vs graceful failover.
  7. Security: ACLs, Protected Mode & TLS — protected mode, least-privilege users, ACL DRYRUN and ACL LOG, and mutual TLS.
  8. Monitoring & Troubleshooting — the slow log, latency monitor, command stats, latency percentiles, hot and big keys, and what to alert on.
  9. Versions, Licensing, Valkey & Upgrades — what the license files say, Redis vs Valkey compared on one machine, and the rolling-upgrade procedure.
  10. Capstone — A Secured, Persistent, Failover-Tested Cluster — a 6-node cluster with ACLs, authenticated replication and AOF, proven by a 13-check acceptance test.

docs.title: After Level 4
docs.text: You can run Redis in production and prove that it behaves as intended. Keep the habit this course has tried to build: before trusting a setting, a library default or a version upgrade, reproduce the failure it's supposed to handle, on a lab you can throw away.

docs.title: 01 · Persistence I: RDB Snapshots & fork()
docs.text: Redis keeps data in memory, so persistence is about one question: after a crash or restart, what comes back? Redis has two mechanisms. RDB writes a compact point-in-time snapshot of the whole dataset. AOF (next lesson) logs every write. This lesson measures RDB on a scratch server (port 6440) holding 3 million keys, about 458 MB.

docs.title: SAVE vs BGSAVE
docs.text:
SAVE writes the snapshot in the server's main thread:

SAVE (foreground) took 1.78 s; the server answered nobody meanwhile

For 1.78 seconds every client was blocked. Never run SAVE on a live server. BGSAVE forks a child process to do the writing, and the parent keeps serving:

BGSAVE -> True
BGSAVE returned in 37.6 ms
rdb_last_bgsave_status: ok
rdb_last_bgsave_time_sec: 3
latest_fork_usec: 23099

The command returned in 38 ms, and the snapshot took 3 seconds in the background while a writer thread kept modifying keys (398,000 writes during the save). The one cost the parent does pay is the fork() itself: 23 ms (latest_fork_usec), during which the server is frozen. Fork time grows with the size of the process's page tables, roughly with memory used, and on large instances (tens of GB) it can reach hundreds of milliseconds. Watch latest_fork_usec on big servers.

The log shows both processes, the parent M and the child C:

5489:M 13 Oct 2026 15:58:06.888 * Background saving started by pid 5495
5495:C 13 Oct 2026 15:58:09.204 * DB saved on disk
5495:C 13 Oct 2026 15:58:09.204 * Fork CoW for RDB: current 0 MB, peak 0 MB, average 0 MB
5489:M 13 Oct 2026 15:58:09.249 * Background saving terminated with success

docs.title: Copy-on-write: the memory you need to reserve
docs.text:
After fork(), parent and child share every memory page. When the parent modifies a page (any write to a key on it), the OS copies that page first, so the child keeps seeing the snapshot moment. Under heavy writes during a save, the copies add up. In the worst case, every page is written and memory use doubles.

Here the log reports CoW as 0 MB, and rdb_last_cow_size was 0, but that is a measurement limitation of this platform, not a fact about the save. Redis computes CoW from Linux's /proc/<pid>/smaps, which macOS doesn't have. Sampling the processes with ps doesn't help either:

parent RSS before: 462 MB
child pid ['5518'] peak child RSS: 457 MB | peak parent RSS: 462 MB

RSS counts shared pages in both processes, so these numbers say nothing about how much was actually copied. On Linux, the Fork CoW log line and rdb_last_cow_size give a real figure. Use them to size headroom: maxmemory plus expected CoW plus buffers must fit in RAM. A common rule of thumb is to keep maxmemory well below the machine's memory on write-heavy instances that snapshot. Also, disable transparent huge pages on Linux, which Redis warns about at startup: with 2 MB pages, writing one byte copies 2 MB instead of 4 KB.

docs.title: What a crash loses
docs.text:
Count 5,000 orders after a snapshot, then kill the server with SIGKILL (no chance to save):

r.set("orders:count", 0)
r.bgsave(); time.sleep(4)
for i in range(5000): r.incr("orders:count")
print("orders:count before crash:", r.get("orders:count"),
      "| changes since last save:", r.info("persistence")["rdb_changes_since_last_save"])

orders:count before crash: b'5000' | changes since last save: 5000

kill -9 <pid>
redis-server --port 6440 --dir … --save ''
redis-cli -p 6440 GET orders:count

* Loading RDB produced by version 8.10.2
* Done loading RDB, keys loaded: 3000001, keys expired: 0.
* DB loaded from disk: 2.299 seconds
0

All 5,000 increments were lost. The counter came back as 0, its value at the last snapshot. With RDB alone, you lose everything since the last successful snapshot. That's the right trade-off for caches and for data you can rebuild, and the wrong one for orders.

Two more facts from that restart:

  • Loading took 2.3 seconds, and the server doesn't accept normal commands until it's done (clients get LOADING). Restart time grows with dataset size, so plan for it in failover and deploy procedures.
  • rdb_changes_since_last_save is the number of writes at risk right now. It's a useful metric to alert on.

docs.title: Save points
docs.text:
When to snapshot automatically is set with save <seconds> <changes> rules, any of which triggers a BGSAVE. The built-in default (Level 1 · 01) is 3600 1 300 100 60 10000. For a cache you can rebuild, save "" (no snapshots) is common. For data you care about, combine RDB with AOF rather than tightening save points to every few seconds, because each snapshot rewrites the whole dataset.

stop-writes-on-bgsave-error yes (the default) makes Redis refuse writes when the last background save failed, for example because the disk is full or the directory isn't writable. It's a loud failure instead of a silent loss of durability. (An attempt to trigger it here by making the directory read-only didn't produce a failed save on this macOS setup, so it isn't demonstrated.) If you turn it off, monitor rdb_last_bgsave_status yourself.

docs.title: Checking a snapshot file
docs.text:
redis-check-rdb validates a file offline:

[offset 101043498] Checksum OK
[offset 101043498] \o/ RDB looks OK! \o/
[info] 3000001 keys read

A file truncated at 50 MB (as a copy interrupted mid-transfer might be):

[offset 50000000] Unexpected EOF reading RDB file
[additional info] While doing: read-object-value
[additional info] Reading key 'k:305343'

Run it on backups before you trust them. A backup that has never been restored is a hope, not a backup.

docs.title: How It Actually Works
docs.text:
BGSAVE calls fork(). The kernel duplicates the process's page tables (not its memory) and marks all pages read-only and shared. That table copy is the 23 ms freeze. The child walks every database and key and serializes them into a temporary file (temp-<pid>.rdb), then fsyncs it and renames it over dump.rdb. Rename is atomic, so dump.rdb is always either the old complete snapshot or the new complete one, never half-written. The parent sees the child exit through waitpid in the event loop and records the result.

The RDB format is compact: a header with the version, then for each key an optional expiry, a type byte, the key and the value in a type-specific encoding (small hashes and sets are stored as their listpack or intset blobs directly, which also makes loading fast), and an 8-byte CRC64 checksum at the end. Strings may be LZF-compressed, which is why 458 MB in memory became a 105 MB file. Loading reverses it and re-encodes each value compactly (Level 2 · 01's exercise 3 relies on this).

Because the snapshot is the state at the moment of fork(), writes that arrive during a long save are in memory but not in the file. They count towards rdb_changes_since_last_save for the next save.

docs.title: Common mistakes
docs.text:
• Running SAVE. It blocks everything for seconds.
  • No memory headroom for copy-on-write. A save under heavy writes can push a full server into swap or the OOM killer.
  • Transparent huge pages enabled on Linux. CoW copies get 512× bigger.
  • Assuming RDB is enough for important data. Everything since the last snapshot is lost in a crash.
  • Ignoring rdb_last_bgsave_status with stop-writes-on-bgsave-error no.
  • Untested backups. Run redis-check-rdb and do a real restore.
  • Forgetting restart time. 2.3 s for 3 M keys here. Minutes for very large datasets.

docs.title: Exercise
docs.text:
1. Measure latest_fork_usec for datasets of 0.5, 1, 2 and 4 GB (DEBUG POPULATE). Is the relationship roughly linear?
  2. On Linux, run BGSAVE with and without a heavy writer and compare rdb_last_cow_size. Then estimate the RAM headroom you'd need for your largest instance.
  3. Corrupt one byte in the middle of a copy of dump.rdb and see what redis-check-rdb reports. Then try starting a server on it. What does the server do?
  4. Configure save 60 1000 and write a script that tells you, at any moment, how many seconds of writes you'd lose in a crash, using rdb_last_save_time and rdb_changes_since_last_save.

docs.title: 02 · Persistence II: AOF, fsync & Hybrid Persistence
docs.text: RDB loses everything since the last snapshot. The append-only file (AOF) narrows that window by logging every write command as it happens. On restart, Redis replays the log. How narrow the window gets depends on one setting, appendfsync, and on understanding which failure you're protecting against. This lesson measures the policies, runs crash tests, and breaks the file on purpose.

docs.title: Turning it on and looking inside
docs.text:
redis-server --port 6451 --dir ./rw --save '' --appendonly yes

Since Redis 7, the AOF is a directory (appendonlydir/) with several parts and a manifest. After three SETs and 100,000 INCRs:

89 appendonly.aof.1.base.rdb
3600137 appendonly.aof.1.incr.aof
102 appendonly.aof.manifest

The incremental file is plain RESP, exactly what clients send (^M is \r):

*2^M
$6^M
SELECT^M
$1^M
0^M
*3^M
$3^M
SET^M
$8^M
greeting^M
$5^M
hello^M
...

It's 3.6 MB to describe a dataset of two keys, because the log records every one of the 100,000 increments.

docs.title: Rewriting: compacting the log
docs.text:
BGREWRITEAOF (or the automatic trigger) forks, writes the current dataset as a new base file, and starts a fresh incremental file:

Background append only file rewriting started

124 appendonly.aof.2.base.rdb
0 appendonly.aof.2.incr.aof
107 appendonly.aof.manifest

file appendonly.aof.2.base.rdb seq 2 type b
file appendonly.aof.2.incr.aof seq 2 type i startoffset 100003

3.6 MB became 124 bytes. The base is in RDB format because aof-use-rdb-preamble is yes by default ("hybrid" persistence: compact snapshot plus a log of what came after). The manifest says which files make up the current AOF. Rewrites happen automatically when the AOF has grown by auto-aof-rewrite-percentage (100%) since the last rewrite and is at least auto-aof-rewrite-min-size (64 MB).

docs.title: The fsync policies
docs.text:
Writing to a file puts the data in the operating system's page cache. Only fsync forces it onto the storage device. appendfsync decides when Redis calls it:

  • always — after every write batch, before replying. Nothing acknowledged is lost even if the machine loses power.
  • everysec (default) — once per second in a background thread. A power loss or kernel crash can lose up to about a second of writes.
  • no — never explicitly. The OS flushes when it chooses (often every 30 s on Linux).

Throughput of SET with redis-benchmark, on this MacBook's internal SSD:

aof=off       SET 50 clients: 160513.64 req/s   1 client: 12763.24 req/s
aof=no        SET 50 clients: 143266.47 req/s   1 client: 11634.67 req/s
aof=everysec  SET 50 clients: 146198.83 req/s   1 client: 11876.48 req/s
aof=always    SET 50 clients:   5719.84 req/s   1 client:    29.67 req/s
  • everysec cost about 9% of throughput against no AOF, which is why it's the default.
  • always collapsed throughput: 5,720 writes/s with 50 clients (Redis batches all writes from one event-loop iteration into one fsync) and under 30 writes per second for a single client waiting for each reply.

Take that last number as a property of this machine, not of Redis. On macOS, Redis flushes with F_FULLFSYNC, which forces the drive to write its own cache to the medium and takes tens of milliseconds. Linux servers with datacenter NVMe drives (with power-loss protection) complete fsync much faster. Measure always on your own production hardware before deciding.

docs.title: What does a crash actually lose?
docs.text:
This test increments a counter as fast as one client can, counts the increments the server acknowledged, kills the server with SIGKILL after 3 seconds, restarts it, and compares:

r = redis.Redis(port=6450, retry=redis.retry.Retry(redis.backoff.NoBackoff(), 0))
pid = r.info("server")["process_id"]
acked = 0
def killer():
    time.sleep(3); os.kill(pid, signal.SIGKILL)
threading.Thread(target=killer).start()
try:
    while True:
        acked = r.incr("acked")             # only count what the server acknowledged
except redis.ConnectionError:
    pass
# restart the server on the same directory, then:
after = int(redis.Redis(port=6450).get("acked") or 0)

appendfsync everysec: acknowledged  24481, recovered  24481, lost 0
appendfsync always  : acknowledged    630, recovered    630, lost 0

Neither lost anything, and that's not a contradiction of the "up to one second" warning. kill -9 kills the process, not the machine. Everything Redis had write()n was already in the kernel's page cache, and the kernel finished writing it to disk after Redis died. everysec only loses data when the operating system or the power fails before the next fsync: a kernel panic, a hypervisor crash, a pulled plug. That couldn't be simulated safely on this laptop, so it isn't measured here. The distinction matters:

Failure no everysec always Redis process crash / OOM kill / kill -9 nothing acknowledged lost nothing lost nothing lost OS crash or power loss up to ~30 s (OS-dependent) up to ~1 s nothing acknowledged

(One subtlety: with everysec, if the disk can't keep up, Redis may delay the next write until the previous fsync completes, so the loss stays bounded at about 2 seconds rather than growing without limit.)

docs.title: Truncated vs corrupt files
docs.text:
A crash during a write can leave a half-written command at the end of the file. Here one is simulated by appending a fragment, *3\r\n$3\r\nSET\r\n$1\r\nc\r\n$1, and restarting:

* DB loaded from base file appendonly.aof.2.base.rdb: 0.001 seconds
# !!! Truncating the AOF appendonly.aof.2.incr.aof at offset 77 !!!
# AOF appendonlydir/appendonly.aof.2.incr.aof loaded anyway because aof-load-truncated is enabled

The server dropped the incomplete tail and started. a and b were intact, and the half-written c simply didn't exist. That's the right behaviour, because an incomplete command was never acknowledged.

Corruption in the middle is different. With one command name changed to SXT:

* DB loaded from base file appendonly.aof.2.base.rdb: 0.001 seconds
# Unknown command 'SXT' reading the append only file appendonly.aof.2.incr.aof

The server refused to start. Silently skipping a command in the middle of history could produce a state that never existed. Note what redis-check-aof said about that same file:

AOF analyzed: filename=…/appendonly.aof.2.incr.aof, size=77, ok_up_to=77, ok_up_to_line=20, diff=0
AOF …/appendonly.aof.2.incr.aof is valid

"Valid", because the tool checks the RESP framing, which was intact. It doesn't know whether SXT is a real command. redis-check-aof --fix repairs framing damage by truncating at the first bad position, which can throw away everything after it. Repair a copy, compare key counts before and after, and prefer restoring from a known-good backup when the damage is in the middle.

docs.title: How It Actually Works
docs.text:
Every write command, after it executes, is appended to an in-memory AOF buffer in RESP form, with SELECT emitted when the database changes. Commands are logged with deterministic effects: an EXPIRE with a relative time is written as PEXPIREAT with an absolute one, so replaying it later gives the same result. Before the event loop goes back to waiting, Redis write()s the buffer to the incremental file. Then, depending on appendfsync, it either fsyncs right away (always, before replies are sent, which is why throughput collapses), asks a background thread to fsync if a second has passed (everysec), or does nothing (no).

A rewrite forks a child, which writes the dataset as the new base (RDB format with the preamble). Meanwhile the parent opens a new incremental file and records new writes there. When the child finishes, the parent atomically updates the manifest to point at the new base and new incremental file, then deletes the old ones. Since the multi-part design (Redis 7.0), there's no need to buffer writes in memory during a rewrite and merge them afterwards, which removed a source of memory spikes and latency in older versions.
