On startup, Redis loads the base (fast, RDB) and replays the incremental files in manifest order. A transaction is logged wrapped in MULTI/EXEC, and an incomplete transaction at the end of the file is treated like any truncated tail.

docs.title: Common mistakes
docs.text:
• Choosing always without measuring on production hardware. It can turn a 100,000-writes/s server into a hundreds-per-second one.
  • Testing durability with kill -9 and concluding everysec loses nothing. Only OS/power failures expose the window.
  • Running redis-check-aof --fix on the only copy. It truncates.
  • Trusting "AOF is valid" to mean the contents are sound. It checks framing only.
  • AOF and RDB in different directories you back up separately. Back up the whole dir, including appendonlydir/ and its manifest.
  • Disks too slow for the write rate. everysec then stalls writers. Watch aof_delayed_fsync in INFO persistence.

docs.title: Exercise
docs.text:
1. Repeat the throughput benchmark with pipelining (redis-benchmark -P 16) for each policy. How much of always's cost does batching recover?
  2. On a Linux VM you can crash (echo c > /proc/sysrq-trigger, only on a disposable VM), run the acknowledged-counter test with everysec and always, and measure the actual loss after the VM reboots.
  3. Generate a 500 MB AOF with auto-aof-rewrite-percentage 0 (disabled), restart and time loading. Then rewrite and restart again. Compare load times.
  4. Corrupt a byte in the middle of a copy of an incremental file so that the RESP framing breaks (change a $5 to $9). Run redis-check-aof and --fix on the copy, and count how many commands were lost.

docs.title: 03 · Replication: PSYNC, the Backlog & Consistency
docs.text: A replica is a Redis server that keeps a copy of another server's data (its primary), updated continuously. Replicas give you a warm standby to fail over to, extra capacity for reads, and a place to take backups without loading the primary. They're asynchronous: the primary acknowledges a write to the client before any replica has it. This lesson watches every part of that on one laptop, a primary on port 6460 and replicas on 6461 and 6462, and ends by losing an acknowledged write on purpose.

docs.title: Starting replication
docs.text:
With a million keys on the primary:

redis-cli -p 6461 REPLICAOF 127.0.0.1 6460
redis-cli -p 6462 REPLICAOF 127.0.0.1 6460

(In a config file it's replicaof 127.0.0.1 6460. Older material says slaveof, which still works.) The primary's log shows the full synchronization:

* Full resync requested by replica 127.0.0.1:6461 (rdb-channel)
* Delay next BGSAVE for diskless SYNC
* Full resync requested by replica 127.0.0.1:6462 (rdb-channel)
* Delay next BGSAVE for diskless SYNC
* Starting BGSAVE for SYNC with target: replicas sockets (rdb-channel)
* Synchronization with replica 127.0.0.1:6461 succeeded
* Streamed RDB transfer with replica 127.0.0.1:6461 succeeded (socket). Waiting for REPLCONF ACK from replica …

and the replica's:

* Done loading RDB, keys loaded: 1000000, keys expired: 0.
* MASTER <-> REPLICA sync: Finished with success

Three things are visible here:

  • Diskless sync (repl-diskless-sync yes, the default): the snapshot is streamed straight to the replicas' sockets instead of being written to disk first.
  • repl-diskless-sync-delay 5: the primary waited 5 seconds (21:40:28 → 21:40:33) so that both replicas, which asked within milliseconds of each other, could share one fork and one stream.
  • (rdb-channel): on this Redis 8 build, the replica opened a separate connection for the snapshot, so the primary can stream new writes on the main replication link while the snapshot transfers. In older versions those writes had to be buffered on the primary for the whole transfer.

Once synced:

role:master
connected_slaves:2
slave0:ip=127.0.0.1,port=6461,state=online,offset=14,lag=1,io-thread=0
slave1:ip=127.0.0.1,port=6462,state=online,offset=14,lag=1,io-thread=0
master_repl_offset:28

The replication offset counts bytes of the replication stream. Each replica reports the offset it has processed, so master_repl_offset − replica offset is the lag in bytes. lag is seconds since the replica last acknowledged.

Replicas are read-only by default:

READONLY You can't write against a read only replica.

docs.title: Short disconnections: partial resync
docs.text:
The primary keeps a replication backlog, a circular buffer of the most recent replication stream (repl-backlog-size, 1 MB by default). Kill the replica connections and they reconnect:

S * Trying a partial resynchronization (request 8a067f3e85013107055154c7e4b7326770bd5ffd:43).
S * Successful partial resynchronization with master.
M * Partial resynchronization request from 127.0.0.1:6461 accepted. Sending 0 bytes of backlog starting from offset 43.

The replica asked to continue from replication ID 8a06… at offset 43, and since the backlog still covered offset 43, the primary just sent what was missing (nothing, here). No snapshot, no reload.

docs.title: Long disconnections: backlog overflow
docs.text:
Now freeze one replica (kill -STOP), drop its connection, write about 4 MB of commands, and resume it:

master_repl_offset now 8346759
M * Partial resynchronization request from 127.0.0.1:6462 accepted. Sending 0 bytes of backlog starting from offset 4157970.
M * Unable to partial resync with replica 127.0.0.1:6461 for lack of backlog (Replica request was: 4157970).
M * Full resync requested by replica 127.0.0.1:6461 (rdb-channel)

The frozen replica needed data from offset 4,157,970, but 4 MB of writes had pushed that out of the 1 MB backlog, so it had to do a full resync: a new snapshot of the whole dataset. On a 50 GB instance that's a fork, gigabytes over the network, and minutes of loading, triggered by a few seconds of network trouble. Size the backlog to cover your longest expected disconnection at your peak write rate. For example, 5 MB/s of replication traffic and 60 seconds of tolerance needs at least 300 MB.

docs.title: WAIT: knowing how many replicas have a write
docs.text:
WAIT numreplicas timeout_ms blocks until at least that many replicas have acknowledged everything this client has written, or the timeout passes, and returns how many did:

127.0.0.1:6460> SET order:1 paid
OK
127.0.0.1:6460> WAIT 1 1000
(integer) 1

docs.title: Losing an acknowledged write
docs.text:
To simulate a network partition, the replica connects through a small TCP proxy that can silently drop traffic:

"""TCP proxy that can simulate a network partition: touch PARTITION file -> bytes are silently dropped."""
import os, socket, sys, threading
LISTEN, TARGET, FLAG = int(sys.argv[1]), int(sys.argv[2]), sys.argv[3]
def pump(src, dst):
    try:
        while True:
            data = src.recv(65536)
            if not data: break
            if not os.path.exists(FLAG): dst.sendall(data)      # partitioned: black-hole the bytes
    except OSError: pass
    finally:
        for s in (src, dst):
            try: s.close()
            except OSError: pass
srv = socket.socket(); srv.setsockopt(socket.SOL_SOCKET, socket.SO_REUSEADDR, 1)
srv.bind(("127.0.0.1", LISTEN)); srv.listen()
while True:
    c, _ = srv.accept(); u = socket.create_connection(("127.0.0.1", TARGET))
    threading.Thread(target=pump, args=(c, u), daemon=True).start()
    threading.Thread(target=pump, args=(u, c), daemon=True).start()

The replica runs with --replicaof 127.0.0.1 6470 (the proxy). One write before the partition, one during it:

127.0.0.1:6460> SET order:1 paid
OK
127.0.0.1:6460> WAIT 1 1000
(integer) 1
                                   ← touch PARTITION
127.0.0.1:6460> SET order:2 paid
OK
127.0.0.1:6460> WAIT 1 500
(integer) 0
(0.54s)

The client got OK for order:2. Then the primary dies and the replica is promoted:

redis-cli -p 6460 SHUTDOWN NOSAVE
redis-cli -p 6461 REPLICAOF NO ONE
redis-cli -p 6461 MGET order:1 order:2

OK
paid

order:2 is gone: the second line of the MGET output is empty (nil). The write was acknowledged, then lost. That's what asynchronous replication means, and no setting removes the possibility entirely. WAIT told the client: it returned 0, meaning "no replica has this yet". An application that must not lose a write can check WAIT's answer and treat 0 as "not safely stored" (retry elsewhere, alert, or refuse to confirm the order). WAIT doesn't make Redis a consensus system. A replica that acknowledged can still fail too, and promotion doesn't pick the most up-to-date replica unless a tool like Sentinel or Cluster does (next lessons).

A first attempt at this demo froze the replicas with SIGSTOP instead of a proxy, and nothing was lost: the bytes were already in the replica's kernel socket buffer and were processed when it resumed. Real partitions drop packets, which is why the proxy discards them.

min-replicas-to-write N with min-replicas-max-lag S makes the primary refuse writes when fewer than N replicas are connected with a lag of at most S seconds. It limits how much an isolated primary can accept (and later lose), at the cost of availability.

docs.title: Reading from replicas
docs.text:
Replicas apply writes slightly after the primary. On this laptop, 10,000 write-then-immediately-read-from-replica cycles never saw a stale value:

read-your-write from replica: 0 of 10000 reads returned the previous value
with WAIT 1 before reading: 0 of 2000 stale

That's a loopback result: the replication stream (microseconds) always beat the client's next round trip. Across a real network, under load, or during a full resync, a replica will return stale data, so don't send reads that need your own latest write to a replica. Use replicas for reads that tolerate a little lag (analytics, listings), or WAIT first.

docs.title: How It Actually Works
docs.text:
A replica connects and sends PSYNC <replid> <offset>: "I have history replid up to offset". The primary has a replication ID and an offset (plus a previous ID, master_replid2, which lets replicas of a promoted replica continue partially). If the ID matches and the offset is still inside the backlog, it replies +CONTINUE and streams the gap. Otherwise it replies +FULLRESYNC <replid> <offset>, forks, and streams an RDB snapshot. Every write command the primary executes is appended to the backlog and sent to each replica's output buffer, in the same effect-based form as the AOF. Replicas acknowledge their offset every second (REPLCONF ACK), which is the lag and what WAIT counts.

When the replica connection's output buffer exceeds client-output-buffer-limit replica (256 MB hard, 64 MB for 60 s soft, Level 2 · 07 showed the defaults), the primary disconnects the replica, which then needs a backlog resync or, failing that, a full one. A replica that can't keep up can get stuck in a loop of full resyncs. Watch for repeated "Full resync" lines in the log.

Expiry is primary-driven: replicas don't delete expired keys themselves. They wait for the primary's DEL, but they hide logically expired keys from readers in the meantime.

docs.title: Common mistakes
docs.text:
• Assuming an acknowledged write is replicated. It isn't, until WAIT says so.
  • A 1 MB backlog on a busy primary. Every blip becomes a full resync.
  • Promoting a replica by hand without checking which replica has the highest offset.
  • Read-your-writes from replicas. It works on a laptop and fails in production.
  • Replicas without persistence behind a primary without persistence that restarts empty. The replicas sync to the empty dataset and wipe themselves. If the primary has no persistence, don't let it auto-restart.
  • Ignoring master_link_status:down on replicas you rely on.

docs.title: Exercise
docs.text:
1. Measure the time of a full resync for 1, 2 and 4 million keys, from the replica's "sync started" to "Finished with success" log lines. Compare disk-based (repl-diskless-sync no) and diskless.
  2. Find the smallest repl-backlog-size that lets a replica survive a 10-second partition while you write 1,000 SETs per second of 1 KB values.
  3. Using the proxy, show that min-replicas-to-write 1 with min-replicas-max-lag 5 makes the partitioned primary reject writes after about 5 seconds. What error do clients get?
  4. Put 50 ms of artificial latency in the proxy and rerun the read-your-write test. How many stale reads do you see now?

docs.title: 04 · High Availability with Sentinel
docs.text: Replication gives you a copy of the data. Sentinel turns that copy into automatic failover. A group of Sentinel processes watches the primary, agrees when it's down, promotes the best replica, reconfigures the other replicas, and tells clients where the new primary is. This lesson builds the standard layout (one primary, two replicas, three Sentinels) on one machine, kills the primary while a client writes, and reads the whole failover from the logs.

docs.title: The setup
docs.text:
Primary on 6480, replicas on 6481 and 6482 (--replicaof 127.0.0.1 6480), all with AOF on. Each of three Sentinels (26379, 26380, 26381) gets a config like this:

port 26379
daemonize yes
logfile /…/sentinel-26379.log
dir /…/l404
sentinel monitor shop 127.0.0.1 6480 2
sentinel down-after-milliseconds shop 2000
sentinel failover-timeout shop 10000
sentinel parallel-syncs shop 1

redis-sentinel sentinel-26379.conf      # same as: redis-server sentinel-26379.conf --sentinel
  • monitor shop 127.0.0.1 6480 2 names the group (shop), its current primary, and the quorum: how many Sentinels must agree the primary is unreachable before it's considered down.
  • down-after-milliseconds 2000 is how long a primary can be unresponsive before a Sentinel suspects it. The default is 30,000. 2 seconds keeps this demo fast. In production, choose it from your tolerance for false alarms against outage length.
  • You only list the primary. Sentinels discover the replicas from the primary and discover each other through a Pub/Sub channel on the monitored servers.

After a few seconds:

127.0.0.1:26379> SENTINEL get-master-addr-by-name shop
1) "127.0.0.1"
2) "6480"
master0:name=shop,status=ok,address=127.0.0.1:6480,slaves=2,sentinels=3
127.0.0.1:26379> SENTINEL ckquorum shop
OK 3 usable Sentinels. Quorum and failover authorization can be reached

ckquorum is worth running after every change: it checks that a failover could actually be authorized.

docs.title: Killing the primary under load
docs.text:
A client finds the primary through the Sentinels and increments a counter every 10 ms. Three seconds in, the primary gets SIGKILL:

import time, os, signal
import redis
from redis.sentinel import Sentinel
sentinel = Sentinel([("127.0.0.1", 26379), ("127.0.0.1", 26380), ("127.0.0.1", 26381)], socket_timeout=0.5)
master = sentinel.master_for("shop", socket_timeout=0.5, decode_responses=True,
                             retry=redis.retry.Retry(redis.backoff.NoBackoff(), 0))
print("client sees master at", sentinel.discover_master("shop"))
pid = redis.Redis(port=6480).info("server")["process_id"]
ok = err = 0; first_err = last_err = None; t0 = time.time()
killed_at = None
while time.time() - t0 < 25:
    if killed_at is None and time.time() - t0 > 3:
        os.kill(pid, signal.SIGKILL); killed_at = time.time(); print("killed primary (pid %d) at t=3.0s" % pid)
    try:
        master.incr("orders"); ok += 1
        if first_err and last_err and not hasattr(master, "_recovered"):
            master._recovered = time.time()
            print(f"writes succeeding again at t={time.time()-t0:.1f}s, master now {sentinel.discover_master('shop')}")
    except (redis.ConnectionError, redis.TimeoutError, redis.ReadOnlyError) as e:
        err += 1; last_err = type(e).__name__
        if first_err is None: first_err = time.time(); print(f"first error at t={first_err-t0:.1f}s: {last_err}")
    time.sleep(0.01)
print(f"ok={ok} errors={err}; write outage ~{master._recovered - first_err:.1f}s")

client sees master at ('127.0.0.1', 6480)
killed primary (pid 7309) at t=3.0s
first error at t=3.0s: ConnectionError
writes succeeding again at t=6.2s, master now ('127.0.0.1', 6482)
ok=1662 errors=225; write outage ~3.2s

Writes failed for 3.2 seconds, then resumed against the new primary, 6482, with no code change and no restart. master_for returns a client that asks the Sentinels for the current primary whenever it reconnects. Afterwards the new primary held orders = 1662, exactly the number of acknowledged increments, so nothing was lost this time (the client wrote slowly and replication kept up; Level 4 · 03 showed it isn't guaranteed).

docs.title: The failover, step by step
docs.text:
The Sentinel that led the failover logged every state change:

21:43:58.964 # +sdown master shop 127.0.0.1 6480
21:43:59.022 # +odown master shop 127.0.0.1 6480 #quorum 2/2
21:43:59.022 # +new-epoch 1
21:43:59.023 # +try-failover master shop 127.0.0.1 6480
21:43:59.032 # +vote-for-leader 1035f0f2c138b0a1e7514158c5df2fd804e39ae7 1
21:43:59.124 # +elected-leader master shop 127.0.0.1 6480
21:43:59.124 # +failover-state-select-slave master shop 127.0.0.1 6480
21:43:59.181 # +selected-slave slave 127.0.0.1:6482 127.0.0.1 6482 @ shop 127.0.0.1 6480
21:43:59.182 * +failover-state-send-slaveof-noone slave 127.0.0.1:6482 …
21:43:59.266 * +failover-state-wait-promotion slave 127.0.0.1:6482 …
21:44:00.045 # +promoted-slave slave 127.0.0.1:6482 …
21:44:00.045 # +failover-state-reconf-slaves master shop 127.0.0.1 6480
21:44:00.096 * +slave-reconf-sent slave 127.0.0.1:6481 …
21:44:01.050 * +slave-reconf-done slave 127.0.0.1:6481 …
21:44:01.115 # +failover-end master shop 127.0.0.1 6480
21:44:01.119 # +switch-master shop 127.0.0.1 6480 127.0.0.1 6482
  1. +sdown (subjectively down): this Sentinel hadn't heard from the primary for down-after-milliseconds, two seconds after the kill.
  2. +odown (objectively down): it asked the others, and the quorum (2) agreed.
  3. +new-epoch, +try-failover, +vote-for-leader, +elected-leader: only one Sentinel may run the failover. They hold an election for a new configuration epoch, and a candidate needs votes from a majority of all Sentinels (2 of 3), whatever the quorum setting.
  4. +selected-slave: the leader picks a replica. Unreachable or long-disconnected replicas are excluded, then it prefers lower replica-priority, then the highest replication offset (most data), then the lowest run ID.
  5. send-slaveof-noone → +promoted-slave: 6482 becomes a primary.
  6. reconf-slaves: 6481 is told to replicate from 6482 (parallel-syncs 1 means one at a time, so not all replicas resync at once).
  7. +switch-master: the new address is published to clients and recorded in every Sentinel's config.

About 2 seconds of the 3.2-second outage was detection (down-after-milliseconds). The rest was the election, promotion and the client noticing.

When the old primary came back, the Sentinels didn't let it resume as primary. They converted it into a replica of the new one:

role:slave
master_port:6482
master_link_status:up

Sentinels also rewrite their own config files to record what they've learned, so a restarted Sentinel remembers the current topology:

sentinel myid 18bfa71c3d54fee364fc1a827079dc5e48e19496
sentinel current-epoch 1
sentinel known-replica shop 127.0.0.1 6481
sentinel known-replica shop 127.0.0.1 6480
sentinel known-sentinel shop 127.0.0.1 26380 1035f0f2c138b0a1e7514158c5df2fd804e…

That means the config file must be writable, and you shouldn't manage it with a tool that overwrites it on every run.

docs.title: Deployment rules
docs.text:
• At least three Sentinels, on independent machines (or zones). Failover needs a majority, and with two Sentinels, losing one blocks every failover.
  • Don't put Sentinels only next to the primary. If that machine dies, they die with it.
  • Quorum ≤ majority. Quorum controls detection, the majority controls authorization.
  • Clients must be Sentinel-aware (master_for in redis-py, and equivalents in other libraries) or go through a proxy that is. A hard-coded primary address defeats the whole setup.
  • Sentinel doesn't prevent split-brain writes on an isolated old primary. Its clients may keep writing there until it's demoted, and those writes are lost. Combine with min-replicas-to-write (Level 4 · 03) to limit the window.
  • Test failover regularly with SENTINEL failover shop, which forces a graceful failover without killing anything.

Everything here ran on one machine, which is fine for learning and useless for availability.

docs.title: How It Actually Works
docs.text:
Each Sentinel sends PING to every monitored server once a second and INFO every few seconds (which is how replicas are discovered). It also publishes a hello message on the __sentinel__:hello channel of each server every 2 seconds, carrying its address, ID and current view of the configuration. That's how Sentinels find one another and converge on the latest configuration, identified by the highest epoch.

Subjective down is a local timeout. Objective down is gathered with SENTINEL is-master-down-by-addr requests to the other Sentinels. The same request, carrying a new epoch and the candidate's ID, doubles as a vote request. Each Sentinel votes at most once per epoch, so at most one leader can win a majority for a given epoch. That's a simplified Raft-style election, used only to pick who performs the failover. Once 6482 was promoted, the leader broadcast the new configuration with epoch 1, and any Sentinel holding an older configuration adopted it.

Promotion itself is REPLICAOF NO ONE plus CONFIG REWRITE on the chosen replica, then REPLICAOF <new primary> on the others. All are ordinary commands, which is why you need the Sentinels' commands to be allowed if you rename or restrict commands with ACLs.

docs.title: Common mistakes
docs.text:
• Two Sentinels, or three on the same host as the primary.
  • down-after-milliseconds too low on a network with hiccups. You get unnecessary failovers (each of which can lose data).
  • Clients connecting to a fixed address. After failover they write to a replica (READONLY errors) or to nothing.
  • Read-only config files for Sentinel. It needs to rewrite them.
  • Assuming no data loss. Failover is asynchronous replication plus a promotion.
  • Never testing. The first failover shouldn't be in production at 3 a.m.

docs.title: Exercise
docs.text:
1. Rerun the kill test with down-after-milliseconds at 1000, 5000 and 30000 (the default). Plot the write outage against the setting.
  2. Kill two of the three Sentinels, then the primary. What happens, and what do the remaining Sentinel's logs say?
  3. Set replica-priority 0 on 6481 and force a failover with SENTINEL failover shop. Which replica is chosen, and can 6481 ever become primary?
  4. Use the proxy from Level 4 · 03 to partition the old primary from the Sentinels but not from a client. Keep writing through that client during the failover and count how many of its writes are lost when the partition heals.

docs.title: 05 · Redis Cluster: Hash Slots, MOVED & ASK
docs.text: Sentinel gives one dataset high availability, but the data still has to fit on one primary, and all writes go to that one machine. Redis Cluster splits the keyspace across several primaries (sharding), each with its own replicas, and handles failover itself without Sentinel. This lesson builds a 6-node cluster (3 primaries, 3 replicas) and explores the rules it imposes on your keys and commands.

docs.title: Creating a cluster
docs.text:
Each node is an ordinary redis-server with cluster mode enabled:

for p in 7100 7101 7102 7103 7104 7105; do
  mkdir -p $p
  redis-server --port $p --dir ./$p --cluster-enabled yes --cluster-config-file nodes.conf \
               --cluster-node-timeout 3000 --appendonly yes --save '' --daemonize yes --logfile ./$p/log
done
redis-cli --cluster create 127.0.0.1:7100 127.0.0.1:7101 127.0.0.1:7102 \
          127.0.0.1:7103 127.0.0.1:7104 127.0.0.1:7105 --cluster-replicas 1 --cluster-yes

(Why 7100 and not the 7000 used in many tutorials? On this Mac, port 7000 is taken by the AirPlay receiver (ControlCenter), and the first attempt failed with [ERR] Node 127.0.0.1:7000 is not configured as a cluster node because the tool was talking to the wrong program. Check ports before blaming Redis.)

The tool assigns slots and pairs replicas with primaries:

M: 7ef3b99d239cba2f5e4a691f3af306ba0703f9ce 127.0.0.1:7100
   slots:[0-5460] (5461 slots) master
   1 additional replica(s)
M: 0e74daaaa2fb05870401488fe38be348fd9fb8b7 127.0.0.1:7101
   slots:[5461-10922] (5462 slots) master
   1 additional replica(s)
M: e705a36b7eaf6608762eb76fb9d7f982826082c1 127.0.0.1:7102
   slots:[10923-16383] (5461 slots) master
   1 additional replica(s)
S: 532f511ae592f611e6c6d6ce752f4e368be6015d 127.0.0.1:7103
   replicates 0e74daaaa2fb05870401488fe38be348fd9fb8b7
...
[OK] All nodes agree about slots configuration.
[OK] All 16384 slots covered.

cluster-config-file nodes.conf isn't for you to edit. Each node writes its view of the cluster there and reloads it on restart. cluster-node-timeout (3 s here) is how long a node can be unreachable before it's considered failing.

docs.title: Hash slots
docs.text:
The keyspace is divided into 16,384 slots. A key's slot is CRC16(key) mod 16384, and each slot belongs to exactly one primary:

127.0.0.1:7100> CLUSTER KEYSLOT user:1000
(integer) 1649
127.0.0.1:7100> CLUSTER KEYSLOT user:1001
(integer) 5712

Slot 1649 is on 7100 and slot 5712 is on 7101. Ask the wrong node and it tells you where to go:

127.0.0.1:7100> SET user:1000 ana
OK
127.0.0.1:7100> SET user:1001 ben
(error) MOVED 5712 127.0.0.1:7101

MOVED means "that slot lives on another node. Update your map and go there." A node never proxies the request for you. With -c, redis-cli follows redirects:

127.0.0.1:7100> SET user:1001 ben
-> Redirected to slot [5712] located at 127.0.0.1:7101
OK
127.0.0.1:7101> GET user:1000
-> Redirected to slot [1649] located at 127.0.0.1:7100
"ana"

docs.title: Multi-key operations and hash tags
docs.text:
A single command (or transaction, or script) can only touch keys in one slot, because one node has to execute it atomically:

127.0.0.1:7100> MSET user:1000 a user:1001 b
(error) CROSSSLOT Keys in request don't hash to the same slot

Hash tags control the slot. If a key contains {…}, only the part inside the first pair of braces is hashed:

127.0.0.1:7100> CLUSTER KEYSLOT {user:1000}:profile
(integer) 1649
127.0.0.1:7100> CLUSTER KEYSLOT {user:1000}:sessions
(integer) 1649
127.0.0.1:7100> MSET {user:1000}:profile a {user:1000}:sessions b
OK

This is why earlier lessons put tags in key names (lb:{arena}:…, rl:{client}:…, api:rl:{client}:…): every key a multi-key operation needs must share a tag. Design the tag around the unit of atomicity in your application (a user, a cart, a tenant, a game). Don't make it too coarse: a tag like {global} puts everything in one slot on one node and defeats sharding.

docs.title: The cluster-aware client
docs.text:
A cluster client keeps a map of slots to nodes, computes the slot of every key locally, and sends each command straight to the right node:

import time
from redis.cluster import RedisCluster, ClusterNode
rc = RedisCluster(startup_nodes=[ClusterNode("127.0.0.1", 7100)], decode_responses=True)
print("nodes known to the client:", sorted(n.name for n in rc.get_nodes()))
p = rc.pipeline()
for i in range(100_000): p.set(f"product:{i}", i)
t = time.perf_counter(); p.execute(); print(f"100,000 SETs via cluster pipeline: {time.perf_counter()-t:.2f}s")
for n in rc.get_primaries():
    print(n.name, "keys:", rc.dbsize(target_nodes=n))
print("MGET across slots:", rc.mget_nonatomic(["product:1", "product:2", "product:3"]))
try:
    rc.mget("product:1", "product:2")
except Exception as e:
    print("plain MGET across slots:", type(e).__name__, e)
try:
    with rc.pipeline(transaction=True) as t:
        t.incr("product:1"); t.incr("product:2"); t.execute()
except Exception as e:
    print("MULTI across slots:", type(e).__name__, str(e)[:90])
with rc.pipeline(transaction=True) as t:
    t.incr("{cart:9}:items"); t.expire("{cart:9}:items", 600); t.execute()
print("MULTI on one hash tag: ok, slot", rc.keyslot("{cart:9}:items"))

nodes known to the client: ['127.0.0.1:7100', '127.0.0.1:7101', '127.0.0.1:7102', '127.0.0.1:7103', '127.0.0.1:7104', '127.0.0.1:7105']
100,000 SETs via cluster pipeline: 0.91s
127.0.0.1:7100 keys: 33309
127.0.0.1:7101 keys: 33386
127.0.0.1:7102 keys: 33309
MGET across slots: ['1', '2', '3']
plain MGET across slots: RedisClusterException MGET - all keys must map to the same key slot
MULTI across slots: CrossSlotTransactionError All keys involved in a cluster transaction must map to the same slot
MULTI on one hash tag: ok, slot 1156
  • From one startup node the client discovered all six nodes (CLUSTER SLOTS/SHARDS).
  • The cluster pipeline split 100,000 commands by node and sent them in parallel, and keys spread evenly: about a third per primary. (The first node holds a few more keys from the earlier redis-cli examples.)
  • mget_nonatomic splits a cross-slot MGET into per-node requests and reassembles the results. As the name warns, the combined read isn't atomic.
  • Cross-slot MGET and transactions are rejected before anything is sent. With a hash tag, a transaction works.

docs.title: Other Cluster restrictions
docs.text:
• Only database 0. SELECT with any other number fails.
  • Lua scripts and Functions must declare their keys, and all of them must be in one slot (Level 2 · 09).
  • Pub/Sub: classic channels are broadcast to every node. Use sharded Pub/Sub (Level 2 · 07).
  • Big keys can't be split. A 10 GB sorted set lives entirely on one node and makes that node the bottleneck.
  • Keyspace-wide commands (SCAN, DBSIZE, FLUSHALL, KEYS) act on one node. Clients must run them per node.

docs.title: How It Actually Works
docs.text:
Every node keeps a full map of the cluster: node IDs, addresses, roles, which primary each replica follows, and the 16,384-slot ownership table, each claim tagged with a configuration epoch. Nodes talk to each other on a second port, the cluster bus (data port + 10,000, so 17100–17105 here), with a binary gossip protocol: every node pings a few others each second, and each message carries the sender's slot ownership and a sample of what it knows about other nodes. Conflicting claims to a slot are resolved by the higher config epoch, which is how a promoted replica's ownership wins over the old primary's.

When a command arrives, the node computes the key's slot (CRC16 of the key or its hash tag, modulo 16,384). If it owns the slot, it executes the command. If not, it replies MOVED <slot> <ip:port> according to its current map. Clients cache the slot map and refresh it on MOVED, so in steady state almost no redirects happen. There's no proxy layer and no central coordinator. ASK is a related, temporary redirect used while a slot is being moved between nodes. The next lesson triggers it.

Why 16,384 slots? Each node's heartbeat carries a bitmap of the slots it owns. 16,384 bits is 2 KB, small enough to gossip constantly, and still allows up to about 1,000 primaries with reasonable balance.

docs.title: Common mistakes
docs.text:
• No hash-tag design before moving to Cluster. Multi-key commands, transactions and scripts start failing with CROSSSLOT.
  • One tag for everything ({app}:…). Everything lands on one node.
  • Hot keys and big keys. Sharding spreads keys, not load within a key.
  • A non-cluster client against a cluster. Every redirect fails or gets followed slowly.
  • Forgetting the bus port in firewalls (data port + 10000). Nodes can't gossip, and the cluster never forms or splits.
  • Running KEYS/SCAN against one node and believing you saw the whole keyspace.

docs.title: Exercise
docs.text:
1. Compute CLUSTER KEYSLOT for {a}b, a{}b, {}a, {a}{b} and a{b. Work out the hash-tag rule from the results (empty braces and unmatched braces behave in specific ways).
  2. Store 100,000 users with keys user:<id>:profile and user:<id>:cart, then redesign the names so a script can update a user's profile and cart atomically. Measure how evenly the redesigned keys spread over the three primaries.
  3. Write a SCAN-over-the-whole-cluster helper with a cluster client, iterating each primary. Why primaries only?
  4. Block the cluster bus port of one primary with the proxy idea from Level 4 · 03 (or stop the node with SIGSTOP) and watch CLUSTER NODES on the others change its flags to fail? and then fail.

docs.title: 06 · Cluster Operations: Resharding, Scaling & Failover
docs.text: A cluster earns its keep when it changes shape without downtime: a new primary to absorb growth, slots moved off a hot node, a node replaced, a failover during maintenance. This lesson does each of those to the 6-node cluster from the previous lesson, holding 100,000 keys, while a client keeps reading and writing. Every operation is measured from the client's point of view: operations completed, errors, and the slowest single operation.

docs.title: Adding a primary and its replica
docs.text:
redis-server --port 7106 … --cluster-enabled yes …     # and 7107, configured the same way
redis-cli --cluster add-node 127.0.0.1:7106 127.0.0.1:7100
redis-cli --cluster add-node 127.0.0.1:7107 127.0.0.1:7100 --cluster-slave --cluster-master-id <id of 7106>

>>> Send CLUSTER MEET to node 127.0.0.1:7106 to make it join the cluster.
[OK] New node added correctly.

A new primary joins with zero slots. It holds no data and serves no keys until slots are moved to it.

docs.title: Moving a slot by hand: the ASK redirect
docs.text:
Moving one slot by hand shows the protocol that clients must handle. Slot 1649 (user:1000 and friends) moves from 7100 to the new node 7106. First, both sides are told what's happening:

redis-cli -p 7106 CLUSTER SETSLOT 1649 IMPORTING <id of 7100>
redis-cli -p 7100 CLUSTER SETSLOT 1649 MIGRATING <id of 7106>
redis-cli -p 7100 MIGRATE 127.0.0.1 7106 user:1000 0 5000      # move one key

Mid-migration, the slot's keys are split between the two nodes:

127.0.0.1:7100> GET user:1000
(error) ASK 1649 127.0.0.1:7106
127.0.0.1:7100> GET {user:1000}:profile
"a"
127.0.0.1:7106> GET user:1000
(error) MOVED 1649 127.0.0.1:7100
127.0.0.1:7106> ASKING
OK
127.0.0.1:7106> GET user:1000
"ana"
  • The source still serves keys it has ({user:1000}:profile). For a key it no longer has, it answers ASK: "try the other node, for this one request".
  • The target refuses with MOVED back to the source, because officially the slot isn't its yet, unless the request is preceded by ASKING, which grants a one-time exception.
  • ASK differs from MOVED in one crucial way: the client must not update its slot map, because the migration might not finish. Cluster clients implement exactly this dance.

The rest of the slot's keys then move with one MIGRATE … KEYS, and CLUSTER SETSLOT 1649 NODE <id> on the nodes makes the new owner official:

[OK] 100005 keys in 4 masters.
M: …7100   slots:[0-1648],[1650-5460] (5460 slots) master
M: …7106   slots:[1649] (1 slots) master

docs.title: Resharding under load
docs.text:
load.py increments random keys through a cluster client for a fixed time and reports errors and the slowest operation:

"""Background load: read/increment random product keys through a cluster client; report errors and latency."""
import random, sys, time, threading
import redis
from redis.cluster import RedisCluster, ClusterNode
seconds = float(sys.argv[1])
rc = RedisCluster(startup_nodes=[ClusterNode("127.0.0.1", 7100)], decode_responses=True)
ops = errs = 0; worst = 0.0; errtypes = {}
end = time.time() + seconds
while time.time() < end:
    k = f"product:{random.randrange(100_000)}"
    t = time.perf_counter()
    try:
        rc.incr(k); ops += 1
    except Exception as e:
        errs += 1; errtypes[type(e).__name__] = errtypes.get(type(e).__name__, 0) + 1
    worst = max(worst, time.perf_counter() - t)
print(f"load: {ops} ops, {errs} errors {errtypes}, worst op {worst*1000:.0f} ms")

With that running, move 1,000 slots from 7100 to 7106 with the standard tool:

redis-cli --cluster reshard 127.0.0.1:7100 --cluster-from <id 7100> --cluster-to <id 7106> \
          --cluster-slots 1000 --cluster-yes

Moving 1000 slots from 127.0.0.1:7100 to 127.0.0.1:7106
Waiting for migration task d15172652a86a6f971d40187ba0859f9ee83efed to complete.
classic reshard of 1000 slots: 1.0 s
load: 158917 ops, 0 errors {}, worst op 48 ms

That "migration task" line was a surprise. The redis-cli shipped with Redis 8.10 didn't move the slots key by key with MIGRATE. It started a server-side atomic slot migration, a feature added in Redis 8.4. The target node's log shows how it works:

* Import task d15172652a86a6f971d40187ba0859f9ee83efed started for slots: 0-999, source address: 127.0.0.1:7100
* RDB channel snapshot transfer completed for the import task.
* Starting to stream accumulated buffer for the import task (85 bytes)

The same mechanism can be driven directly from the target node:

redis-cli -p 7106 CLUSTER MIGRATION IMPORT 6000 6999
redis-cli -p 7106 CLUSTER MIGRATION STATUS ALL

id 9e9f5759da709d795d7567123ffdddcc709fbf59 slots 6000-6999 source 0e74daaa… dest 546a8e77… operation import
state completed last_error  retries 0 … start_time 1791908390282 end_time 1791908390303 write_pause_ms 0

* Import task 9e9f… started for slots: 6000-6999, source address: 127.0.0.1:7101
* RDB channel snapshot transfer completed for the import task.
* Successfully streamed accumulated buffer for the import task, applied offset: 86
* Import task 9e9f… is ready to takeover slots: 6000-6999
* Import task 9e9f… completed for slots: 6000-6999 (imported 6110 keys)
load: 76925 ops, 0 errors {}, worst op 67 ms

The 6,110 keys moved in 21 ms of task time (start_time to end_time), the reported write pause was 0 ms, and the client saw no errors. Instead of the key-by-key MIGRATE and ASK dance, the target receives a snapshot of the slots (like a replica's full sync, over an RDB channel), then the writes that happened meanwhile, then takes ownership in one step. No client ever sees the slot half-moved.

This is very new. Older redis-cli versions, older servers and other forks still use the classic MIGRATE-based method, during which clients get ASK redirects and multi-key operations on a migrating slot can fail with TRYAGAIN. Know which one your versions use before planning a big reshard. redis-cli --cluster rebalance uses the same machinery to even out slots across primaries, optionally weighted.

docs.title: Failover: killed vs graceful
docs.text:
Killing a primary (SIGKILL on 7101) under load:

kill: action at t=3.0s; ops=96211 errors=163 {'ConnectionError': 163}; errors spanned 4.3s

The replica's log:

S 21:50:32.551 * FAIL message received from 7ef3b99d… about 0e74daaa…
S 21:50:32.552 # Cluster state changed: fail
S 21:50:33.212 * Starting a failover election for epoch 8.
S 21:50:33.253 * configEpoch set to 8 after successful failover
M 21:50:33.254 * Cluster state changed: ok

Other nodes declared 7101 failed after cluster-node-timeout (3 s). Its replica 7103 waited a short, rank-based delay, asked the primaries for votes, won epoch 8 and took over the slots. Client errors spanned 4.3 s, and all 163 were ConnectionErrors from requests routed to the dead node. Requests for other slots kept succeeding. Note the Cluster state changed: fail line, though: with the default cluster-require-full-coverage yes, a node that sees uncovered slots refuses all queries with CLUSTERDOWN until coverage returns. Here that state lasted only about 0.7 s on the replica, and the client didn't record any CLUSTERDOWN errors. If a shard stays down (primary and replica both lost), it would stop the whole cluster. Setting the option to no keeps healthy slots available (Exercise 3).

A graceful failover for maintenance: run CLUSTER FAILOVER on the replica (7104, replica of 7102):

CLUSTER FAILOVER on 7104 -> b'OK'
manual: action at t=3.0s; ops=129708 errors=0 {}

S * All master replication stream processed, manual failover can start.
S * Starting a failover election for epoch 9.
S * configEpoch set to 9 after successful failover

Zero errors. A manual failover makes the primary pause clients, waits until the replica has processed the entire replication stream, and only then switches roles. No acknowledged write can be lost, which is unlike the kill. Always fail over gracefully before taking a primary down for patching.

The killed node, restarted, rejoined as a replica of the node that replaced it:

role:slave
master_port:7103

[OK] 100005 keys in 4 masters.
[OK] All nodes agree about slots configuration.
[OK] All 16384 slots covered.

docs.title: How It Actually Works
docs.text:
Failure detection is gossip-based. When a node hasn't answered pings for cluster-node-timeout, the observer flags it PFAIL (possibly failing) and mentions that in its gossip. When a primary collects PFAIL reports about a node from a majority of primaries, it marks the node FAIL and broadcasts a FAIL message. That's the line in the replica's log.

Replica promotion is an election among primaries. The failed primary's replicas wait a delay of about 500 ms + random + rank × 1000 ms, where replicas with more replicated data get a lower rank and go first. Then they request votes for a new config epoch. Each primary votes once per epoch, so a majority vote can elect only one replica. The winner takes the slots and announces them with the new epoch, which overrides the old claim everywhere. This is why a cluster needs at least three primaries: with two, losing one leaves no majority to elect a replacement.

A manual failover adds a handshake. The replica asks its primary to stop accepting writes and send its current offset. The replica waits until it has processed up to that offset, and then runs the election without the delay. Hence no lost writes.

Classic slot migration keeps the slot in MIGRATING/IMPORTING states while MIGRATE moves keys one batch at a time (each key is serialized, restored on the target with RESTORE, and deleted from the source, atomically per key). That's what produces ASK for keys that already moved. Atomic slot migration (8.4+) replaces this with a replication-like transfer of the whole slot range followed by an ownership switch, observed above as one 21 ms task.

docs.title: Common mistakes
docs.text:
• Fewer than three primaries. No majority means no automatic failover.
  • Replicas on the same host as their primary. One machine failure takes out both.
  • Killing primaries for maintenance instead of CLUSTER FAILOVER on the replica first.
  • cluster-require-full-coverage yes when partial availability would be acceptable.
  • Assuming every tool version reshards the same way. Classic migration produces ASK/TRYAGAIN, and atomic migration doesn't. Check before production.
  • Forgetting to rebalance after adding a primary. It sits empty.
  • Hand-editing nodes.conf. Let the cluster manage it.

docs.title: Exercise
docs.text:
1. Remove node 7106 from the cluster without losing data: move its slots away (reshard or CLUSTER MIGRATION), then redis-cli --cluster del-node. What happens if you try del-node while it still owns slots?
  2. Rerun the kill-failover test with cluster-node-timeout at 1000 and 15000 ms and compare the error span.
  3. Set cluster-require-full-coverage no on all nodes, kill a primary and its replica, and measure how many of the load script's operations still succeed.
  4. Using the manual SETSLOT … MIGRATING/IMPORTING method, migrate a slot containing a 2-million-element sorted set. What happens to latency on the source while that single MIGRATE runs? How does that compare with atomic migration?

docs.title: 07 · Security: ACLs, Protected Mode & TLS
docs.text: A default Redis server trusts anyone who can open a TCP connection to it, with full power to read every key, delete everything, rewrite its configuration and load modules. Redis servers exposed to the internet are routinely found and abused. This lesson closes the doors in layers: network exposure, authentication, per-user permissions and encryption in transit.

docs.title: Layer 1: who can connect at all
docs.text:
A server started with no configuration listens on all interfaces (bind * -::*), but protected mode is on. With no password set for the default user and no explicit bind, it accepts connections only from loopback. Connecting from the machine's LAN address (192.168.97.73) to a server on port 6490:

DENIED Redis is running in protected mode because protected mode is enabled and no password is set for the default
user. In this mode connections are only accepted from the loopback interface. If you want to connect from external
computers to Redis you may adopt one of the following solutions: 1) Just disable protected mode … 4) Set up an
authentication password for the default user. …

That's a safety net, not a security model. The moment you set a bind address or a password, protected mode steps aside and your configuration is all that stands between the server and the network. With --bind 127.0.0.1, the LAN address doesn't even accept the TCP connection:

Could not connect to Redis at 192.168.97.73:6490: setsockopt(TCP_NODELAY): Invalid argument

(That odd error text is how this build of redis-cli on macOS reports a refused connection.) In production: bind to private interfaces only, firewall the port (and the cluster bus port, +10000) to the hosts that need it, and never expose Redis to the internet, even with a password.

docs.title: Layer 2: users and permissions (ACLs)
docs.text:
Since Redis 6, authentication is per user, and each user has rules about which commands, keys and Pub/Sub channels it may use. A fresh server has one user:

127.0.0.1:6490> ACL LIST
1) "user default on nopass sanitize-payload ~* &* +@all"

nopass with +@all on ~* (all keys) and &* (all channels) means anyone can do anything. Create users per application, by the principle of least privilege:

127.0.0.1:6490> ACL SETUSER cache-app on >s3cret-cache-pw ~cache:* resetchannels -@all +@read +@write +@keyspace -@dangerous
OK
127.0.0.1:6490> ACL SETUSER reporter on >s3cret-report-pw ~* resetchannels -@all +@read -@slow +info|stats
OK
127.0.0.1:6490> ACL SETUSER admin on >s3cret-admin-pw ~* &* +@all
OK
127.0.0.1:6490> ACL SETUSER default off
OK

Reading the rules:

  • on / off enables or disables the user. >password adds a password, which is stored as a SHA-256 hash, as ACL LIST shows (#9a3039b1…).
  • ~cache:* limits keys to that pattern. resetchannels removes all Pub/Sub channel access.
  • -@all +@read +@write +@keyspace -@dangerous starts from nothing, then adds command categories, then removes the dangerous ones. ACL CAT lists the categories, and ACL CAT dangerous lists 60 commands on this version, including flushdb, keys, save, debug, module|load, client|kill, acl|setuser, replicaof and info.
  • +info|stats allows one subcommand argument (INFO stats) and nothing else from INFO.
  • Disabling default means unauthenticated clients can do nothing.

Before rolling rules out, check them without running anything with ACL DRYRUN:

127.0.0.1:6490> ACL DRYRUN cache-app SET cache:product:1 x
OK
127.0.0.1:6490> ACL DRYRUN cache-app SET session:1 x
"User cache-app has no permissions to access the 'session:1' key"
127.0.0.1:6490> ACL DRYRUN cache-app FLUSHALL
"User cache-app has no permissions to run the 'flushall' command"
127.0.0.1:6490> ACL DRYRUN reporter KEYS *
"User reporter has no permissions to run the 'keys' command"
127.0.0.1:6490> ACL DRYRUN reporter INFO stats
OK
127.0.0.1:6490> ACL DRYRUN reporter INFO server
"User reporter has no permissions to run the 'info' command"

Then as the application:

$ redis-cli -p 6490 GET x
NOAUTH Authentication required.

127.0.0.1:6490> AUTH cache-app wrong-password
(error) WRONGPASS invalid username-password pair or user is disabled.
127.0.0.1:6490> AUTH cache-app s3cret-cache-pw
OK
127.0.0.1:6490> ACL WHOAMI
(error) NOPERM User cache-app has no permissions to run the 'acl|whoami' command
127.0.0.1:6490> SET cache:product:1 widget
OK
127.0.0.1:6490> GET session:42
(error) NOPERM No permissions to access a key
127.0.0.1:6490> FLUSHALL
(error) NOPERM User cache-app has no permissions to run the 'flushall' command
127.0.0.1:6490> CONFIG SET maxmemory 1mb
(error) NOPERM User cache-app has no permissions to run the 'config|set' command

Note ACL WHOAMI being refused. It's in the @connection category, which -@all removed. Start-from-nothing rules need care: client libraries may run HELLO, CLIENT SETINFO, SELECT or PING when they connect. Add +@connection (or the specific commands) if your library fails to connect with a narrowly scoped user.

Every denial is recorded in ACL LOG (here read as admin), with the user, the command or key, and the client's address. It's the first place to look when an application breaks after an ACL change, and a good thing to alert on:

1)  1) "count"
    2) (integer) 1
    3) "reason"
    4) "command"
    5) "context"
    6) "toplevel"
    7) "object"
    8) "config|set"
    9) "username"
   10) "cache-app"
   ...
   14) "client-info"
       "id=6 addr=127.0.0.1:57076 … cmd=config|set user=cache-app …"

Persist users with an ACL file (aclfile /etc/redis/users.acl, then ACL SAVE/ACL LOAD) or user lines in redis.conf. Don't leave them only in memory, where a restart would lose them. Replicas, Sentinels and cluster nodes need users too: masteruser/masterauth for replication, sentinel auth-user/auth-pass for Sentinel.

The old approach of rename-command FLUSHALL "" still exists, but ACLs replace it: they're per user, visible and auditable.

docs.title: Layer 3: encryption in transit (TLS)
docs.text:
Passwords and data cross the network in clear text unless you enable TLS. The Homebrew build includes TLS support. First, a private CA and certificates for the server and one client:

openssl genrsa -out ca.key 2048
openssl req -x509 -new -nodes -key ca.key -sha256 -days 30 -subj "/CN=redis-lab-ca" \
  -addext "basicConstraints=critical,CA:TRUE" -addext "keyUsage=critical,keyCertSign,cRLSign" \
  -addext "subjectKeyIdentifier=hash" -out ca.crt

openssl genrsa -out redis.key 2048
openssl req -new -key redis.key -subj "/CN=localhost" -out redis.csr
printf "subjectAltName=DNS:localhost,IP:127.0.0.1\nauthorityKeyIdentifier=keyid,issuer\nbasicConstraints=CA:FALSE\nkeyUsage=digitalSignature,keyEncipherment\nextendedKeyUsage=serverAuth\n" > server.ext
openssl x509 -req -in redis.csr -CA ca.crt -CAkey ca.key -CAcreateserial -days 30 -sha256 -extfile server.ext -out redis.crt

openssl genrsa -out client.key 2048
openssl req -new -key client.key -subj "/CN=cache-app" -out client.csr
printf "authorityKeyIdentifier=keyid,issuer\nbasicConstraints=CA:FALSE\nkeyUsage=digitalSignature,keyEncipherment\nextendedKeyUsage=clientAuth\n" > client.ext
openssl x509 -req -in client.csr -CA ca.crt -CAkey ca.key -CAcreateserial -days 30 -sha256 -extfile client.ext -out client.crt

Those extension lines matter. The first version of these certificates was minimal, and redis-cli accepted it, but Python 3.14 rejected it twice:

[SSL: CERTIFICATE_VERIFY_FAILED] certificate verify failed: Missing Authority Key Identifier (_ssl.c:1082)
[SSL: CERTIFICATE_VERIFY_FAILED] certificate verify failed: CA cert does not include key usage extension (_ssl.c:1082)

Recent Python versions verify certificates in OpenSSL's strict X.509 mode by default, which requires extensions that many quick-start tutorials leave out. If one client connects and another doesn't, compare their TLS libraries' strictness before blaming the server.

Start a TLS-only server (--port 0 disables the plain-text port):

redis-server --port 0 --tls-port 6491 --tls-cert-file redis.crt --tls-key-file redis.key --tls-ca-cert-file ca.crt

* Ready to accept connections tls

$ redis-cli -p 6491 PING
Error: Connection reset by peer
$ redis-cli --tls --cacert ca.crt -p 6491 PING
Error: Server closed the connection
$ redis-cli --tls --cacert ca.crt --cert client.crt --key client.key -p 6491 PING
PONG

A plain-text client is refused. A TLS client without a client certificate is refused too, because tls-auth-clients defaults to yes (mutual TLS). Set it to optional or no if clients should authenticate with ACL passwords only. From Python:

r = redis.Redis(port=6491, ssl=True, ssl_ca_certs="ca.crt", ssl_certfile="client.crt", ssl_keyfile="client.key")
print("python over TLS:", r.ping())

python over TLS: True
no client cert: ConnectionError Error while reading from localhost:6491 : (1, '[SSL: TLSV13_ALERT_CERTIFICATE_REQUIRED] tlsv13 alert certifica…

TLS has a cost. redis-benchmark with 50 clients doing GET:

GET plain: 164203.61 req/s  TLS: 121654.50 req/s

That's about 26% less throughput on this laptop, from encryption and the TLS record layer on Redis's main thread. Long-lived pooled connections avoid repeating the handshake. Use TLS whenever traffic crosses a network you don't fully control, and budget for the cost. Replication and cluster bus traffic can be encrypted too (tls-replication yes, tls-cluster yes).

docs.title: How It Actually Works
docs.text:
On every command, Redis checks the connection's authenticated user. First, is the command (or the subcommand, or for rules like +info|stats, the first argument) allowed by the user's command bitmap? Then the command's key specifications (metadata saying which arguments are keys, and whether each is read or written) are checked against the user's key patterns. Patterns can be split as %R~ (read) and %W~ (write) for finer control. That's why ACLs need no per-command special cases, and why scripts and Functions must declare their keys (Level 2 · 09): the server checks KEYS before running them, and checks again on every redis.call.

Passwords are stored only as SHA-256 hashes, so ACL LIST doesn't reveal them. Denials go into a bounded in-memory log (acllog-max-len).

TLS is implemented with OpenSSL inside the connection layer. After the handshake, the same RESP bytes flow over an encrypted channel. tls-auth-clients yes makes the server request and verify a client certificate against tls-ca-cert-file during the handshake, before any command can be sent. By default the certificate's identity isn't mapped to an ACL user. This 8.10 build also has a tls-auth-clients-user setting (off by default) for authenticating clients as an ACL user derived from their certificate, but it wasn't tested for this lesson. Usually mTLS and ACL passwords are combined.

docs.title: Common mistakes
docs.text:
• Exposing Redis to the internet. Bind privately and firewall it, password or not.
  • Only setting requirepass. Every client then shares one all-powerful identity. Use ACL users per application.
  • Leaving default on with nopass after creating users.
  • +@all for applications. Grant categories and key patterns, and remove @dangerous.
  • Users only in memory. Use an ACL file and ACL SAVE.
  • Minimal certificates that one TLS stack accepts and another (Python 3.13+) rejects. Include proper extensions.
  • Plain-text replication across networks when client traffic is encrypted.
  • Ignoring ACL LOG. Denials are often the first sign of a misconfiguration or an intrusion attempt.

docs.title: Exercise
docs.text:
1. Create a queue-worker user that can only use streams under jobs:* (XREADGROUP, XACK, XAUTOCLAIM, XADD), and verify with ACL DRYRUN that it can't read cache:* keys or run FLUSHDB.
  2. Give reporter read-only access to cache:* via %R~cache:* and write access to reports:* only. Test both directions.
  3. Run a primary and replica where replication requires a dedicated replicator user. Which permissions does that user need? Use ACL LOG on the primary to find out by trial and error.
  4. Measure TLS overhead with redis-benchmark at 1, 10 and 100 clients and with pipelining (-P 16). When is the overhead smallest?

docs.title: 08 · Monitoring & Troubleshooting
docs.text: When an application team says "Redis is slow", Redis itself can usually tell you exactly why: which command, from which client, how long it took, how often it happens, and which key. This lesson plants four classic problems in an otherwise healthy workload, then finds each of them with Redis's built-in instruments, the way you would during an incident.

docs.title: Planting the problems
docs.text:
A scratch server (port 6495, allkeys-lfu, latency-monitor-threshold 50) gets 300,000 normal keys and one 400,000-field hash. After a burst of ordinary traffic, four mistakes are run:

import random, time, threading, redis
r = redis.Redis(port=6495, decode_responses=True)
r.execute_command("DEBUG", "POPULATE", "300000", "item", "200")
p = r.pipeline(transaction=False)
for i in range(400_000):
    p.hset("big:catalog", f"sku{i}", "x" * 50)
    if i % 20000 == 0: p.execute()
p.execute()
r.config_resetstat(); r.slowlog_reset(); r.execute_command("LATENCY", "RESET")
# normal traffic plus three bad habits
for i in range(20000):
    r.get(f"item:{random.randrange(300000)}")
    if i % 1000 == 0: r.get("hot:config")
for _ in range(500): r.get("hot:config")
r.hgetall("big:catalog")                             # 1. reading a huge hash in one go
r.keys("item:1*")                                    # 2. KEYS on 300k keys
r.eval("local n=0 for i=1,3000000 do n=n+i end return n", 0)   # 3. a CPU-heavy script
r.delete("big:catalog")                              # 4. synchronous delete of a big key
print("done")

docs.title: SLOWLOG: which commands were slow
docs.text:
The slow log records every command whose execution took longer than slowlog-log-slower-than microseconds (default 10,000, so 10 ms), keeping the last slowlog-max-len entries:

127.0.0.1:6495> SLOWLOG GET 5
1) 1) (integer) 4
   2) (integer) 1791908690
   3) (integer) 43839
   4) 1) "DEL"
      2) "big:catalog"
   5) "[::1]:57218"
   6) ""
   7) (integer) 2
2) 1) (integer) 3
   2) (integer) 1791908690
   3) (integer) 14929
   4) 1) "EVAL"
      2) "local n=0 for i=1,3000000 do n=n+i end return n"
      3) "0"
   5) "[::1]:57218"
   6) ""
   7) (integer) 3
3) 1) (integer) 2
   2) (integer) 1791908690
   3) (integer) 24196
   4) 1) "KEYS"
      2) "item:1*"
   ...
4) 1) (integer) 1
   2) (integer) 1791908690
   3) (integer) 40213
   4) 1) "HGETALL"
      2) "big:catalog"
   ...

All four planted problems, newest first. Each entry has an ID, a Unix timestamp, the duration in microseconds (the DEL blocked the server for 43.8 ms, HGETALL for 40.2 ms, KEYS for 24.2 ms, the script for 14.9 ms), the command and arguments, the client address and name, and, new in 8.10 per COMMAND DOCS, the original argument count. Name your connections (CLIENT SETNAME, or the client_name option in libraries) so the sixth field tells you which service sent the command.

What the slow log doesn't include is time spent waiting in the queue, network time or time writing the reply. A client can see 200 ms while the slow log shows nothing, if the server was busy with someone else's slow command. That is the head-of-line blocking from Level 1 · 01.

docs.title: LATENCY: when the server stalled
docs.text:
The latency monitor records events (command execution, fork, AOF fsync, expiry cycles, eviction) that exceed latency-monitor-threshold milliseconds, as a time series. At 50 ms nothing was recorded, since the worst command was 43.8 ms. With the threshold at 10 ms and the problems run again:

127.0.0.1:6495> LATENCY LATEST
1) 1) "command"
   2) (integer) 1791908706
   3) (integer) 48
   4) (integer) 48

The command event peaked at 48 ms. There's one sample per event type per second, holding the worst value, so all the slow commands that second collapsed into one point. LATENCY DOCTOR turns the history into advice:

1. command: 1 latency spikes (average 48ms, mean deviation 0ms, period 1.00 sec). Worst all time event 48ms.

I have a few advices for you:

- Check your Slow Log to understand what are the commands you are running which are too slow to execute. …
- Deleting, expiring or evicting (because of maxmemory policy) large objects is a blocking operation. If you have very
  large objects that are often deleted, expired, or evicted, try to fragment those objects into multiple smaller objects.

Where the slow log tells you which commands, the latency monitor also covers stalls no command is responsible for: fork (Level 4 · 01), aof-fsync-always, expire-cycle, eviction-del. Turn it on in production with a threshold a little above your normal p99. It's cheap.

docs.title: commandstats and latency percentiles: the aggregate view
docs.text:
INFO commandstats accumulates calls and time per command since the last CONFIG RESETSTAT:

cmdstat_hgetall:calls=2,usec=76755,usec_per_call=38377.50,rejected_calls=0,failed_calls=0,slowlog_count=2,slowlog_time_ms_sum=76.75,slowlog_time_ms_max=40.21
cmdstat_del:calls=2,usec=92676,usec_per_call=46338.00,rejected_calls=0,failed_calls=0,slowlog_count=2,slowlog_time_ms_sum=92.68,slowlog_time_ms_max=48.84
cmdstat_keys:calls=2,usec=47579,usec_per_call=23789.50,rejected_calls=0,failed_calls=0,slowlog_count=2,slowlog_time_ms_sum=47.58,slowlog_time_ms_max=24.20
cmdstat_eval:calls=1,usec=14929,usec_per_call=14929.00,rejected_calls=0,failed_calls=0,slowlog_count=1,slowlog_time_ms_sum=14.93,slowlog_time_ms_max=14.93
cmdstat_get:calls=20520,usec=30521,usec_per_call=1.49,rejected_calls=0,failed_calls=0
cmdstat_hset:calls=400000,usec=155547,usec_per_call=0.39,rejected_calls=0,failed_calls=0

This is the most useful single view for "where does Redis spend its time?". The 20,520 GETs together cost 30 ms. The two DELs cost 93 ms. Sort by usec, not by calls. On this version the slow-log counters are included per command, so you can graph "slow calls of command X" directly. rejected_calls (refused before running: ACL, OOM, wrong arity) and failed_calls (errored while running) are worth alerting on.

INFO latencystats gives per-command percentiles:

latency_percentiles_usec_get:p50=1.003,p99=8.031,p99.9=15.039
latency_percentiles_usec_hgetall:p50=36700.159,p99=40370.175,p99.9=40370.175
latency_percentiles_usec_keys:p50=23461.887,p99=24248.319,p99.9=24248.319

A GET's p99 of 8 µs says the server isn't the problem for normal reads. Anything slower that the clients see is queueing behind the big commands, or the network.

docs.title: Finding the keys
docs.text:
$ redis-cli -p 6495 --hotkeys
[00.00%] Hot key "item:185595" found so far with counter 5
...
$ redis-cli -p 6495 --memkeys
Biggest string found "item:185595" has 254 bytes

--hotkeys reads each key's LFU counter, so it needs an LFU eviction policy, which is why this server uses allkeys-lfu. It found no key standing out (counters of 4–5 are random traffic), and the reason is instructive: hot:config was requested 520 times but never existed, so it has no LFU counter. Such requests show up only in keyspace_misses:

keyspace_hits:620002
keyspace_misses:520

A hot missing key is a classic bug: a cache that's never populated, or a typo in a key name. Neither --hotkeys nor --bigkeys will find it. MONITOR (briefly) or client-side logging will. --memkeys and --bigkeys find big keys like big:catalog before they cause trouble.

docs.title: What to watch continuously
docs.text:
Metric (INFO) Why used_memory vs maxmemory, mem_fragmentation_ratio headroom, swapping (ratio < 1 on Linux), fragmentation evicted_keys, expired_keys eviction means the cache is too small, or wrongly configured keyspace_hits / keyspace_misses cache effectiveness, and missing hot keys instantaneous_ops_per_sec, cmdstat_* usec load and where time goes connected_clients, blocked_clients, rejected_connections connection leaks, maxclients (10,000 here) client_recent_max_output_buffer slow consumers, big replies rdb_last_bgsave_status, aof_last_write_status, latest_fork_usec persistence health and fork cost master_link_status, replica offsets, repl_backlog_* replication health and lag slowlog_count per command, LATENCY LATEST stalls

Exporters for Prometheus and similar systems scrape these fields. Whatever you use, alert on trends and thresholds, not just "is it up?".

docs.title: A troubleshooting checklist
docs.text:
1. Is the server slow, or the client waiting? Compare client-side latency with latencystats. If the server's p99 is microseconds, look at queueing (slow log), the network, or the client (pool exhaustion, Level 1 · 09).
  2. Slow log for O(N) commands on big keys, KEYS, long scripts and big deletes.
  3. Latency monitor for forks, fsyncs and expiry or eviction stalls.
  4. Memory: near maxmemory? Evicting? Swapping (mem_fragmentation_ratio < 1 on Linux)?
  5. Clients: CLIENT LIST sorted by omem (output buffers) or idle. One subscriber or MONITOR can be the culprit.
  6. Persistence: a fork every few seconds on a big instance? AOF appendfsync always on slow disks?
  7. The host: CPU steal on VMs, transparent huge pages, swap. Redis can't see these directly, but redis-cli --intrinsic-latency 30 on the server host measures how much latency the machine itself adds.

docs.title: How It Actually Works
docs.text:
Every command runs inside a wrapper that takes a monotonic timestamp before and after execution. The difference feeds commandstats (sums), a per-command HDR histogram (latencystats, with percentiles chosen by latency-tracking-info-percentiles), the slow log (if above the threshold) and the latency monitor's command event (if above its threshold). That's why all four views agreed on 40–48 ms for the planted commands: they're the same measurement aggregated differently. Other latency events (fork, fsync, expire cycle) are timed around those operations in the same way.

The slow log is a fixed-length in-memory list. Arguments are truncated (32 arguments, 128 bytes each), so it's safe to leave on, but entries scroll away quickly on busy servers, so ship them to your log system. The LFU counter that --hotkeys reads is the 8-bit logarithmic counter from Level 3 · 02, exposed by OBJECT FREQ, which --hotkeys calls for each key while scanning.

docs.title: Common mistakes
docs.text:
• Raising slowlog-log-slower-than until the log is quiet. Keep it at 10 ms or lower and investigate.
  • Reading only the slow log when the issue is forks, fsyncs or eviction. Use the latency monitor too.
  • Sorting command stats by calls. Time (usec) is what blocks the server.
  • Unnamed client connections. Incidents take longer when you can't tell which service sent KEYS *.
  • Leaving MONITOR running, which is itself a performance problem (Level 1 · 02).
  • Monitoring only availability. Memory, evictions, replication and persistence fail silently.

docs.title: Exercise
docs.text:
1. Set slowlog-log-slower-than 0 for 10 seconds on a busy lab server (it logs everything), then summarize which commands and clients dominate. Set it back afterwards.
  2. Reproduce a fork latency event: populate 2 GB and run BGSAVE with latency-monitor-threshold 10. What does LATENCY DOCTOR advise?
  3. Write a small exporter that prints, every 5 seconds, the hit ratio, ops/s, used memory, evicted keys and the top 3 commands by usec (deltas, not totals).
  4. Plant a hot missing key in an application and find it two ways: with keyspace_misses trends and with a 2-second MONITOR capture piped through sort | uniq -c | sort -rn | head.

docs.title: 09 · Versions, Licensing, Valkey & Upgrades
docs.text:
"Which Redis?" used to have one answer. Since 2024 there are two major lineages with the same heritage: Redis itself and Valkey, a fork. Managed services may run either, or something compatible. This lesson covers what the licenses say (from the license files that ship with the software), compares Redis 8.10.2 and Valkey 9.1.2 on the same machine, finds where they're no longer interchangeable, and ends with how to upgrade safely.

Not legal advice

The summary below is a reading of the license files included with the installed software. Whether a license fits your use (particularly if you offer Redis as a service to others) is a question for your legal team, using the current license texts.

docs.title: What the license files say
docs.text:
The Homebrew Redis 8.10.2 package ships LICENSE.txt, which begins:

Starting with Redis 8, Redis Open Source is moving to a tri-licensing model with all new Redis code
contributions governed by the updated Redis Software Grant and Contributor License Agreement.
After this release, contributions are subject to your choice of: (a) the Redis Source Available License v2
(RSALv2);or (b) the Server Side Public License v1 (SSPLv1); or (c) the GNU Affero General Public License v3 (AGPLv3).
Redis Open Source 7.2 and prior releases remain subject to the BSDv3 clause license as referenced
in the REDISCONTRIBUTIONS.txt file.

In outline, the history is:

  • Up to 7.2: BSD 3-Clause, a permissive open-source license.
  • 7.4 (2024): dual-licensed under RSALv2 and SSPLv1, both source-available licenses that restrict offering Redis as a competing managed service. Neither is OSI-approved open source.
  • 8.0 and later (2025): a third option, AGPLv3, was added, which is an OSI-approved open-source license with network-copyleft obligations.

The Valkey 9.1.2 package ships COPYING:

SPDX-License-Identifier: BSD-3-Clause

BSD 3-Clause License

Copyright (c) 2024-present, Valkey contributors

Valkey was forked from Redis 7.2.4 in 2024 (under the Linux Foundation) when Redis moved away from BSD, and it remains BSD-licensed. That heritage is visible in its INFO:

redis_version:7.2.4
server_name:valkey
valkey_version:9.1.2

Valkey reports redis_version:7.2.4 so that clients and tools that check the version keep working. valkey_version is the real one. Redis 8.10.2 reports redis_version:8.10.2.

docs.title: Same commands, different defaults
docs.text:
The core of both is the same: data types, RESP, persistence, replication, Cluster. Every Level 1 lesson works on either. The differences are in defaults and in what each project has added since 2024. Running the same CONFIG GETs against both servers:

                        Redis 8.10.2   Valkey 9.1.2
lazyfree-lazy-user-del       no            yes
lazyfree-lazy-expire         no            yes
lazyfree-lazy-eviction       no            yes
lazyfree-lazy-user-flush     no            yes
hash-max-listpack-entries    512           512
io-threads                   1             1
maxmemory-policy             noeviction    noeviction

The lazy-free defaults differ. On Valkey a plain DEL of a huge key is already non-blocking. On this Redis build it blocked for 281 ms (Level 1 · 04) unless you use UNLINK or change the setting. Code that's fine on one can stall the other.

Command availability, checked with COMMAND INFO on each server:

DELEX        redis:delex      valkey:(none)
DIGEST       redis:digest     valkey:(none)
HSETEX       redis:hsetex     valkey:hsetex
HGETEX       redis:hgetex     valkey:hgetex
HEXPIRE      redis:hexpire    valkey:hexpire
XACKDEL      redis:xackdel    valkey:(none)
XNACK        redis:xnack      valkey:(none)
VADD         redis:VADD       valkey:(none)
FT.SEARCH    redis:FT.SEARCH  valkey:(none)
JSON.SET     redis:json.set   valkey:(none)
BF.ADD       redis:bf.add     valkey:(none)
COMMANDLOG   redis:(none)     valkey:commandlog
  • Hash field expiry exists on both, and HSETEX … EX 60 FIELDS 1 f v worked identically.
  • SET … IFEQ worked on both. Redis's DELEX and DIGEST don't exist on Valkey.
  • Redis's stream additions (XACKDEL, XNACK, and XADD … IDMP) don't exist on Valkey. XADD s IDMP p1 i1 * a 1 failed there with ERR Invalid stream ID specified as stream command argument, because Valkey parsed IDMP as an ID.
  • Vector sets are built into Redis 8. The JSON, search and probabilistic commands are modules in both worlds. Redis ships its own. Valkey has separate modules of its own (for JSON, Bloom filters and search), which weren't installed or tested here, so their compatibility isn't assessed.
  • Valkey has commands Redis doesn't, such as COMMANDLOG (a generalization of the slow log).

The BITCOUNT discrepancy from Level 2 · 02 is a reminder that implementations also differ in bugs: Valkey counted correctly where this Redis build didn't.

docs.title: The file formats have diverged
docs.text:
Both servers wrote an RDB snapshot of the same small dataset. The headers differ:

REDIS0015
VALKEY080

Valkey 9.1.2 loading Redis 8.10.2's file:

# Can't handle RDB format version 15
# Fatal error loading the DB, check server logs. Exiting.

Redis 8.10.2 loading Valkey 9.1.2's file:

# Wrong signature trying to load DB from file
# Fatal error loading the DB, check server logs. Exiting.

Neither can read the other's snapshots. The same goes for the other binary paths. A Valkey replica of a Redis 8.10 primary failed to sync:

# Failed to load RDB
* Reconnecting to PRIMARY 127.0.0.1:6500 after failure

and DUMP payloads from Redis were rejected by RESTORE on Valkey:

RESTORE profile:1 into Valkey: DUMP payload version or checksum are wrong

What did work was a logical copy: reading values with ordinary commands on one server and writing them with ordinary commands on the other:

logical copy: {b'name': b'Ana', b'plan': b'pro'}

So moving between the two lineages, in either direction, at these versions, means a logical migration: dual writes from the application, or a copy tool that SCANs and re-writes keys type by type (with TTLs), followed by a cut-over. That's not a file copy or a replica promotion. Plan for it before choosing, and re-test with the versions you actually run, since compatibility can change from release to release. (Moving from Redis ≤ 7.2 to Valkey was designed to be a drop-in, because Valkey started from 7.2.4. That wasn't tested here.)

docs.title: Upgrading within one lineage
docs.text:
Within Redis (or within Valkey), the documented rule is that newer versions load older RDB files and accept replication from older primaries, not the other way round. (This course only had one version of each installed, so that direction wasn't tested here.) That makes the standard zero-downtime upgrade:

  1. Read the release notes for every version you're skipping: changed defaults, deprecated commands, new reserved behaviour. The COMMAND DOCS history fields seen in this course (8.4.0 Added 'IFEQ'…) come from those changes.
  2. Upgrade replicas first. Stop a replica, install the new version, start it, and let it resync from the old primary.
  3. Fail over to an upgraded replica: gracefully with SENTINEL failover or CLUSTER FAILOVER (Level 4 · 06 measured zero client errors for the latter).
  4. Upgrade the old primary, now a replica, last.
  5. Don't use new features until every node is upgraded. A new command written to the new primary would fail to replicate to an old replica, and an RDB written by the new version can't be loaded by the old one, which removes your rollback path. Keep the old version's snapshot until you're sure.

Test the whole procedure, including rollback, on a staging copy with production-like data and traffic.

docs.title: How It Actually Works
docs.text:
An RDB file starts with a magic string and a format version (REDIS0015). Each release can add new encodings (new types, new listpack layouts, field TTL metadata, stream extensions), and the loader rejects files whose version it doesn't know rather than misreading them. Valkey changed the magic string itself (VALKEY080), so a Redis loader stops at the first bytes ("Wrong signature"). Replication full syncs and DUMP payloads use the same serialization with a version and checksum trailer, which is why all three paths failed the same way, while ordinary commands (whose wire format, RESP, both still speak) succeeded.

Because the RESP protocol and core command semantics are shared, client libraries mostly work against both. Library features that depend on server-specific commands (Redis's client-side cache helpers, search and JSON helpers, newer stream commands) work only where the server has them.

docs.title: Common mistakes
docs.text:
• Assuming "Redis-compatible" means file-compatible. Snapshots, replication and DUMP didn't cross between these versions.
  • Relying on defaults that differ (lazy freeing here). Set important options explicitly in your config.
  • Using new commands in libraries or scripts before every node and environment supports them.
  • Upgrading the primary first, or without a tested rollback.
  • Choosing a license by headline. Read the actual license texts for the versions you deploy, and involve legal counsel for service offerings.
  • Pinning to "latest" in containers. Pin exact versions and upgrade deliberately.

docs.title: Exercise
docs.text:
1. Write a logical migration tool that copies every key from one server to another using SCAN, TYPE, PTTL and type-specific reads and writes (string, hash, list, set, zset, stream). Verify it by comparing DBSIZE and a sample of values, and run it from Redis 8.10 to Valkey 9.1.
  2. Compare CONFIG GET * on both servers and list every parameter whose default differs. Which differences could change application behaviour?
  3. Run the Level 1–3 project test suites (URL shortener, leaderboard, API guard) against Valkey. Which tests fail, and why?
  4. Draft an upgrade runbook for a 3-shard Cluster with one replica per shard, including the exact CLUSTER FAILOVER steps, health checks between steps, and how you'd roll back after step 3.

docs.title: 10 · Capstone — A Secured, Persistent, Failover-Tested Cluster
docs.text:
The capstone puts Level 4 together into one deployment and, more importantly, into an automated acceptance test that proves the deployment does what it claims. The test checks the topology, the security rules, the persistence settings, a kill -9 of a primary under write load (with an exact accounting of which writes survived), the dead node coming back, and a full restart of every node.

Everything runs on one machine on ports 7200–7205. That proves the configuration and the procedures, not availability: a real deployment puts each primary and its replica on different hosts or zones.

docs.title: The design
docs.text: Concern Choice From Scale-out 3 primaries × 1 replica, Redis Cluster Level 4 · 05–06 Partial availability cluster-require-full-coverage no Level 4 · 06 Durability AOF everysec + RDB save 300 100 Level 4 · 01–02 Data-store memory policy maxmemory 256mb, noeviction Level 3 · 02 Large-key safety lazyfree-lazy-user-del yes, lazyfree-lazy-expire yes Level 1 · 04 Limit writes that can be lost min-replicas-to-write 1, min-replicas-max-lag 10 Level 4 · 03 Confirmed durability per write application calls WAIT 1 and checks the answer Level 4 · 03 Access control default off; admin, replicator and app users in an ACL file Level 4 · 07 Network bind 127.0.0.1 (a private interface in real life) Level 4 · 07 Observability latency-monitor-threshold 25 Level 4 · 08

docs.title: The users
docs.text:
users.acl:

user default off
user admin on >admin-Pa55-change-me ~* &* +@all
user replicator on >repl-Pa55-change-me +psync +replconf +ping
user orders-app on >app-Pa55-change-me ~{order}:* ~order:* resetchannels -@all +@read +@write +@string +@hash +@stream +@connection +wait +cluster|slots +cluster|shards +cluster|nodes -@dangerous
  • default off: no anonymous access.
  • replicator can only do what replication needs (PSYNC, REPLCONF, PING). Every node uses it as masteruser, so replicas authenticate to their primaries, including after a failover changes who is primary.
  • orders-app is limited to order:* keys (and the {order} hash tag), to string, hash and stream commands, to WAIT, and to the cluster-topology commands a cluster client needs to discover nodes. @dangerous is removed.

The passwords are lab examples. In production they come from a secret store, and the ACL file is readable only by the Redis user.

docs.title: The node configuration
docs.text:
node.conf.tpl (rendered per node by up.sh):

port PORT
bind 127.0.0.1
